article_text: RIPLEY, W.Va. - The Jackson County Chamber of Commerce focused on the future of local industry and infrastructure during its monthly meeting at the Cedar Lakes Conference Center on March 10. Chamber President Cinda Francis opened the meeting by sharing updates on upcoming civic events and ongoing professional development programs. "The Chamber is proud to co-sponsor the first Meet the Candidates Night with WMOV," Francis said. "This will be at Cedar Lakes at 6 pm on April 14. With so many candidates, this will be a very good opportunity for voters to have personal conversations." Francis also noted that the Jackson County Leadership program remains active. Participants recently traveled to the State Capitol to meet with legislative leaders and observe the West Virginia government in action. Some members also attended the March 3 Ripley City Council meeting. "Both were valuable experiences," Francis said. The meeting's featured speaker, Veronica Lewis, director of the Jackson County Development Authority (JCDA), provided insights into the region's business support strategies. "What does economic development mean?" Lewis asked. "It is such a broad term." Lewis outlined seven core pillars that define the JCDA's approach to economic development: Retention and Expansion: Identifying existing businesses and determining how to help them grow. Workforce Development: Focus on skills training and labor availability. Industrial and Site Development: Preparing physical locations for business use. Infrastructure Improvement: Enhancing the fundamental systems of the county. Quality of Life: Focusing on community development to attract residents. Marketing: Strategic promotion of the region. Small Business Support: Providing resources for local entrepreneurs. Lewis emphasized that site readiness is the most critical factor for sustained growth. "We have a lot of flat land, but are we competitive?" Lewis said. "Water and sewer, two of my favorite subjects, are vital. If we don't have those in place, there will be no development." To address these needs, Lewis has initiated quarterly meetings with the county's public service districts (PSDs) and municipalities since taking the lead at the JCDA. "I want to know what their expansion plans, financing, and strategies are," Lewis said. "It's critically important that we take care of our PSDs." Beyond industrial infrastructure, Lewis expressed a commitment to the county's entrepreneurial community. "These are a passion of mine," Lewis said. "Small businesses, or those with an idea, I want to know if you need help, what your growth plans are, and where you need me. I have access to resources." The JCDA will host a small business development event on March 25, featuring a business coach available for one-on-one, 30-minute consultations. The coach will analyze individual business needs and offer follow-up assistance at no cost. The event is organized by Lauren Kelley, Lewis's assistant at the JCDA. "I could not do this job without Lauren," Lewis said. "She keeps things moving and me organized. She is a lifesaver." Lewis concluded her presentation by highlighting several major investments currently shaping Jackson County, including: Constellium's $150 million investment (including a $75 million Department of Energy match) for two new SmartMelt furnaces. The upcoming cancer center at Jackson General Hospital. The development of the Donohew luxury apartment complex. The progress of TIMET, which is slated to begin operations by the end of 2026. Charleston Area Medical Center's (CAMC) purchase of land for future development. When asked to identify the county's primary strengths and hurdles, Lewis pointed to the local community as the deciding factor for outside investors. "Our people are our greatest asset," Lewis said. "If I can get prospective businesses here, they fall in love with the people. Our biggest weakness is the water and sewer in some parts of the county. And generational land that is not able to be developed yet is somewhat of a frustration." For more information regarding JCDA programs or assistance, contact 304-372-1151 or visit www.jcda.org. The Jackson County Chamber of Commerce meets monthly; details are available at www.jacksonchamberwv.org. SANDYVILLE, W.Va. - Motorsports was not something Diana Casto thought much about while growing up on a farm in Ripley, but her perspective eventually shifted. Casto, a 1995 graduate of Ripley High School, admits she originally knew nothing about race cars. "If it had a manual transmission and a clutch, it was a tractor or a truck," Casto said. "I was a typical small-town kid who didn't get out much." During high school, her time was occupied as a member of the Future Farmers of America and a player on the softball team. It wasn't until years later, when she met her second husband, Dana Casto - a substitute school bus driver for Jackson County - that she was introduced to racing. Casto, who has now driven a school bus herself for 10 years, has developed a deep passion for the sport. "Meeting Dana, I grew out of that farm phase," she said. "He was into race cars and motorsports, so I guess you could say I went from one type of horsepower to another." Casto competes in 10 races per season with the North Carolina-based Southeast Gassers Association (SEGA). She has been involved with the organization for five years. "A gasser is the way the car sits, down in the back end and raised in the front end," she said. "It's a vehicle that runs on gas, not alcohol or anything like that." The couple first connected with SEGA through a Facebook group. "Dana had contacted them and asked why they didn't have an automatic class," Casto said. "Just an innocent question, and that started a conversation." The Castos now race across the Eastern United States, including North Carolina, South Carolina, Mississippi, Georgia, Tennessee, Kentucky, and Ohio. Casto noted that when she first began racing, she used a 306 sbf engine in her 1964 Ford Falcon. "That was pretty much just a beefed-up street motor, that was my training wheel," she said with a laugh. "My first passes were not pretty, but by the middle of my second season, I had the car running bracket numbers, so we decided it was time for an upgrade. I am now running a 314 sbf." While she frequently competes against men, Casto believes it is vital for more women to enter the driver's seat. "I welcome and encourage all girls and women alike to come see us race, come sit in my car, because you can be anything you want to be," she said. "Don't ever let anyone tell you that you can't do something just because you are a girl." Casto is set to begin her sixth season racing her "Quick Draw" Falcon on April 11 at Shadyside Dragway in Shelby, North Carolina. "I have placed in the top 10 every year for the past five years," she said. "I am so ready and excited to get started on my sixth year of this sport." To offset the expenses associated with the sport, the Castos have partnered with Shandy Broom of Swiftees in Ripley to raise funds. "Shandy has helped us open an online store for SEGA Quick Draw merchandise," Casto said. "We have shirts, hats and so much more for our fans to purchase." Supporters can view merchandise at https://swiftees.printavo.com/merch/quick-draw-racing-2026. The Castos are always looking for ways to improve and are seeking sponsors to assist with the upcoming season. Updates are available on their Facebook pages, "Dana And Diana Casto" and the build page "SEGA Quick Draw 64 Falcon." RAVENSWOOD, W.Va. - After 30 years of service to her community, Teresa Thacker is saying goodbye to the insurance industry and hello to retirement. What began as a job eventually turned into what Thacker describes as a "lifelong calling." Her career path started unexpectedly while working at a photography studio in Gallipolis, Ohio. "There was a State Farm office right next door," Thacker said. "I would see the ladies go out and inspect cars. I have always had a passion for cars, so I thought it looked interesting. I decided it was something I might want to check out." A few years later, Terry Pyles opened his State Farm agency in Point Pleasant. "I had insurance with State Farm and the girls at the office said I would be really good at it, so I applied and the rest is history," Thacker said. About five years into the job, she left Pyles's office to join Allstate. "Allstate approached me about opening up my own agency in Jackson County, so I did," she said. After some time with Allstate, Steve Tygrett of Erie Insurance approached her about opening an Erie location in Ravenswood. "I left Allstate and opened Erie in Ravenswood in January of 2003," Thacker said. "We expanded to the town of Mason in Mason County with Hometown Insurance. Then when Steve was ready to retire, we sold that location to get two offices in one county." The Ripley branch followed, opening in October 2014. Throughout the decades, Thacker found the most meaning in the personal connections she made with her clients. "Helping people with their ups and downs of life has been my favorite part of the job," she said. "Rate increases were my least favorite." Thacker credited her staff as a primary pillar of her success. "I have always had the greatest staff," she said. "They care as much for our clients as I do. Insurance is about more than policies; it's about taking care of your neighbors and friends." For those considering a career in the industry, Thacker offered a simple piece of advice. "Always do the right thing by the customer," she said. As she steps away, Thacker expressed confidence in the future of the agency and its clients. "David Swor will be stepping into the role of serving our valued clients moving forward," she said. "He brings over 20 years of Erie Insurance experience, integrity and a genuine care for others that I know this community deserves. I have every confidence that they will be in excellent hands, and I am grateful knowing the agency will continue with the same commitment and personal service." Thacker said she believes a higher power played a role in the transition, noting that David is the "perfect" person to carry on the legacy of service to the community. One thing that Thacker said will continue is the annual Cops and Bobbers event. "We will continue to host them for the community," she said. "They are always a big hit with everyone." Now that she has officially retired, Thacker said her focus has shifted entirely to her family. "Ultimate sleepovers, it's all about the grandkids and that is what they love," Thacker said with a laugh. "Working around the farm and creating landscaping projects for Dickie (her husband) also tops the list. We don't travel a lot, but we may do some of that. We are really just content with being here on the farm, it's where we love to be." RIPLEY, W.Va. - Jackson County Delegates Jonathan Pinson, R-Mason, and Happy Joe Parsons, R-Jackson, have cast their support behind a $5.5 billion General Revenue budget for fiscal year 2027. The budget, which covers the period beginning July 1, 2026, has been sent to Gov. Patrick Morrisey for his consideration. Both delegates noted that the spending plan includes a 5% reduction in personal income tax rates-half of the 10% reduction originally proposed by the governor-and a 3% pay increase for state employees, including teachers, service personnel, and members of the West Virginia State Police. Pinson said that adoption and foster care programs will receive nearly $40 million more than current funding levels, and that Medicaid funding will increase by about $28 million. "These directives were moved from the surplus section of the budget to the primary Policy and Programming Budget to ensure the funding is secure," Pinson said. "Additionally, Medicaid waiver programs receive more than $5 million above current-year funding levels." Parsons pointed out that the budget also includes $117 million for the Hope Scholarship as part of the budget bill. He explained that the total of approximately $230 million dedicated to the Hope Scholarship will be comprised of last year's budget surplus and a separate appropriation. Parsons also listed infrastructure and environmental initiatives, along with local roads and flood-resilience efforts, as highlights of the plan, though he did not provide additional specific details on those items. Both delegates touted the passage of HB 4001, which would create TEAM-WV Corp., a private nonprofit organization designed to promote economic development, job creation, job retention, and business recruitment. "TEAM-WV would not operate as a state agency but would instead serve as a non-governmental partner to the Department of Commerce, helping increase our state's competitiveness in attracting private investment and new businesses," Pinson said. Parsons added that he sees this agency as having the most long-lasting effect of the session's initiatives. "TEAM-WV is aimed at boosting economic development all across the state," Parsons said. "Several of our neighboring states are already successfully using this type of policy, and we need to do the same." Finally, Pinson shared information regarding HB 4191, which addresses childcare challenges throughout the state. "The bill stabilizes reimbursement rates for childcare providers and expands tax credits for employers who help provide childcare services for their employees," Pinson said. "Employers could receive a tax credit equal to 50% of their investment in childcare facilities, as well as 50% of the cost of operating childcare services for employees." The 2026 Legislative session is scheduled to conclude at midnight on March 14.

article_text: CHARLESTON, W.Va. - A timeline for the West Virginia Public Service Commission's consideration of NextEra Energy's application for a high-voltage electricity transmission line has been set. The PSC issued an order Wednesday, March 18, setting the timeline which includes a deadline for those affected property owners who wish to file objections, as well as the date for a public hearing and the date a decision is due from the PSC. The process is expected to take at least a year. NextEra filed the application for a Certificate of Public Convenience & Necessity, with authorizes the construction of the MidAtlantic Resiliency Link, on Jan. 30. The high-voltage line is proposed to stretch from Greene County, Pennsylvania, to Frederick, Virginia, crossing over portions of the Eastern Panhandle of West Virginia - including Mineral, Hampshire, Preston, and Monongalia counties - and Western Maryland - including Allegany and Garrett counties. The line, as proposed, will stretch for 107.5 miles and have the capability of carrying 500 kilovolts (500,000 votes) of electricity. Since word of NextEra's plans for the line began circulating last year, those property owners who would be affected by the chosen path, as well as various elected officials who represent those property owners, have spoken out against the line. According to documents from the PSC, the citizen-led group West Virginians Against Transmission Injustice, or WATI, filed a petition to intervene on Feb. 6; a group of individual landowners referred to as the Intervenor Group, who live in or near the proposed route for the line, filed a petition on Feb. 12; the West Virginia Energy Users Group filed a petition on March 3; the Hampshire County Commission filed a petition on March 9; and the Preston County Commission filed a petition on March 10. In their petition, WATI alleged that the line would create "potential impacts to land use, environmental resources, property values, and electric rates." The Hampshire County Commissioners stated that the siting of the transmission line would "affect county residents, landowners, scenic and historic resources, and local communities ..." as well as adversely affect "the county's tax base, economic development, and the overall quality of life of its residents. The Preston County Commissioners said the proposed MARL project "could affect residents, landowner, natural resources and local communities within Preston County..." and that it could adversely "affect privately owned property, agricultural lands and working farms, scenic and natural resources, and the county's long-term economic vitality." In addition, the PSC's own Consumer Advocate Division filed a petition on Feb. 10, citing its "statutory duty to represent ratepayers' interests and the potential rate impacts of the MARL project." The application itself as originally filed by NextEra was revised at the PSC's direction twice as the state regulatory commission requested additional information. The PSC's Consumer Advocate Division raised additional concerns about the applications, "including the level of detail provided concerning existing transmission facilities and the disclosure of potential rate impacts to affected customers." According to CAD, NextEra's application was "prematurely filed because the cost allocations and rate impacts ...were not fully determined at the time of filing." In their finding issued on March 18, the Public Service Commission directed NextEra to publish it's revised version of the siting application in each affected county, and to notify, by certified mail, each affected property owner of the preferred corridor for the line. The deadline of June 1, 2026, was set for any other entities wishing to file petitions to intervene in the process. In preparation for that, a series of public meetings have been scheduled around the area to help inform the public about how the intervention process works. Meetings are scheduled as follows: - Thursday, March 26, 6-8 p.m. at Brookedale Farm, Georges Run Road, Fort Ashby. - Monday, March 30, 6:30-8 p.m. at Slanesville Ruritan Building, 6458 Bloomery Pike, Augusta. - Tuesday, March 31, 6:30-8 p.m. at Hampshire High School, 157 Trojan Way, Romney. - Wednesday, April 1, 6-9 p.m. at Cheat Lake Volunteer Fire Department, 409 Fairchance Rd., Morgantown. - Saturday, April 4, from 10 a.m. to noon at Old Capon Bridge Middle School, 75 Capon School St., Capon Bridge. - Saturday, April 11, from 10 a.m. to noon at Brookedale Farm, Georges Run Road, Fort Ashby, and the Slanesville Ruritan Building, Bloomery Pike, Augusta. - Sunday, April 12, from 1-4 p.m. at North Preston Senior Center, 13549 N. Preston Hwy., Bruceton Mills. The meetings are being hosted by West Virginians Against Transmission Injustice and are open to all concerned citizens. An evidentiary hearing is set for Oct. 26-30 and Nov. 2 at the PSC building in Charleston. A decision on the application is expected by March 6, 2027. PIEDMONT, W.Va. - Former Piedmont Council member Greg Harvey is now a Distinguished Mountaineer. Harvey, who successfully steered the City of Piedmont through their many water woes since the 2019 closure of Verso Luke mill and spearheaded the project to finally secure and implement an independent water source for the city, was honored for his efforts March 18 with a proclamation from Gov. Patrick Morrisey. Del. Rick Hillenbrand, who represents Piedmont as part of his House District 88, presented Harvey with the honor during the regular meeting of the mayor and council. Saying that he appreciates all the hard work of the city officials and many residents of Piedmont, Hillenbrand noted that "there are some who go above and beyond," and Harvey was definitely one of those. "Piedmont's water issues can best be described, in the words of the Grateful Dead, as 'a long, strange trip,' but there's one individual who really held the banner and wore the cloak of doing what was needed for Piedmont to get to where it is," Hillenbrand said. Hillenbrand also explained that the Distinguished Mountaineer Award, bestowed by the Governor, is not a common honor. "If you look it up, not a whole lot of people have gotten one," he said. The award citation credited Harvey for "playing a pivotal role in resolving the City of Piedmont's water crisis since 2019. "His selfless efforts have ensured a safe and secure water supply for Piedmont residents, breaking dependence on external providers," the citation stated. Harvey credited the current and former mayor and council for their efforts, and noted that "this is everybody's award" as he accepted the honor. Former mayor Paula Boggs presented Harvey with a cake celebrating his recognition. Although retired from the council, Harvey continues as the city's water administrator, overseeing the completion of the well water project and the search for funding for a second well to be used as a backup water source. WESTERNPORT, Md. - With a little over a month left to officially declare as a candidate, only one person has filed papers to run for office in the Town of Westernport. Allen Shapiro, currently serving as finance commissioner, has filed to run for re-election, according to town clerk Laura Freeman-Legge. In addition to his seat on the council, the seat currently held by water commissioner James Wills is coming open this year, along with the mayoral position. Mayor Judy Hamilton has indicted she will not be running for re-election. Hamilton is in her second two-year term as mayor, having been overwhelmingly returned to office in 2024 as a write-in candidate. Prior to her two terms as mayor, she served a term as a commissioner. Shapiro was elected in 2018 and although he did not seek a second term, was appointed in 2025 to fill a vacancy on the council. Wills was appointed to fill a vacancy in 2023. The seats currently held by streets commissioner Kirk Ketterman and police commissioner Catherine Mock, who were both elected in 2024, do not come open this year. Commissioners serve four-year terms. Any registered voter within town limits may run for office, as long as he or she is able to secure at least 25 signatures of registered voters who are residents of the city. Filing fee for mayor is $10 and commissioner is $5. Deadline to submit the candidacy papers back to the city office is Tuesday, April 28, at 4 p.m. The last day to register to vote is May 5, and the last day to request an absentee ballot is May 11. May 19 is designated as Revision Day, when residents not qualified to vote will be removed from the town's books. The election is set for Tuesday, May 26. All absentee ballots must be returned before the polls close on that day. CHARLESTON, W.Va. - The projected cost of NextEra Energy's portion of the Mid-Atlantic Resiliency Link transmission line has more than doubled, according to new analysis from the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis. The line, approved in December 2023 by regional transmission operator PJM, was originally expected to cost $441 million. NextEra now estimates its share will total $960 million. The project still requires regulatory approval from state public utility commissions along its proposed route, which primarily runs through West Virginia to supply power to a cluster of data centers in northern Virginia. PJM's planning documents cite rapidly growing data center energy demands in Northern Virginia as the main driver for the line. A 2025 IEEFA report used MARL as a case study to call for reform in PJM's transmission cost allocation methodology, arguing that data centers - not ratepayers - should bear the cost of new infrastructure needed to serve them. NextEra applied to the West Virginia Public Service Commission in January for a certificate to build its segment of the 500 kV interstate line. Another portion of the project in West Virginia, to be built by FirstEnergy, has not yet filed an application. IEEFA's revised analysis indicates West Virginia ratepayers will shoulder $572 million in costs over the 40-year life of the project-more than triple the group's 2025 estimate of $185 million. The line will provide no direct benefits to West Virginia, as NextEra has no customers in the state. The updated estimate includes capital, operational, and construction work in progress charges, broken down for residential, commercial, and industrial customers. West Virginia regulators recently granted "intervenor status" to a coalition of local governments and grassroots groups, giving them the ability to participate in hearings, submit evidence, cross-examine witnesses, and receive all filings. The Preston County Commission has been among the most proactive opponents. Commissioners recently unanimously approved a Petition for Leave to Intervene, formally establishing the county as an official party in the PSC proceedings. Commission President Hunter Thomas said the status allows the commission to advocate for residents' concerns and interests in hearings, testimony, and evidence submission. Residents, including farmer and local activist Beth Ann Bassio, praised the commission's leadership and urged others to get involved. Bassio said intervention is critical due to potential impacts on property values and the county's tax base and warned that West Virginians could bear financial costs for a project primarily serving out-of-state data centers. Hampshire County Commission also secured intervenor status, citing concerns that the transmission line could traverse scenic and historic resources, reduce property values, negatively affect the local tax base, and impact quality of life. County officials emphasized their responsibility to oversee potential impacts on county-owned properties and emergency service coordination. The PSC granted intervention to West Virginians Against Transmission Injustice (WATI), a grassroots group representing residents and farmers across Monongalia, Preston, Mineral, and Hampshire counties. WATI members argue that the project threatens property values, local environmental resources, and electricity rates. A separate "Intervenor Group" of Hampshire County landowners was recognized to challenge proposed routing corridors passing through or near their private property. The PSC has imposed strict transparency requirements on NextEra following objections from commission staff and the Consumer Advocate Division regarding public clarity. NextEra must now send notice via certified mail to every owner of surface real estate within the "preferred corridor" of the line. Regulators also mandated that public notices use bold type to clearly direct residents to interactive project maps. Additional petitions to intervene in the case are due by June 1. Formal evidentiary hearings are scheduled to begin in Charleston on Oct. 26, with a final PSC decision expected by March 6, 2027.

article_text: KINGWOOD, W.Va. - Preston County students delivered a strong performance at the recent West Virginia State Science Fair, with six of seven projects placing and two students earning special honors. Maintaining a longstanding record of excellence, Preston County students earned top marks across various categories. Officials noted the achievement is particularly remarkable as the state-level competition becomes more intense each year. Among the participants, Mariah Titchenell and Lexa Galloway took first place in the state competition. Second-place honors went to Brooke Burns, Eileen Parks and Nathan Bernatowicz. Catalina Richards and Harper Dick earned third place. School officials also recognized Kamryn Hayes, who represented Preston County in one of the toughest categories at the competition. Science Fair Coordinator Deb Zigray praised students for their abilities and impressive performances in a competition that featured a wide variety of topics this year. "I was very pleased with the students," she said. At the high school level, the two top-placing Preston County students also received special awards, according to Zigray. Titchenell's project, "Comparative Analysis of Vitamin C Degradation Across Cooking Methods," earned high marks for scientific exploration and received the Naval Award. The Naval Award recognizes outstanding projects in science, technology, engineering and mathematics. Galloway's project, "Dirty to Clean: Which Method Works Best?" earned the Regional Stockholm Junior Water Prize, an award that recognizes innovation in addressing significant water challenges. Zigray said it was fantastic to see Preston County students again earn top marks and special awards at the state fair, recalling last year where students Ethan White and Donald "Travis" Parks also received notable awards for their outstanding projects. "They all made Preston County proud," she said, "because the projects this year were absolutely amazing, and the topics at state were really out there." Zigray added the state science fair has become an even more challenging competitive scene, with the level of competition increasing as students present more impressive and in-depth projects. Even at the local level, students are increasing their efforts. Recently, local participants have introduced unique and complex topics. Zigray added that at the elementary level, this year's projects were so well-prepared that it was difficult to select the top winners. Science fair judge Jeff Zigray encountered a similar situation with the high school projects, noting that students put significantly more effort and depth into their work this year. "There are different topics every year, but this year, the display boards were fantastic, presentations are being memorized more, and there were a lot of very good interviews," Deb Zigray said. "I couldn't be prouder of them," she added. Officials of Preston County Schools now turn their attention to the upcoming Regional Social Studies Fair. CHARLESTON, W.Va. - The West Virginia Legislature wrapped up work on several priorities Saturday night as the 2026 regular session came to a close, with a tax cut and pay raise making it but a bill aimed at protecting children whose parents are being investigated for child welfare issues failing in the final hours. The Legislature gaveled in for its annual 60-day session on Jan. 14, introducing more than 2,700 bills over the last nearly nine weeks. Heading into the final hours of the session, lawmakers passed 152 state Senate bills and 151 House of Delegates bills. The Legislature completed work on Senate Bill 392, Gov. Patrick Morrisey's bill to cut personal income tax rates by 5% retroactive to Jan. 1, returning $125 million to taxpayers when fully implemented. The House amended the bill Friday to remove a proposed increase in vape and e-cigarette taxes, with the Senate agreeing Saturday. "We made a firm commitment during my time in the Legislature, in particular the last few years, to lessen the tax burden on our citizens as best we can," said state Sen. Trenton Barnhart, R-Pleasants. "This 5% tax cut on the personal income tax is another step towards eventually getting to zero, and we're excited to be able to provide some much-needed tax relief to our citizens." State Sen. Mike Oliverio, R-Monongalia, said the 5% cut in personal income tax rates was one of several ways the Legislature has worked to help West Virginians with affordability issues in recent years. "We're hearing from our constituents that many are experiencing an affordability crisis with expenses going up and the impact of costs," Oliverio said. "We passed a ... tax reduction a couple of years ago, and today we've added to that with an additional 5% reduction in personal income tax. "We passed a rebate on personal property tax where we return dollars to citizens who have paid their personal income tax," Oliverio continued. "We have eliminated the state income tax for our seniors with respect to their Social Security. ... We are trying today to increase the homestead exemption for our seniors and those that are disabled. We're trying to address this affordability crisis." Morrisey has pressured lawmakers during the session to pass a full 10% cut in personal income tax rates, though his budget only accounted for the loss in revenue from a 5% reduction. In a statement posted to social media Saturday, Morrisey thanked lawmakers for the tax relief they provided. "West Virginians will be able to enjoy some more money in their paychecks very soon," Morrisey said. "Today, the Legislature passed a 5% income tax reduction. This is a start, but we will accept the win and then begin efforts to lower income taxes even more in the future!" House Bill 4765, providing an average 3% pay raise for teachers, school service personnel and employees of the West Virginia State Police, got over the finish line with 10 minutes to spare before midnight after the Senate agreed to recede from an amendment adopted Friday to include locality pay for those workers in counties with higher median incomes and costs of living. A 3% pay raise for other state employees paid through the general revenue budget was included in Senate Bill 250, the finalized budget bill for fiscal year 2027. Morrisey first proposed the raise during his State of the State address kicking off the session. House Bill 5537, the latest vehicle for Raylee's Law, died Saturday night after the bill was drowned in debate on multiple amendments meant to water down its provisions. The bill would prohibit a county board of education from approving a request for home school instruction for an enrolled public school student if there is a pending child abuse or neglect investigation against the child's parent or guardian. The legislation, which has been offered for several years by House Minority Whip Shawn Fluharty, is named for Raylee Jolynn Browning, who died in 2018 from child abuse after her father pulled her from public school. Fluharty, who had placed a photo of Raylee outside the House chamber earlier Saturday, was livid at the bill's failure. "We sat on it for 8 hours ... and now all these amendments are popping up and we know damn well why it is," said Fluharty, D-Ohio. "This is abhorrent behavior. Disgusting government. When you're done here tonight, after you kill this bill again ... go out there and at least have the guts to look at her. Have the guts. I don't think you do. This is ridiculous." While the House rejected all the amendments and passed the bill 94-1 with four absent or not voting, it was too late for the Senate to receive the message after it adjourned sine die. Del. Elliott Pritt, R-Fayette, pleaded with members to not delay passage of the bill. "If we amend this bill or change it in any way, this bill dies tonight. which I do think is probably the outcome that some in this room want," Pritt said. "That's fine, that's their prerogative, I respect that. But what I can't respect ... is that we have a moment here to do something to protect children that are in harm's way. That is a fact, and I'm very sorry if that fact is very uncomfortable for some of you to deal with." Opponents of Raylee's Law argued that the Senate amendment incorporating it into the bill was poorly drafted. "I don't care what time it is. Our job is to write good law. And we need to write good law, and we need to protect kids," said Del. Adam Burkhammer, R-Lewis. "Let's do the right thing here. Or we can play political games and think we're getting some kind of win by passing the bill that's before you that will not protect one single child. It's flawed." The Senate amended the House message to Senate Bill 890, changing the school calendar from days to hours. The Senate amendment put the bill back to a 900-hour limit that was originally in the bill. The House agreed to the Senate's amendment Saturday in a 93-3 vote with three members absent While the bill remains permissive, allowing county school systems to continue to use the traditional 180-day calendar, Oliverio renewed his opposition to the change earlier Saturday. "This is the bill that reduces high school attendance by 23 days," Oliverio said. "The House attempted to make an amendment to our bill to reduce it by 14 days. Either way, I think it's a step in the wrong direction ... Our children need instruction time. They need quality instruction." House Bill 5453, which gutted a proposal for county school systems to switch from the current seven-step state school aid formula to a new block grant model beginning with the 2029-30 school year, died when the House did not take up the Senate message in the bill before midnight. The Senate Finance Committee's strike-and-insert amendment to HB 5453 would have wiped out the proposed block grant funding model in its entirety. Instead of a flat supplemental fund, the amendment integrated special education needs directly into the net enrollment calculation used for the basic foundation program. The House accepted the Senate's amendment Saturday night to House Bill 5381, relating to a comprehensive energy development policy and plan for the Office of Energy, 91-5, with three members absent or not voting. HB 5381 would restructure the state's Office of Energy with the Department of Commerce, empowering it with the creation of a comprehensive state energy policy that utilizes diverse resources like coal, natural gas, nuclear and renewables as part of Morrisey's 50 by 50 initiative to increase the state's production of electricity from 16 gigawatts to 50 gigawatts by 2050. Key provisions in HB 5381 include the incorporation of the Office of Coalfield Community Development and a new mandate to ensure electrical grid stability. "The purpose of this amendment is to empower the Office of Energy to develop a comprehensive energy development policy, a comprehensive grid stabilization plan, and to test the stability of West Virginia's energy grid," explained Senate Majority Whip Ben Queen, R-Harrison. "The office will prepare a comprehensive energy policy and a plan for implementation that embraces coal, natural gas, nuclear energy, hydropower, hydrogen and geothermal energy." The amendment removes the provisions of Senate Bill 420, the West Virginia First Energy Act, which would encourage electric utility companies to reach a 69% operational utilization rate for coal-fired power plants by offering financial incentives tied to cost recovery. The amendment also removes references to renewable energy, such as wind and solar. "This is a vote about electric rates," said Del. Evan Hansen, D-Monongalia, who voted not to concur. "This is a vote about whether we as a body, we as a state, are going to not play favorites and pick and choose what type of energy is allowed in our energy plan, but to consider all types of energy ... not to presuppose that you know what's best for the people of West Virginia or what's going to be cheapest." KINGWOOD, W.Va. - Officials of the Preston High School Theatre Department are set to present their next show for the season, "Shrek the Musical," a Broadway stage adaptation of the DreamWorks Animation film and the book by William Steig, with book and lyrics by David Lindsay-Abaire and music by Jeanine Tesori. Coming off the tails of their recent performance of Arthur Miller's "The Crucible," the PHS Theatre crew is now shifting gears for a musical that embraces classic comedy and family fun, yet still aims to maintain all of the demanding technicality a performance could offer, officials said. Drama teacher Leah DeLauder said ticket sales for the coming show have already started "going crazy," adding that this musical has been the most anticipated show in her time teaching at Preston High School. "I think it will surpass 'The Addams Family' (musical) in 2023, which we sold 1,100 tickets for," she said. DeLauder added that she estimates over 2,200 people could come out to see the new show. The new musical will certainly be a change of pace for those at the theater, as it requires a ton of props, features various location sets, and also requires a lot of prosthetics, which is a new challenge for those in the department, she added. Additionally, the musical will boast a large cast with 34 participants. Many are freshmen gearing up to take on a variation of dancing and singing choruses along with a huge group to play fairytale creatures, DeLauder said. One of the new challenges for the students has been to conceptualize how much they really will have to do for the show - from the acting to setting the stage and more. "It's going to be fantastic, but nobody gets to sit down and rest," she added. "It is a huge show, but we're all going through this journey together." DeLauder added that some of the current seniors of the department are taking on the four big parts in the show - a bittersweet moment, as many of them will be graduating soon. Those in the department were looking forward to the show, especially since it delivers a great message, inspires joy and is perfect for kids and adults alike, she said. The show follows the story of Shrek and Fiona from the movie and has all the big moments that people expect, along with some musical theater elements. Additionally, the musical will feature a lot of wonderful messages about individuality and about embracing how someone should be proud of how they are a unique individual, she said. While many are familiar with the movie, there likely will be a large group of people who will find some greater messages in the musical than they did with the motion picture, she said. "It really brings home the community aspect of being unique and finding your people," she said. Given current circumstances in the world's environment, best described as "hostile" by DeLauder, she noted that embracing happiness and joy is more than necessary. "We need some joy, we need some laughter and we need to feel that being ourselves is always a positive thing," she said. Transitioning from a very technically strict and heavy play like "The Crucible," DeLauder added that they certainly wanted to lighten things up for the year, but students still wanted to do something detail-oriented. And even though the two shows may seem extremely different, they both carry many of the same messages in a strange way, she said. "The idea of 'othering' people always causes chaos - it happens in 'The Crucible' when we are with other people, and it happens in the swamp in Shrek when we are with other people - and we don't see people for who they are, good or bad," she said. From a teaching perspective, taking the time to see those similarities across two very different genres of performance is a wonderful way for students to understand that the same messages and stories are in lots of different places and in history especially. For the musical, the PHS Theatre also will offer showings to Kingwood Elementary, Central Preston, the Bruceton School, Terra Alta East Preston and South Preston, DeLauder said, adding that cadets from the Mountaineer ChalleNGe Academy are also set to attend a showtime. The public showtimes will run from Thursday, March 19, to March 22. The shows will begin at 7:30 p.m., running from Thursday through Saturday at the Preston High School Theatre. The Sunday matinee will begin at 2:30 p.m. Student night is set for Friday, and student tickets will be $5. Regular tickets for the show are $7 and proceeds will go to support the PHS Theatre program and pay for play royalties for the coming year. KINGWOOD, W.Va. - Officials with the Preston County Clerk's Office are reminding voters of significant changes for the upcoming election cycle to ensure residents remain informed and able to exercise their right to vote. Preston County Clerk Dave Sypolt and his staff have been working to prepare for the May primary election. A central part of those efforts involves educating the public on key legislative changes that could affect voters this season. Sypolt said one of the most important changes this year is the requirement of a voter ID amid the closed Republican primary. According to the Secretary of State's Office, under new state voter ID laws, West Virginia voters must show an approved form of photo identification at the polls during early voting or on Election Day. All forms of ID must be valid and not expired. The change comes after Gov. Patrick Morrisey signed House Bill 3016 into law in 2025. The bill also provided voters the option of requesting a voter registration card with their photo from the West Virginia Secretary of State's Office. Additionally, HB 3016 made a number of previously accepted forms of ID - such as a state-issued hunting and fishing license or a recent utility bill - no longer valid. "We want to make the laws as simple as possible in West Virginia," Morrisey said. "No photo ID, no vote." This law does not apply to absentee-by-mail voting or any person who falls under an exception. Under the new law, voters can use several accepted forms of ID according to the West Virginia Secretary of State's office, including: A West Virginia license or state-issued ID A driver's license from another state A U.S. passport or passport card An employee ID with photo issued by local, state, or federal government A U.S. military ID with photo A voter registration card with a photo issued by a West Virginia county clerk or the Secretary of State An ID issued by the Division of Motor Vehicles without a photo, for voters who swear and affirm that they belong to recognized religious communities that prohibit them from being photographed. Of the IDs listed, one exception can be made for voters 65 years of age or older if their ID is expired. In this case, the ID is still acceptable if the document was not expired on the voter's 65th birthday. Sypolt said this will be the first year that photo ID is required. "In the past, a photo ID could be used for identification, but now you must have at least a photo ID - there are some nuances to that as well," he said. There are three other exceptions to the voter ID requirement involving a signed, sworn statement by an adult who has known the voter for six months or more. Those vouching must have known the voter for at least six months, must show a valid photo ID with their current name and address, and must sign an affidavit confirming the voter's identity. Sypolt elaborated that the new ID requirements are another way to assure that the person casting a ballot is the person who is registered to vote. "I have never believed there was voter fraud in Preston County, or for that matter, in any of the neighboring counties. I've never felt that there was a problem with that. But in some areas, maybe there has been," he said. Sypolt added that the first line of defense against voter fraud is maintaining an accurate voter registration list, a task his office spends many hours keeping up to date. Besides the voter ID requirements, officials stressed that voters must be aware of the closed Republican primary ballot. Independent and non-party voters will not be able to vote on a Republican ballot during the primary. However, those voters will still have the opportunity to vote on nonpartisan matters, such as levies, municipal elections, and the board of education. Independent and non-party voters will be able to participate in the general election without needing to change their affiliation because everyone uses the same ballot, officials said. Those wishing to participate in the Republican primary can still do so by changing their voter affiliation to Republican. The deadline to make this change is April 21, Sypolt added. As for the election itself, Sypolt said he expects an average year for voter turnout, though there is room for variation. Several competitive races are contributing to local interest, including the Kingwood municipal election, several candidates seeking seats on the Preston County Commission, and various races for the state Senate and House of Delegates. "My prediction is that we will have approximately half of the turnout that we had last time," Sypolt said. "There was a lot of interest in the 2024 election because of the national ticket." For this midterm, Sypolt estimated the county would likely see 40% to 45% voter participation. He added that while lower turnout is expected for midterms, more people seem to be paying closer attention to the election process this year, which he noted is a positive sign for participation. Sypolt explained that due to the closed Republican primary, more voters have re-registered to participate, which further indicates increased public engagement. Overall, officials said their goal this year is an informed voter population, especially given the changes that could impact an individual's ability to cast a ballot. Sypolt encouraged community members to tell their family, friends, and neighbors about the updates so more people are ready to vote in the May primary. For more information, residents can visit www.wvsos.gov or contact the Preston County Clerk's office at 304-329-0070 during regular business hours. MORGANTOWN, W.Va. - The United Way of Monongalia and Preston Counties celebrated the conclusion of its 2026 fundraising campaign Thursday evening with a community gathering at the West Virginia Botanic Garden, highlighting both the campaign's success and the organization's broader community impact. The campaign celebration, held at the Terrace at Tibb's Run, brought together nonprofit partners, business leaders, volunteers and supporters to mark the close of the annual campaign. Executive Director Brandi Helms opened the event by emphasizing that United Way's work extends far beyond its annual fundraising effort. "One of the things we like to highlight is that United Way's work happens year-round, not just during the campaign," Helms said. Through West Virginia 211, the health and human services resource line the local United Way manages for Monongalia and Preston counties, the organization answered 1,324 calls in 2025, connecting residents with resources such as food assistance, after-school programs and financial help. The calls resulted in 7,729 referrals to community services. Helms also highlighted volunteer and outreach programs, including the annual Day of Caring, sponsored by Burke & Herbert Bank. Last year the event engaged 302 volunteers, who completed 26 service projects and contributed nearly 1,200 hours of community service. Food security remains another major focus. Through the Helpful Harvest program, based at Hazel's House of Hope, United Way partnered with 52 feeding programs and food pantries serving nearly 7,600 individuals over the past year. The facility also distributed nearly $1 million in donated household goods through partnerships with local agencies and national organizations such as Baby2Baby. Seasonal initiatives also supported hundreds of local families. In partnership with West Virginia Radio Corporation, the organization revived its Cans for the Community food drive last fall, collecting more than 3,400 food items. During the holiday season, United Way also worked with Christian Help to distribute toys and food to families, reaching 1,149 children and more than 1,600 individuals. Helms said that when all programs are combined, United Way provides roughly $2.5 million in direct assistance to the community each year. The evening also celebrated the success of the 2026 campaign, which raised $1.2 million to support United Way programs and its 24 funded partner agencies across Monongalia and Preston counties. Campaign Chair Dave Thomas said the milestone reflected the strength of community support. "Tonight we celebrate reaching the $1.2 million goal," Thomas said. "But what's more important is how we reached it. The United Way campaign is truly a grassroots effort supported by individuals, businesses and organizations throughout our community." More than 1,300 individual donors contributed to the campaign, accounting for about 13 percent of total funds raised. Corporate donations from 50 local companies made up another 24 percent, while workplace campaigns-employee contributions through payroll deduction-represented the largest share at 49 percent. "It's not one big donor or one corporate check," Thomas said. "It's thousands of people giving what they can. That's what makes this campaign - and this community - so special." During the celebration, Thomas was also presented with the Timothy P. Saub Community Leader Award, recognizing his leadership and commitment to philanthropy during the campaign. Helms praised Thomas for his dedication and his focus on strengthening local impact. "He really dug into the campaign this year," she said. "His leadership helped bring individuals and companies together around the idea that what we do here truly makes a difference locally."

article_text: KINGWOOD, W.Va. - Preston County Board of Education members reviewed and approved the proposed levy rates for fiscal year 2026-27 during their most recent meeting, moving forward with the district's annual budget process. In accordance with West Virginia State Code §11-9-12, the proposed rates were presented for approval and authorization. The board will now submit the rates to the State Board of Education and the State Auditor's Office for final approval, officials said. Superintendent Brad Martin said the levy rate is not an excess school levy, but is the base levy rate set by the state that will fund the schools. Reviewing and establishing the rate is a process that the board must undertake on an annual basis, Martin added. During the discussion, board members reviewed the rates and discussed the differences between Class I and Class II tax brackets, among other details. According to the proposed rates, the levy estimate for each $100 of assessed valuation is as follows: Regular Levy - As determined by the Legislature per W.Va. Code §11-8-6f. General Current Expense Levy: Class I: 19.40¢ Class II: 38.80¢ Class III/IV: 77.60¢ Additionally, the net amount to be raised by the levy for FY 2026-2027 is $10,242,101 for the General Current Expense Levy. Board members approved the levy rates. Katrina Kerstetter, accountant for the Preston Board of Education, spoke to the proposed levy rates, clarifying that they are the state's dedicated levy rates applied for the county. Additionally, the proposed numbers are what is used to formulate the district's budget from year to year, she said, adding that the rate, which is set by the state, has not changed since her time working with the district. Kerstetter added that while the total levy amount appears to have increased, it is because assessed property values have risen. This indicates that the tax base for the district has grown, she said. To view the schedule of proposed levy rates, visit https://go.boarddocs.com/wv/preston/Board.nsf/Public. In other business: - Board members approved additions to the extended employment, supplemental, and extracurricular scale for the 2025-26 school year, adding a boy's track coach position and a GED examiner to the scale. - Martin said the district's waiver regarding the 180-day calendar requirement was approved by West Virginia State Superintendent of Schools Michelle Blatt. The waiver was requested for four days between January 26 and January 30, 2026, which were included in Gov. Patrick Morrisey's emergency declaration. With the approval of the waiver and a recent "snow day," the final day for students is now scheduled for Friday, May 29. Additionally, Tuesday, April 7, which was originally an instructional make-up day, will now be a day off for students and 200-day staff. This change maintains the district's original spring break schedule, Martin said. West Virginia regulators recently granted "intervenor status" to a coalition of local governments and grassroots groups, giving them the ability to participate in hearings, submit evidence, cross-examine witnesses, and receive all filings. The Preston County Commission has been among the most proactive opponents. Commissioners recently unanimously approved a Petition for Leave to Intervene, formally establishing the county as an official party in the PSC proceedings. Commission President Hunter Thomas said the status allows the commission to advocate for residents' concerns and interests in hearings, testimony, and evidence submission. Residents, including farmer and local activist Beth Ann Bassio, praised the commission's leadership and urged others to get involved. Bassio said intervention is critical due to potential impacts on property values and the county's tax base and warned that West Virginians could bear financial costs for a project primarily serving out-of-state data centers. Hampshire County Commission also secured intervenor status, citing concerns that the transmission line could traverse scenic and historic resources, reduce property values, negatively affect the local tax base, and impact quality of life. County officials emphasized their responsibility to oversee potential impacts on county-owned properties and emergency service coordination. The PSC granted intervention to West Virginians Against Transmission Injustice (WATI), a grassroots group representing residents and farmers across Monongalia, Preston, Mineral, and Hampshire counties. WATI members argue that the project threatens property values, local environmental resources, and electricity rates. A separate "Intervenor Group" of Hampshire County landowners was recognized to challenge proposed routing corridors passing through or near their private property. The PSC has imposed strict transparency requirements on NextEra following objections from commission staff and the Consumer Advocate Division regarding public clarity. NextEra must now send notice via certified mail to every owner of surface real estate within the "preferred corridor" of the line. Regulators also mandated that public notices use bold type to clearly direct residents to interactive project maps. Additional petitions to intervene in the case are due by June 1. Formal evidentiary hearings are scheduled to begin in Charleston on Oct. 26, with a final PSC decision expected by March 6, 2027. KINGWOOD, W.Va. - Preston County Commissioners recently held several special sessions to gather public input on the proposed Special Emergency Ambulance Service Fee (county EMS ordinance) which aims to support Emergency Medical Service in the future. During the most recent meeting, commissioners, Preston County EMS Director Henry McDonald, and attorney Wendy Greve presented draft version No. 14 of the ordinance. McDonald presented the costs associated with operating an ambulance, including data on personnel, equipment, and licensing saying that it is roughly $900,000 a year just to run one outfitted ALS ambulance, 24/7, 365 days a year. McDonald added that for the population for Preston County, four ambulances are recommended, just for emergency response. Explaining the legislative authority for the ordinance, McDonald said that in 1975 West Virginia made county commissions responsible for providing EMS, yet provided no funding for the mandate. Under this action, West Virginia State Code §7-15-17 empowers county commissions to impose a "special emergency ambulance service fee." McDonald elaborated that under the code, the commission has the authority to apply the fee at its own discretion without public input; however, the commission opted to hold public meetings for feedback. McDonald walked through the entire ordinance for those in attendance. Notably, Section 4 deals with the establishment of the fee. According to the latest version of the ordinance, Section 4 states: "Each Special Emergency Ambulance Service Fee imposed under this ordinance shall be for emergency ambulance service provided for a Preston County fiscal year July 1st to June 30th. The Special Emergency Ambulance Service Fee established by this ordinance shall be one hundred sixty-five dollars ($165) per living unit per fiscal year." The fee imposed on living units is assessed against the unit itself. The owner of record is designated solely as the billing and payment agent. The ordinance states: "Nothing herein shall be construed to impose personal liability upon any tenant as a user of emergency ambulance services." Residents who have been granted a property tax Homestead Exemption by the assessor shall pay a discounted fee of $75 on their owner-occupied residential unit. The ordinance also applies to local commerce, stating: "The Special Emergency Ambulance Service Fee established by this ordinance shall be one hundred sixty-five dollars ($165) per business entity per fiscal year." Nonprofit businesses will not be required to pay the fee. Landlords are responsible for the payment of any tenant of a living unit. Any landlord or person required to pay more than three fees in a calendar year shall have the right to have the full amount of their yearly payment prorated over a 12-month period. For example, a landlord who owns 10 units with 10 tenants would owe a yearly fee of $1,650. The landlord would be allowed to make 12 monthly payments of $137.50. Any business entity operated inside a residential living unit shall be required to pay only the living unit fee. Commission President Hunter Thomas spoke regarding the choice of a standard fee for both residential and business entities, noting the commission had explored various other structures. However, it was discovered that many options besides the flat fee would not hold up to a legal challenge. Thomas elaborated that they had worked through several possibilities, like square footage or employee numbers, only to find they would likely be struck down by the West Virginia Supreme Court. As for how the money would help existing agencies, McDonald said the goal is not to fund every EMS agency in the county, but to ensure that all currently available EMS remains available. If the ordinance passes and a fee is established, each emergency ambulance agency in the county would have to sign a service contract, officials said. Within that contract, agencies would report the areas they cover and their response times, etc. That data would be used to determine how much money is disbursed to agencies that meet the requirements, McDonald said. Thomas added that the county has no authority or oversight over existing agencies because they are independent nonprofit entities, unless the commission provides them funding. With recent support provided to agencies, the commission has only performed direct invoice payment or reimbursement, he added. With funding through the ordinance, however, the service contract would hold agencies to certain expectations and standards. Officials said this would require agencies to open their books to the commission and answer fiscally to the commission. Thomas added that the county has already moved forward with licensing and permitting a county ambulance. The county will soon purchase an ambulance using General County dollars to provide non-emergency transports. Thomas said the idea would be to take over transports to free up existing agencies to focus on emergency calls. Revenue generated through the county truck would be used to backfill into existing agencies. In the event of an agency closing, the county truck would provide redundancy to cover the service area immediately, he added. McDonald noted that two EMS agencies in West Virginia recently closed within 24 hours of each other. When asked how many employees the county would need, McDonald answered that they would need 12 full-time providers to run the truck 24/7. Community member Jim Maier asked about the logic behind the $75 homestead exemption fee when the ideal fee is $165 across the board. Commissioner Don Smith noted that those with a homestead exemption are typically citizens living on a fixed income, representing roughly one-fifth of the entities in the county. Commissioner Samantha Stone spoke about the process of working through the ordinance with the EMS Advisory Board. The initial goal, she said, was to establish a lower fee of $50 to $100, but after finding data on the deficits leading to agency closures, they landed on the $165 fee. Thomas added that the justification for the homestead exemption was looking out for senior citizens. Community members expressed concerns and asked if there was consideration for a fee that was more representative of the whole population. Commissioners noted they are limited by the structure of the state code. Smith said that in the past, the West Virginia Association of Counties had tried to lobby for a 1% sales tax that commissions could apply to areas outside of municipalities for fire and EMS, but the legislation never took hold. Thomas added that the commission is limited in how it can structure the fee, specifically because it cannot be based on monetary aspects like revenue from taxes. Under West Virginia State Code, fees must be distinguished from taxes. While taxes are assessed based on economic value, the fee must be based on the potential users of the service being funded which limits the parameters, officials said. Community members continued discussions, citing issues with the state's failure to offer greater support for EMS. Community members and commissioners also held deeper discussions on the specifics of the ordinance, reviewing the language and discussing the definitions provided within the document along with the application of the ordinance fee for seasonal units. KINGWOOD, W.Va. - Board members continued to review and approve reductions in force and transfers, which sparked further discussion and concerns for cuts of specific Career and Technical Education offerings during a recent meeting. The board has continued to work through the RIF and transfer process, now set for a total of 40 positions. Superintendent Brad Martin explained that transfers being considered must be completed by April 1, clarifying that the most recent meeting was the last opportunity to do so. However, the deadline for RIFs is May 1 and can be taken up for consideration at future meetings, he added. Elaborating on the RIF and transfer process, Assistant Superintendent Angie Varner said that due to the recent loss of 283 students in enrollment for the school year, Preston County Schools had to consider 40 positions to remain within the confines of the state aid formula. Varner added that while the cuts are being made, there are still pending changes with kindergarten enrollment, which is currently starting to increase. This change could result in the district adding back a few positions that were cut. Officials noted that cuts must be made to remain within the requirements of the state aid formula. If Preston County Schools goes over its budgeted limit, the state will look at the district's financial records and could flag them for not being financially responsible, thus the reason for the difficult decisions. Board members talked through a variety of issues regarding the cuts - like the impacts of maintaining courses such Information Technology 1 and Information Technology 2, along with offerings like the Cisco Networking Academy, an IT and cybersecurity curriculum for students. Part of the issue with some classes - and part of the reasoning for their selection for being cut - is due to a general decrease of student interest, not just general enrollment downtrends, officials said. Board members discussed how student interest has waned in IT-related courses and how the district would go about offering other IT curriculums that could attract students. During the discussion, board members also focused on three career and technical education offerings that were to be cut, including Diesel Technology, an Auto Collision class, and an agriculture position for Preston County middle schools, all of which were to be cut due to decreasing enrollment, officials said. Board member Michael Hovatter asked about the Auto Collision class, saying there was a certain need for skilled workers in that field in the community. Varner added that the course had been selected due to "dismal" student sign-ups. Varner elaborated on the selection process, saying that when cuts are made, using Preston High School as an example, the process first looks at electives because they are not required. Some electives are taken out, though they don't want to, but that's done because they have to ensure the core required classes are provided. The next step is to look through the courses with the lowest class enrollments, Varner said. Board member Beth Noss stressed concerns over the cut of the Diesel Technology class, saying there would still be some students who are trying to become CTE completers in that field of study. Noss added that if the position is done away with, how will the district get a teacher who is certified in diesel technology to help students complete? Martin said there were current instructors who could help students reach completer status, but added that he understood the concerns of finishing the work with someone who is certified in the subject. Noss added that she was concerned that students who want to complete in the course could be left out, and motioned to separate the decision on the Diesel Technology RIF until another date to be further reviewed. Board members approved the service and personnel agendas but separated out the Diesel Technology class to be tabled and reviewed at a future meeting. KINGWOOD, W.Va. - Officials are gearing up for the next event leading to the 84th Preston County Buckwheat Festival: the annual Preston County Buckwheat Festival Royalty Pageant, where the next King Buckwheat and Queen Ceres will be named April 18. It is known that the effort required to produce the Buckwheat Festival is a yearlong undertaking. Best said by several Buckwheat general chairmen, "once one festival ends, the other begins." Amid all the work and planning is arguably one of the most important traditions leading up to the annual festival: the Royalty Pageant. Officials said the event is the culmination of a rigorous review for the next sets of royals, often regarded as "the best of the best" who will go on to represent the festival and Preston County. 84th Buckwheat Festival chairman Mike Shaffer said that currently the farm visits and interviews have been completed in the current selection process for King Buckwheat. Additionally, the royalty court is set with 11 escorts in total, which is a strong showing for the year. The 84th Preston County Buckwheat Festival senior escorts include: Brycen Brown, Hayden Cole, Brayden Miller, William Fields, Max Huggins, Nick Bernatowicz, Coen Thomas, Kaleb Stone, Brody McCleary, Blake Jennings and Riley Mayfield. Among them, five escorts are completing the process to become the next King Buckwheat, including Mayfield, Brown, Stone, McCleary and Bernatowicz. The field of candidates for the next Queen Ceres is also strong, made up of senior princesses Alyssa Friend, Khloe Kelly, Allyson Teets, Leighton Biermann, Sarah Jeffries, Mariah Titchenell, Caralie Fultz, Stella Taylor, Sophie Zinn, Lyla Fisher and Raegan Teter. Speaking to the selection process for king, Mike Shaffer added that the farm visits are conducted by selected judges who are from outside the Preston County community. An additional three judges, different from the farm judges, are also selected for the interview processes. Mike Shaffer added that it has been a very competitive year, regarding the current group of youths as "outstanding." Speaking to that point, Mike Shaffer added that each king candidate is provided 90 minutes to showcase their farm and the best they have to offer during the farm visit - a task that the candidates managed while keeping the judges' attention for the entire duration. Ultimately, the rigorous process ties to a deeper importance of the royalty court for the Buckwheat Festival, as they will go on to represent the county and promote the festival, officials said. All of the court will be representative of the county, Mike Shaffer said, but as always the top six will hit the road, attend parades throughout the region and represent the county across the state. For the pageant process, judges from outside the area will be brought in. The goal of all of this is to provide competitive integrity and allow for the youths' achievements to stand on their own, officials said. Pageant coordinator Shelley Shaffer said the tradition of the pageant is tied to the history of the festival itself. "The pageant has been around forever," she said, adding that there will be some returning traditions this year for the pageant. In the spirit of this year's theme, "Back to our roots," the pageant will again feature a dancing number for the top youths - a tradition that the community cherished but had lost after the impact from COVID, she said. Shelley Shaffer said she is really looking forward to continuing to work with the courts, adding that in her career as a preschool teacher, she naturally deals with children rather than young adults. The pageant itself is about supporting the youth of the community and celebrating their success, she said. She said that she has loved getting to know the top 11 escorts and all the senior princesses. Ultimately, Shelley Shaffer said she hopes to see all the candidates have fun, enjoy their time, be the best they can be and shine. Shelley Shaffer added that she hopes to see everyone at the pageant. The Preston County Buckwheat Festival Royalty Pageant will be held April 18 at the Craig Civic Center, with doors opening at 5 p.m. and the pageant starting at 6 p.m. Tickets are $10 and will be available at the door. Buckwheat Festival merchandise will also be available at the event.
