article_text: MERCERVILLE, Ohio - A ribbon-cutting ceremony was held Wednesday at South Gallia High School for the new South Gallia Health Clinic, a facility officials say will transform health care access for South Gallia students, faculty and the surrounding community. The new health care center is one of several projects underway in Gallia County. In partnership with Holzer Health System and backed by a $2.8 million award, the Gallia County Local School District began taking patients at the clinic in December. An opening ceremony was originally scheduled for February but was postponed due to a winter storm. Officials say the facility will offer comprehensive primary care, behavioral health, dental and vision services to students, district staff and local residents. The center will be staffed by Holzer team members, including a nurse practitioner and a certified medical assistant trained in registration duties. Vision services will be provided by a Holzer optometrist, while dental care will be offered by a local dentist. Nationwide Children's Hospital is also a supporting partner for the new facility. Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine visited Gallia County in March 2024 to announce the Appalachian Children's Health Initiative, with more than $64 million in funding awarded to the Appalachian Children Coalition to support the creation or expansion of community and school-based health clinics, the launch of health care-focused workforce development programs and more. Funding for the Appalachian Children's Health Initiative was awarded through the larger Appalachian Community Grant Program, which invested $500 million into Ohio's 32-county Appalachian region. This investment was spearheaded by DeWine's administration with support from the Ohio General Assembly. John Carey, director of the Governor's Office of Appalachia, spoke at the event, along with Holzer CEO Todd Fowler, Mary Kay Irwin of Nationwide Children's Hospital and Randy Leite of the Appalachian Children Coalition. The ceremony was hosted by Gallia County Schools Superintendent Phillip Kuhn. Kuhn highlighted the major advantage of having health services available on campus for students. "There's really a big push in Ohio to cut down on absenteeism, and this is definitely going to support that, and we are excited about that," Kuhn said. Carey said the clinic at South Gallia is an ideal example of why the initiative was launched. "It's important that communities like South Gallia are recognized. The state sees you, and you're just as important as anybody else," Carey said. Fowler underscored the impact the facility has already had on the rural community, with more than 370 patients treated since the clinic opened. He noted that the number represents both students and adults in the community. "We've treated adults here as well, who might not have had easier access otherwise. We've always said about school-based health care that schools are the center of the community, and that's where things happen," Fowler said. Leite applauded the collaboration among project partners, noting their shared focus on prioritizing children's health. He extended special thanks to the leadership at Holzer and Nationwide Children's Hospital. "No child should face barriers for the care they need. And the fact is, for a long time there was a huge barrier, because health care was not here, it was someplace else many miles away," Leite said. Irwin spoke on the positive impact the clinic is already having on absenteeism. "The students who have accessed care here have saved an average of 4.7 hours of seat time. One of the things with school-based medicine that we really want to do is we want to prevent children from missing school because they are trying to find a way to treat their health care needs. When children have to leave school and go to an appointment, oftentimes they don't come back that day," Irwin said. The ceremony included student participation, with the South Gallia band and choir performing the national anthem. Additionally, student Blaise Davison led the Pledge of Allegiance, and student MichaelAnne Ours introduced Carey. Following the close of the speaking engagements, the ceremony moved outside for the formal ribbon-cutting, which was followed by tours of the new clinic. POINT PLEASANT, W.Va. - The Mason County Board of Education approved a series of personnel actions, travel requests and contracts during its regular meeting Tuesday. Board president Jared Billings presided, joined in person by Vice president Meagan Bonecutter and members Ashley Cossin and Dale Shobe. Board member Bo Burgess participated by telephone, while Superintendent Melissa Farmer was also present. The board recognized Hannan eighth-graders Zoe Haddock and Lacey Berks for their achievements as participants in the West Virginia Music Educators Association. The students were not present at the meeting to receive their certificates. Curriculum directors Erin Tolliver and Walter Raynes presented a report on the i-Ready program. Tolliver told the board there were improvements at the elementary level in reading, but math still needs improvement. She noted funding has been approved to hire four additional academic coaches. Raynes said there were improvements at the high school level, but not nearly at the desired levels. He told the board that creative efforts are underway at all three county high schools to improve test scores. Tolliver, Raynes and board members agreed that the program's mixed results require further analysis. Farmer told the board that the students aboard a bus involved in a minor accident Tuesday were unharmed. She commended aide Lori Thomas for the care she provided to the students. Farmer said plans for roofing and paving projects at county schools are being finalized. She also noted summer school has been scheduled for the week of Aug. 6. Treasurer Charles Fish submitted a financial report to the board showing revenue collection and expenditures are on schedule with forecasts. Board members approved Brent Hereford, Jayna Lowery, Michael Marerro and Alisha Wallis as drivers for the 2025-26 school year after verification of their driving records through the West Virginia Department of Motor Vehicles. Christina Nelson was approved for out-of-state travel to Washington, D.C., March 30-31, 2026, to attend the School Nutrition Association Congressional Briefing at no cost to the board. Cossin noted that Nelson was selected as the sole representative for the state. Steve Richardson was also approved for out-of-state travel to Forney, Texas, April 22-24, 2026, to attend an OC Site Tour funded through the Perkins Grant. The board also approved a list of volunteers from Beale Elementary and Point Pleasant Junior/Senior High School for the 2025-26 school year. In professional personnel matters, the board approved the employment of Joel Beattie as HVAC teacher at the Mason County Career Center effective March 26, 2026, and John Robinson as a substitute teacher for the 2025-26 school year. Due to a reduction in force, contracts for Hannah Allinder, MaKayla Atkins, Shenna Muniz, Emily Parsons, Lydia Rhodes and Morgan Snyder will be terminated effective June 30, 2026. The board also placed Crystal Beller, Nicole Carr, Amber Grubb, Amelia Hudnall, Logan Raynes and Chelsea Troy on the transfer and subsequent assignment list for the 2026-27 school year, along with William Cottrill, whose contract will be reduced from 261 days to 240 days due to declining student enrollment. Contract reassignment agreements were approved for Peyton Ball, moving from second grade to fourth grade at New Haven Elementary; Barbara Michelle Mitchell, from fourth grade to third grade at Point Pleasant Intermediate School; Rebecca Roll, from Title I to first grade at Beale Elementary; and Amy Miller, transitioning from VoAg teacher at the Mason County Career Center to a combined VoAg and Project Lead the Way teaching role at the career center and Wahama Junior/Senior High School. Among service personnel actions, the board accepted the resignations of Ernest Bryant and Joshua Selman from the maintenance department effective March 16 and March 12, 2026, respectively. Georgia Hart, a custodian at Leon Elementary, was granted up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave under the Family and Medical Leave Act. Transfers were approved for Joshua Mattox, who will move from bus route 2029 to route 142, and James Walker, who will transfer from custodian at Point Pleasant Junior/Senior High to custodian at Hannan Junior/Senior High, both effective March 26, 2026. The board approved the employment of Leah Cochran for an unassigned bus route, Rickie Murphy as a bus operator for route 184 and Anna Will as a custodian at New Haven Elementary, all effective March 26, 2026. Additional hires included Takoda Kiser as substitute bus operator, Sarah Lynch as substitute cook, Carlina Mullins as substitute secretary and Patricia Newsome as substitute aide for the 2025-26 school year. Several reclassifications were approved in accordance with state code, including Cynthia Chapman from secretary III/receptionist to executive secretary/receptionist retroactive to July 1, 2024, Pam Neece and Terri Watterson from secretary II to secretary III retroactive to July 1, 2024, and Kourtney Long from secretary II to secretary III retroactive to July 1, 2025. The board approved a mutual agreement adjusting Gena Jeffers' contract from a 261-day secretary position to a 240-day position at Point Pleasant Junior/Senior High effective July 1, 2026, due to declining enrollment. Due to a reduction in force, service personnel contracts for Angela Bartee, Misty Clutter, Kayla Ellis, Sly Gearheart, Shannon Pauley, Delilah Payne and Kaitlyn Smith will be terminated effective June 30, 2026. Patricia Gilkey, Beth Hodges, Shannon Pauley, Amanda Stanley and Susan Williamson were placed on the transfer and subsequent assignment list for the 2026-27 school year. In extracurricular matters, the board accepted the resignation of Matthew Cottrill as assistant varsity football coach at Point Pleasant Junior/Senior High effective Jan. 7, 2026, along with the resignations of Sherry Pullin as tutor/interventionist effective March 9, 2026, and Paige Roush as soccer coach for the 2026-27 school year effective March 12, 2026. The board approved the employment of Ronda Matheny as a supplemental custodian at the Mason County School for Success on an as-needed basis effective March 26, 2026. David Darst was approved as assistant varsity boys track coach and Lori Danford as junior high golf coach at Point Pleasant Junior/Senior High for the 2025-26 school year. John Bonecutter, Greg Danford, Casey Killingsworth, David McCutchen, Christopher Miller and Roger Wood were approved as unpaid athletic assistants at Point Pleasant Junior/Senior High. Alan Barnitz was approved as assistant varsity track coach at Wahama Junior/Senior High, while Anthony Jeff Jodon and Chris Knapp were approved as unpaid athletic assistants at Wahama. Danielle Wilson was approved as junior high head softball coach at Hannan Junior/Senior High for the 2025-26 school year. The board approved a memorandum of understanding with the West Virginia Department of Education to hire four academic coaches to support kindergarten through sixth grade English language arts and math using grant funding. A contract with Thrasher Architecture and Engineering was also approved to upgrade security entrances at Point Pleasant Intermediate School and Point Pleasant Junior/Senior High, funded through School Building Authority grants. In financial matters, the board appointed members to the audit committee to procure audit services for fiscal years ending June 30, 2026, through June 30, 2028. The board also approved the ratification of orders, transfers and supplements, including checks totaling $1,237,095.95. The next regular business meeting is scheduled for April 14 at 6 p.m., followed by a statutory business meeting at 10 a.m. on April 21 and another regular business meeting April 28. Both meetings will be held at the Mason County Board of Education Office. BIDWELL, Ohio - A new $6.1 million speculative industrial building is coming to Gallia County, with officials saying the project will help attract jobs and strengthen the region's manufacturing footprint. DEIP II LLC and the Community Improvement Corporation of Gallia County, in collaboration with multiple state and regional partners, announced plans to construct a 50,000-square-foot facility at the Dan Evans Industrial Park. The building will be located on a 10-acre site within the 77-acre SiteOhio Authenticated industrial park and will be designed for manufacturing, warehousing and light industrial use. Construction is expected to begin this spring, with completion anticipated in early 2027. The project is being supported by a $2 million JobsOhio grant through the Ohio Site Inventory Program, along with $1 million from the All Ohio Future Fund to assist with site preparation and utilities. JobsOhio President and CEO J.P. Nauseef said the investment will help position Gallia County for future economic growth. "The Dan Evans Industrial Park is a vital driver of business expansion and job creation in Gallia County," Nauseef said. "Investing in the site alongside state and local partners empowers Southeast Ohio to further build on its manufacturing legacy, with new companies having the opportunity to quickly utilize an exceptional speculative building upon completion." Officials said the facility will be expandable up to 250,000 square feet and available for lease or purchase once completed. Patrick Saunders, president of the Community Improvement Corporation of Gallia County, said the building will serve as a key tool in attracting new industry. "By constructing this building, Gallia County will have a tremendous asset to attract additional industrial investment," Saunders said. "The CIC is focused on the betterment of Gallia County through economic development and this building will be a powerful tool to accomplish that objective." The Ohio Site Inventory Program was created to develop properties that are not currently being built by the private market but have proven demand and economic benefits. State officials say the program helps improve Ohio's ability to compete for new business investments and job creation opportunities. The Dan Evans Industrial Park is located less than one mile from U.S. 35 and within a day's drive of more than 60% of the U.S. population. Established in 1998, the park is home to multiple businesses and sits near major industrial investments across the Ohio Valley, including Nucor Steel's $4 billion sheet mill in Apple Grove, West Virginia. Gallia County Economic Development Director Taylor Stepp said the project addresses a longstanding gap in available industrial space. "For many years Gallia County has not possessed available square footage suitable to attract industrial investment," Stepp said. "This spec building will add much needed industrial inventory to land a new industrial park tenant, which will yield new jobs and investment for Gallia County. We are thankful for the investment that CIC of Gallia County, JobsOhio and the Ohio Department of Development have made into Gallia County." The Gallia County Commissioners supported the project through a Community Reinvestment Area tax abatement aimed at assisting with development and marketing efforts. "Bringing new, well-paying jobs to Gallia County is a top priority for the Commission and this project will help do just that," the commissioners said in a joint statement. "We look forward to supporting the eventual tenant of the spec building as they invest in Gallia County." Matt Abbott, president and CEO of Ohio Southeast Economic Development, said the project will help leverage the region's workforce. "This industrial park's location will allow access to our region's labor surplus and support continued growth in Gallia County," Abbott said. "We were pleased to work with the Gallia County Community Improvement Corporation and DEIP II to provide assistance for this spec building project." GALLIPOLIS, Ohio - The Gallia County Local School District Board of Education approved a wide range of administrative, financial and personnel items during its regular meeting on Monday, including the 2026-2027 school calendar, equipment purchases and multiple staffing changes. Board President Paula Whitt presided, joined by Vice President Beth James and members David Small and Larry Carter. Superintendent Phillip Kuhn and Treasurer Jack Webb were also in attendance. As part of the superintendent's report and general consent agenda, board members approved minutes from the Feb. 21 regular meeting, along with bills, payroll and financial statements. Donations were accepted and the 2026-2027 school calendar was adopted. The board also adopted a policy on misbranded foods and cultivated-protein food projects, waiving the first reading in order to comply with House Bill 10, which took effect March 20 and requires districts to implement a policy as soon as possible. A first reading was approved for policies addressing artificial intelligence and mandatory kindergarten entrance age, with final adoption scheduled for April. Members approved entering into a master service agreement with the Metropolitan Educational Technology Association beginning July 1 for the upcoming school year. The board also approved bids of $146,228 each for the purchase of two buses and a $69,229 bid for a 2025 Chevrolet Silverado 3500 with a utility bed. The superintendent was authorized to seek bids for asphalt surfacing and resurfacing at South Gallia High School and Southwestern Elementary, along with asphalt sealing and striping at Vinton Elementary, Hannan Trace Elementary, Southwestern Elementary and South Gallia High School. Board members approved a student trip for South Gallia High School College Credit Plus American history students to travel to Philadelphia from May 4-6. The trip will be conducted in partnership with the Gallia-Vinton Educational Service Center, with expenses covered by a grant and the service center. The 2026-2027 tax budget was approved as presented by the treasurer, along with a memorandum of understanding between Holzer Health Systems and the district for operation of the South Gallia Health Clinic. Under personnel actions, the board accepted resignations from Stephen Brown, teacher and head girls basketball coach at River Valley High School; Chris Hill, associate athletic director at River Valley High School; Jay Lambert, assistant varsity boys basketball coach at South Gallia High School; Mallory Massie, varsity volleyball coach at River Valley High School; and Corey Small, varsity girls basketball coach at South Gallia High School. Chris Hill was approved for employment as assistant principal and athletic director at River Valley Middle School on a two-year contract beginning Aug. 1, with salary and benefits set according to the administrative salary schedule. The board also approved Todd Boothe for a 60-month contract as director of technology and buildings and grounds beginning with the 2026-2027 school year, and Sandra Plantz for a 36-month contract as TAG/federal programs coordinator, both contingent upon proper certification and background checks. Supplemental positions were approved for the 2025-2026 school year, including Kaleb Taylor as junior varsity softball coach, Josh Fury as volunteer softball coach and Colton Bradley as volunteer baseball coach at River Valley High School, along with Ethan Lawler as head junior high track coach at South Gallia Middle School. Additional approvals included Chris McComas and Morgan Stanley as assistant varsity baseball coaches at South Gallia High School at half salary and Amanda Gilbert as assistant varsity softball coach. POINT PLEASANT, W.Va. - A 2005 Point Pleasant High School graduate has released a debut children's book inspired by a real-life rescue story involving her dog. Beth Nicole Hynes has authored "Where's Winnie?," which follows the journey of her 9-pound rescue dog that went missing for 21 days in the rural woods of Indiana before being found with the help of community members. Hynes said the experience highlighted for her the importance of kindness and support from others, themes reflected in the book, which is aimed at children ages 3 to 7. The release marks the first project under her brand, Bunny Tales, with plans to support animal rescue efforts through future initiatives. Hynes spoke this week on the remarkable story that inspired her book. The story began when Hynes, who now splits her time between Chicago and Puerto Rico with her husband and two children, was visiting her mother-in-law's summer home in LaPorte, Indiana. Winnie, a 9-pound "sato" - a term for Puerto Rican mixed-breed dogs - had been rescued by Hynes while she was pregnant. Known for being timid, Winnie's fear was triggered during a routine potty break, leading her to bolt into the surrounding woods. "She was terrified of everyone," Hynes said. "When dogs go missing, sometimes they just go into survival mode. They don't really listen to anyone, and she was scared of everyone anyway, except for me." Despite being a newcomer to the area, Hynes was met with an outpouring of support from the LaPorte community. A post on a local lost dog Facebook page was shared hundreds of times, keeping the search at the forefront of residents' minds. Community members helped post flyers, set humane traps and even brought in a scent-tracking dog. Others frequently stopped Hynes to offer tips and encouragement, with some even removing her search signs after Winnie was found so she would not have to worry about them. "No matter where you are, it's the people who show up for you that make all the difference," Hynes said. On the 21st day of the search, Hynes received the call she had been hoping for. A local resident found Winnie in his yard, though the dog was in rough condition. After being stabilized at a local veterinary clinic, Winnie was transferred to Purdue University's veterinary hospital, where she spent 10 days in intensive care. While Winnie suffered a permanent injury to one eye from burrs, she made a near-full recovery. The experience left a lasting impression on Hynes, who had vowed to write a book about the ordeal if Winnie was found. "Where's Winnie?" tells a gentler version of the story aimed at children. In the book, Winnie goes on an adventure, asking other animals if they have seen her owner, believing it is Hynes who is lost. The book concludes with the real-life story and photos of the actual Winnie. Hynes is already working on her next project, another dog-based story inspired by her now departed dog Huey, who received a "spirit award" at the Catholic school where her mother-in-law teaches, due to his popularity with the faculty and student body. The book will follow a day in Huey's life at the school, where he was a frequent visitor. Hynes began college at Marshall University after graduating from Point Pleasant in 2005. She later transferred to Ohio University because they offered a program more suited to her interests. During her time there, she met her future husband, who was originally from Chicago. She says her family still resides in the local area. "Where's Winnie?" features illustrations by Polya Bulba, an artist based in Serbia, and is available now for purchase on Amazon.

article_text: Quick take: The health system generated $16.8 billion in national economic activity in FY24 and supports one in every 14 jobs in West Virginia, underscoring its role as the state's largest private employer and a central economic engine. Billions in capital investments, including expansions at flagship and regional hospitals, have reduced patient outmigration by keeping advanced care and specialized services in-state. Created by the Legislature to protect local health care, WVU Medicine now spans 25 hospitals across four states while remaining West Virginia-based and focused on improving health outcomes and community stability statewide. MORGANTOWN, W.Va. - WVU Medicine generated $16.8 billion in total national economic activity during the 2024 fiscal year, supporting more than 56,000 jobs statewide and reinforcing its role as both West Virginia's largest private employer and a major driver of the state's economy, according to a newly released study. The report, conducted by consulting firm Tripp Umbach and released by West Virginia University, details the broad financial and employment impact of the WVU Medicine health system, which operates 25 hospitals across West Virginia, Maryland, Ohio and Pennsylvania and employs more than 35,000 people. Within West Virginia alone, WVU Medicine's economic footprint totaled $11.2 billion. That figure includes $7.1 billion in direct spending - such as payroll, medical supplies, capital construction and operating expenses - along with $4.1 billion in indirect and induced economic activity as those dollars circulated through local businesses and communities. WVU Medicine President and CEO Albert Wright said the report offers a snapshot of how effectively the health system is fulfilling its mission to improve health outcomes while serving as an economic engine for the state. "When you look at the report, it's just a snapshot in time of how effective we are at carrying out our health and teaching missions and whether we are making a positive impact on the state," Wright said. "It's awe-inspiring and very humbling to be part of an organization that is doing really good things for West Virginia." According to the study, WVU Medicine supports 56,224 jobs statewide, meaning one in every 14 jobs in West Virginia is either directly provided by the health system or supported through its supply chain and employee spending. Of those, 26,452 positions are direct WVU Medicine employees, while an additional 29,772 jobs are supported indirectly. Economic benefits are spread across the state through regional hubs, including Morgantown, Charleston, Beckley, the Eastern Panhandle, the Northern Panhandle and southern West Virginia. The Morgantown region alone accounted for $5.4 billion in economic impact and supported more than 26,500 jobs. Beyond employment, the report found WVU Medicine-related activity generated $686.5 million in state and local tax revenue during the fiscal year - approximately $1 out of every $8.32 collected by state and local governments. Wright said the system's growth strategy over the past decade has focused on expanding care at flagship facilities such as J.W. Ruby Memorial Hospital and WVU Medicine Children's while also building a statewide network designed to improve population health. "We've built a network of hospitals that covers the state from Bluefield and Parkersburg to Jefferson County and everywhere in between," Wright said. "That allows us to have a population health footprint to take care of our communities." The report also highlights significant capital investment by the health system. WVU Medicine has invested roughly $3 billion in capital projects over the past 10 years, with plans for an additional $3 billion over the next decade, according to Wright. Those investments include new towers, hospital expansions and upgraded facilities in multiple regions of the state. A key goal of those investments has been reducing patient outmigration by offering advanced care within West Virginia. The study credits developments such as the WVU Medicine Children's Hospital and expanded neuroscience and heart transplant programs with keeping patients - and health care dollars - in the state. Wright also pointed to the origins of WVU Medicine, which was created by an act of the state Legislature in 1986 amid concerns that out-of-state, for-profit hospital systems could reduce local investment. "I think the report shows how well we are executing on that original vision," Wright said. "We're making investments in health care that probably wouldn't be made if those decisions weren't being made right here in West Virginia."

article_text: Quick take: The West Virginia Legislature opens its 60-day session Wednesday, which will followed by Governor Morrisey's State of the State address Morrisey aims to cut and simplify the state personal income tax by 5-10%, expand child and dependent care credits, boost business bonus depreciation, and restructure historic and tourism tax credits The governor plans legislation to reduce out-of-state placements, create a revolving fund for new or renovated child welfare facilities, and address federal audit findings highlighting systemic gaps in foster care and adoption oversight. CHARLESTON, W.Va. - On Wednesday the West Virginia Legislature will convene for its 2026 regular session, kicking off a 60-day period of lawmaking and advocacy at the State Capitol. The session will adjourn at midnight on March 14. Mid-session deadlines include Feb. 17 for the final introduction of House bills and Feb. 23 for Senate bill introductions. To ensure all measures receive the required three readings before the session concludes, key committee and crossover deadlines include Feb. 2 for submission of legislative rule-making review bills, March 1 as the final day for bills to be reported out of committees in their house of origin, and March 4 for the last day to consider bills on a third reading in their house of origin, excluding budget or supplementary appropriation bills. Jan. 14 will also feature the annual State of the State address from Gov. Patrick Morrisey. The governor has said his budget proposal will include pay increases for teachers, school service personnel, members of the West Virginia State Police, correction officers, and other state employees on the state's payroll. "In my budget for next year, for Fiscal Year 2027, we will have a pay raise for state employees, period," Morrisey said. "That's going to include teachers; that's going to include school service personnel. That's going to include our hardworking State Police and so many of the people, the correction officers, who are working hard every day to make West Virginia a better place to live, to work and to play." Morrisey said the amount of the raises has not yet been set. "We're getting to the final stages of our budget that will be coming out during this State of the State," he said. "So as we get closer to that, we might have more color to add, and most assuredly, it'll be all public by the time of the State of the State. But I want to try to work collaboratively with our colleagues in the House and Senate." During the Legislature's interim meetings in December, Revenue Secretary Eric Nelson said the process of preparing the governor's budget proposal is well underway. "One thing that Gov. Morrisey has instilled in not only the budget team and revenue team, but all agencies, is to look for efficiencies," Nelson said. "How can we be structurally balanced, not just right now, but going forward?" Nelson said staff from both the House and Senate Finance committees were working with the Department of Revenue as final adjustments continued, and that the administration remained "cautiously optimistic" while focusing on keeping long-term spending in line with revenues as the Fiscal Year 2026 budget comes together. "We're in a good position," Nelson said, "but we always have a cautionary tone on our revenue front." Morrisey has also outlined a package of tax cuts and tax code changes he plans to pursue during the session, arguing that strong state revenues allow for broader relief while keeping the budget balanced. The governor said his top priority for the session is cutting and simplifying the state personal income tax to help residents cope with higher living costs and to keep West Virginia competitive with neighboring states that are also lowering taxes. "Our total general revenue collections are about 5% above estimate," Morrisey said. "That's about $120 million more than estimated. That means we can afford to do a tax cut." He said the administration is targeting an additional income tax reduction of at least 5% to 10%, though he emphasized final numbers would be negotiated with lawmakers. Morrisey said the proposal builds on earlier income tax reductions enacted in recent years and is aimed at rewarding work, putting more money back in residents' pockets and making the state more attractive to businesses and investors. "Cutting the income tax is probably the cleanest way to help all individuals in West Virginia afford everyday life," he said. The governor pointed to revenue trends as evidence the state can sustain additional tax cuts. Despite a nearly 6% income tax rate reduction last year, Morrisey said income tax collections are nearly flat this fiscal year, while consumer sales tax collections are up nearly 10%. He also cited actions by neighboring states, noting that Kentucky and Ohio are moving forward with income tax reductions in 2026. Morrisey said West Virginia must keep pace or do better to remain competitive. In addition to income tax cuts, Morrisey said his administration will seek to bring parts of West Virginia's tax code into closer conformity with recent federal tax changes. Those include expanding the child and dependent care tax credit by increasing the state match from 35% to 50%, and allowing businesses to fully expense qualified property by increasing bonus depreciation from 60% to 100%. Morrisey said the proposals would particularly benefit small businesses and encourage investment and expansion in the state. The governor also announced plans to restructure the state's Historic Rehabilitation Tax Credit by creating a single, unified section in the tax code. He said the current framework is fragmented and inconsistent, creating uncertainty for applicants and limiting the program's effectiveness as an economic development tool. The proposed changes, he said, would streamline approvals, improve predictability, and better align the credit with broader economic development goals. Another proposal would expand the Tourism Development Act tax credit, which Morrisey said has already attracted more than $390 million in investment since its creation, including $295 million over the past eight years. Under the plan, investors in tourism-related projects, particularly lodging and visitor infrastructure, could receive sales and use tax credits tied to growth generated by their developments. Morrisey said the plan would allow businesses to reinvest new tax revenue back into their projects without creating significant risk to the state. The governor said the tax proposals are part of a broader strategy focused on cutting red tape, streamlining permitting, and investing in infrastructure, including water, sewer, broadband, and health care. He said he has been in discussions with House and Senate leadership and is optimistic about reaching agreement. "I believe we can deliver meaningful tax relief without sacrificing essential services," he said. "If we're reducing taxes, cutting red tape and investing in infrastructure, West Virginia is going to be in a great place to win." Morrisey also announced plans to work with state lawmakers on a bill aimed at reducing out-of-state placements for children in West Virginia's child welfare system. The bill will be a step toward returning all West Virginia children in the system to the state, the governor said. "I'm not here to give you a date on that, but we want to do that," he said. "That needs to be our goal, and we need to be very aggressive about that." There were a total of 5,960 child welfare placements as of October, the most recent data available, according to information from the West Virginia Department of Human Services. Of those, kinship placements accounted for 48.6%, and the rate of out-of-state residential placements was 6.4%, or about 381 children. Morrisey said he also wants to establish a new, revolving investment fund that would be used to construct new state-owned child welfare facilities and to renovate and repair existing state facilities. "The goal is to take that revolving fund (and), as you put money in, to refurbish the facilities, and you bring people home. We think we can actually save money as a result, and then we can reinvest it back into the program, with the goal of eventually eliminating out-of-state placements," he said. Morrisey's plan followed West Virginia Department of Human Services Secretary Alex Mayer outlining an aggressive reform effort addressing deep-rooted issues in adoption, foster care, residential care, and case management. The initiative responds to a federal audit released last month that drew attention to longstanding structural problems in the state's child welfare system. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General found that 91% of screened-in child abuse and neglect reports during the audit period did not meet federal or state requirements. Key deficiencies included missing written notifications, delayed assessments, incomplete interviews, unnotified mandated reporters, inadequate safety plans, and incomplete risk assessments. Officials cited staff shortages, high caseloads, and inconsistent adherence to policies as contributing factors.

article_text: CLARKSBURG, W.Va. - Clarksburg Council on Thursday approved the city's Fiscal Year 2026-2027 budget and advanced an amended rental housing registration ordinance. Council also held the first reading of an ordinance that would permit cigar and smoking lounges within city limits. The budget includes $18,546,864 for the city's General Fund, $7,230,000 for the Sales and Use Tax Fund and $1,762,750 for the Robinson Grand Performing Arts Center. Council approved the budget following a public comment period during which no one spoke. Also Thursday, council approved on first reading an ordinance establishing a rental housing registration program, but not before first discussing the ordinance and approving two amendments proposed by council member Will Hyman. The ordinance would create a licensing, permitting, inspection and enforcement framework for rental properties citywide. Rental properties would be subject to inspection, with owners paying a $20 initial inspection fee. A $150 compliance fee would be assessed if violations are not corrected. The amendments proposed by Hyman would establish grace periods for landlords found to be in violation. Under the amendments, property owners would have 24 hours to correct life safety violations and seven days to correct standard violations outside of a defined winter season, Nov. 1 through March 31. Violations identified during the winter season would carry an extended correction timeline for seasonal repairs. "The goal of the amendment is to allow landlords and property owners to have a grace period before they're immediately given a $150 violation," Hyman said. Council members also flagged a desire to amend the ordinance, before its second reading, to require more frequent inspections of repeat violators rather than the standard two-year inspection cycle. Vice Mayor Jerry Riffle framed the ordinance as a long-overdue step. "We have a slumlord issue in this city. If you don't know it, you're not paying attention. And it's one of the biggest issues that we have," Riffle said. "I think I've been on council for almost four or five years now, and at this point I would say I failed on something that I promised everybody when I first ran - it was fixing the slumlord issue. This is the biggest step we've made." Council member Marc Jackson also spoke in favor of the ordinance. "This isn't an attack on landlords by any means, but this is a means to start to upgrade the standards by which the people in our city live," Jackson said. Council also approved on first reading an ordinance regulating cigar lounges, cigar bars and smoking lounges, establishing HVAC ventilation standards, licensing, permitting, inspection and enforcement requirements for them. Council's action follows a failed vote by the Harrison-Clarksburg Board of Health to adopt a variance that would permit cigar and smoking lounges under the 2010 Clean Indoor Air Act of the Harrison-Clarksburg Health Department. "So we brought it back up, and it's passed," Mayor Jim Malfregeot said. "You've got to understand, it's a very strict rule for a cigar bar. The ventilation has got to be top-notch, and whoever does that will have to follow regulations to the T, or it won't happen. And, you know, our vote among council in here passed 7-0. If you don't want to be near cigar smoking, then don't go." Council members also took time to congratulate the Robert C. Byrd High School swim teams on their state tournament performances. The boys team won the Division II state championship, and the girls team finished fifth among 14 competing teams. "To see a state champion, that's just amazing. That just gave me goosebumps," said council member Wayne Worth. Council began the meeting with a prayer and moment of silence for Landon Isaiah Jackson, a Clarksburg resident and United Technical Center student who passed away in a car wreck Wednesday. MORGANTOWN, W.Va. - Jerome Powell, chairman of the Federal Open Market Committee, which is the governing body of the Federal Reserve, announced Wednesday that the national bank would maintain interest rates for the second time this year. He also said he would stay in his post - even past his term's end - until a new successor is confirmed by Congress. Powell said he would not leave the board entirely until the investigation into his handling of renovations of the Fed's headquarters was "well and truly over." Powell's term as chair ends May 15, but his governorship does not expire until 2028. Still, traditionally, FOMC chairs have stepped down entirely from the board of governors once their term of leadership ends. "For many, many years, it has been the case that chairmen just stepped down ... from the board altogether when their chairmanship expires. But that hasn't been legally required, that's just been the tradition," West Virginia University economist John Deskins said, noting the tenures of past Fed Chairs Janet Yellen, Ben Bernanke, Alan Greenspan and Paul Volcker. Citing precedent in federal law, Powell said he would continue to serve as chair until lawmakers install his successor. In January, President Donald Trump announced he had picked former Fed Governor Kevin Warsh for the role, but the Senate has yet to schedule the start of the confirmation process, lending credence to concerns that the new chairman will not be formally recognized until after the end of Powell's term. In relation to the investigation, "[Powell's] saying, 'I'm going to break tradition because I want to see this investigation through to make sure that it is a legitimate investigation and that we have the opportunity to respond properly, and that nothing that's happened has been distorted through the investigation,'" Deskins said. Powell has asserted that the investigation into his handling of the Fed headquarters renovation was politically motivated, as Trump has pushed the chairman to cut interest rates, going so far as to verbally attack Powell for his decision not to do so. Deskins called the situation all-around "unprecedented," but said he was confident the chairman would not be breaking tradition "absent an investigation." "The political situation is so unusual right now that maybe it's reasonable for him to stay on until a new chairman is confirmed, because we don't know if Warsh is going to be confirmed or not, given the political fighting around the Fed," Deskins continued. Deskins decried recent politicization of the Fed, saying, "It's supposed to be independent of politics." "I think it's a scary time, because the Fed should be a stable force in the country and shouldn't be subject to political pressure," he said. "Politicization of the Fed is what's leading to these unprecedented times." A politicized central bank, Deskins said, is dangerous. This is because the Fed is supposed to make level-headed decisions that provide long-term benefits to the economy and keep inflation near the target rate, instead of allowing interest rates to be bent to political whims in order to increase the popularity of the party in power. Drastically cutting rates, as Trump has frequently asked for, would stimulate economic growth and job growth in the short run. But an increased rate of inflation would follow in the months to come. "There's a lag with inflation," Deskins explained. "Cut rates now, it will spur growth. ... But the inflation might not really be so bad until six months or a year later." The executive branch stimulating the economy through monetary policy prior to an election is "very common in third-world countries," Deskins said. And it "helps the executive stay in power. And then the pain - the inflation - doesn't happen until after the election is over." "This is exactly why economists have been arguing for independent central banks for decades. And this is exactly why literally every rich country in the world has an independent central bank," he said. Although Trump has signaled to the Fed governors and Powell time and time again that he has wanted drastic interest rate cuts, the board has instead enacted conservative fiscal policy. Deskins said this is preferable to the president's desires, even as Americans face significant inflationary pressures due to tariffs and higher gas prices because of oil tankers stranded in the Strait of Hormuz since the onset of the U.S. war against Iran. But Deskins noted that gasoline is not the only commodity that is set to see prices rise. Supply chain constraints on fertilizers, also due to the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, put strain on the agricultural sector and could cause food prices to increase beyond just the cost of fuel for transporting goods from producer to distributor. "If the Fed were to lower rates, that would do more to drive inflation," Deskins said, "... which would hurt struggling Americans more. So the Fed is worried about keeping inflation down, and ... the most important thing to help struggling families is to make sure that we don't have another surge in inflation like we had in 2022." Raising rates is a stronger way for the Fed to tamp down on inflationary pressures. But Deskins said he wouldn't expect the FOMC to consider such a move unless the war persists and inflation continues to rise over the longer term. "The Fed doesn't want to act rashly, so I wouldn't expect them to raise rates this soon," he said. CHARLESTON, W.Va. - West Virginia regulators have opened the door for local residents and county officials to challenge a proposed high-voltage transmission line cutting through the Eastern Panhandle and North Central regions of the state. The Public Service Commission of West Virginia issued an order Wednesday granting "intervenor status" to a broad coalition of local governments and grassroots organizers. The project, the MidAtlantic Resiliency Link, is a 500 kV interstate line proposed by NextEra Energy Transmission MidAtlantic. While the project spans multiple states, the PSC is currently weighing the "convenience and necessity" of the 58.9-mile segment slated for Monongalia, Preston, Mineral and Hampshire counties. The Preston County Commission has been among the most proactive local governments in opposing the project. Last week, commissioners unanimously approved a Petition for Leave to Intervene in the PSC case . That formally established the county as an official party in the proceedings. Preston Commission President Hunter Thomas said the status allows the commission to participate in hearings, submit testimony and evidence, cross-examine witnesses, and receive all filings and updates. He said the move is intended to advocate for the concerns and interests of county residents. Preston residents, including farmer and local activist Beth Ann Bassio, praised the commission's leadership and encouraged others to get involved. Bassio said intervention is critical due to potential impacts on property values and the county's tax base and warned that West Virginians could bear financial costs for a project that primarily serves out-of-state data centers. The Hampshire County Commission also secured a seat at the legal table, arguing that the project would traverse "scenic and historic resources" and could negatively affect the local tax base and quality of life. County officials emphasized their responsibility to oversee impacts on county-owned properties and emergency service coordination. Individual landowners are also banding together. The PSC granted intervention to West Virginians Against Transmission Injustice, a grassroots group representing residents and farmers across all four affected counties. WATI members allege the project poses a direct threat to property values, local environmental resources and ultimately electricity rates. A separate "Intervenor Group" of Hampshire County landowners was recognized specifically to challenge proposed routing corridors passing through or adjacent to their private property. The commission's order also imposed strict transparency requirements on NextEra. Following objections from PSC staff and the Consumer Advocate Division regarding public clarity, the company must now send notice via certified mail to every owner of surface real estate within the "preferred corridor" of the line. Regulators also mandated that NextEra use bold type in public notices to clearly direct residents to interactive project maps. The legal battle is expected to intensify over the coming months. The PSC has set a June 1 deadline for additional petitions to intervene. Formal evidentiary hearings are scheduled to begin in Charleston on October 26, with a final decision required by March 6, 2027. DUBAI, United Arab Emirates - Israel pounded Tehran with airstrikes Friday as Iranians marked Nowruz, or the Persian New Year, in the midst of a war that has sent shock waves through the global economy and risked drawing Iran's Arab neighbors directly into the conflict. Activists reported hearing strikes around Iran's capital. The attacks came a day after Israel pledged to refrain from more strikes on a key Iranian gas field and Iran intensified attacks on oil and natural gas facilities around the Gulf. Heavy explosions shook Dubai early Friday as air defenses intercepted incoming fire over the city, where people were observing Eid al-Fitr, the end of the holy Muslim fasting month of Ramadan, and mosques made the day's first call to prayers. Iran kept up its wave of attacks launched at Israel that have sent millions of people to shelters, with sirens sounding across a wide swath of the north, from Haifa to the Galilee to the border with Lebanon. It came after an intense day that saw more than a dozen missile launches on Thursday alone, according to Israel's military. Global fuel supplies have been under intense pressure because of Iran's stranglehold on the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway through which a fifth of the world's oil is transported. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Thursday that, at the request of President Donald Trump, Israel will hold off more attacks on Iran's South Pars gas field. Iranian strikes in retaliation have led to already elevated global energy prices further surging and spurred Gulf allies to call for Trump to rein in Netanyahu. Since the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Feb. 28, Iran's top leaders have been killed and the country's military capabilities have been severely degraded. Netanyahu said in a televised address that Iran no longer has the ability to enrich uranium or make ballistic missiles, although he did not provide evidence. Still, Iran - now led by the son of the supreme leader killed in the war's opening salvo - remains capable of missile and drone attacks. Brent crude oil, the international standard, briefly surged above $119 a barrel, up more than 60% since the war started. The European benchmark for natural gas prices also rose sharply and has roughly doubled in the past month. U.N. Security Council meets over Iran's attacks on Gulf states The United Nations Security Council held an urgent closed meeting Thursday during which Gulf countries stressed the need for Iran to halt attacks on them, said Bahrain's U.N. Ambassador Jamal Alrowaiei, the Arab representative on the U.N.'s most powerful body. But Iran has showed no signs of backing down. Saudi Arabia said its SAMREF refinery in the Red Sea port city of Yanbu was hit. Saudi Arabia had begun pumping large volumes of oil west toward the Red Sea to avoid the Strait of Hormuz. Qatar, a key source of natural gas for world markets, said Iranian missiles that caused extensive damage to the Ras Laffan liquefied natural gas facility, reduced its exports by about 17 percent and will cost about $20 billion in lost revenue a year. The damage will take up to five years to repair, even though production at the facility had already been halted after earlier attacks. Two oil refineries in Kuwait and gas operations in Abu Dhabi also were targeted by Iran, authorities said. Underscoring the danger to ships in the region, a vessel was set ablaze Thursday off the United Arab Emirates' coast and another was damaged off Qatar. Efforts to bypass the strait were also under pressure: An Iranian drone hit a Saudi refinery on the Red Sea, which the country had hoped to use as an alternative route. Meanwhile, the UAE said Friday it disrupted what it called "a terrorist network funded and operated by Lebanon's Hezbollah and Iran," arresting its operatives. It accused the men of laundering money while "operating within the country under a fictitious commercial cover" that sought to carry out schemes that would threaten the country's financial stability. It published images of five prisoners on its state-run WAM news agency, without identifying the men. Netanyahu says Iran's military has been severely hit At Thursday's news conference, Netanyahu said: "Iran's air defenses have been rendered useless, their navy is lying at the bottom of the sea. ... Their air force is nearly destroyed." He said he hopes the Iranian people will rise up against the Islamic Republic that has ruled for nearly a half-century. There's been no sign of any organized opposition since the war began, after Iranian authorities crushed mass protests in January. The prime minister's comments to foreign journalists came amid difficult days for Trump and Netanyahu, with a top U.S. intelligence official resigning and claiming Israel pushed Trump into the war, and Israel's attacks on South Pars, which led to Iran's retaliatory strikes on the region's oil and gas fields. "I misled no one," Netanyahu said. "And I didn't have to convince President Trump about the need to prevent Iran from developing its nuclear program." Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said that U.S. forces were attacking deeper into Iranian territory, with warplanes hunting Iranian boats in the strait and dropping 5,000-pound bombs on underground weapons-storage facilities. Trump says he is not deploying troops to Iran Iran condemned Israel's attack on South Pars, the Iranian part of the world's largest gas field, located offshore in the Persian Gulf and owned jointly with Qatar. With some 80% of power generated in Iran coming from natural gas, according to the International Energy Agency, the attack threatens the country's electricity supplies. After Trump requested Israel not attack South Pars, he also warned on social media that if Iran continued striking Qatar, the U.S. would "massively blow up the entirety" of the field. Asked later about the possibility of U.S. ground troops being deployed to Iran, Trump responded: "No. I'm not putting troops anywhere." Death toll climbs in third week of war More than 1,300 people in Iran have been killed during the war. Israeli strikes against the Iranian-backed Hezbollah militant group in Lebanon have displaced more than 1 million people, according to the Lebanese government, which says more than 1,000 people have been killed. Israel says it has killed more than 500 Hezbollah militants. In Israel, 15 people have been killed by Iranian missile fire. Four people were also killed in the occupied West Bank by an Iranian missile strike overnight. At least 13 U.S. military members have been killed. CLARKSBURG, W.Va. - After the White House released a new set of terms for fully funding the Department of Homeland Security, Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., expressed her frustration with the Democratic Party for rejecting the offer. "This is a dangerous situation," Capito said. "Chuck Schumer and his party are putting this country at risk by not funding the Coast Guard and not funding our TSA agents. "We know about 10% [of TSA agents] are beginning to walk off the job. It's spring break. It's Easter. Lots of families are traveling. You see photos of Austin, Texas, or Dallas where the security lines are out of the door. We're lucky in West Virginia, where we have smaller airports and so far it's been containable. "Actually, in talking with some of our airports, they're beginning to see TSA agents that can't fulfill their obligations or won't fulfill their obligations if they're not getting paid over 34 days." The DHS comprises many agencies beyond TSA, including the Coast Guard, Federal Emergency Management Agency, and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the agency at the center of the funding disagreement. After ICE came under fire for violent arrests and two separate shootings of U.S. citizens, Congress failed to reach an agreement on funding DHS after Democrats set terms seeking to reform ICE. Funding lapsed and has left the department without funds since Feb. 13. "This is going to start to impact us more locally," Capito said. "I'm very concerned about the overall abilities for cybersecurity, for some investigations that go on in terms of violent crime and drugs. Pick up the phone and call your senators, particularly Democratic senators, and say, 'Reach a compromise.' "[Democrats] asked for a compromise from the president on ICE. They got a compromise of more funding for cameras, more inspector general reports, more identification so that you can see who the agent is. These are things that the Democrats have been asking for, so I don't know why they just won't take it." One ask that the president did not fulfill in his offer is banning face coverings for ICE agents, a major point of contention. Capito believes the Democratic Party is refusing to cooperate in an effort to defund law enforcement as a whole. "When they defund ICE, they're also defunding the investigative part of ICE that looks at tracing not just illegals, but illegal shipments of drugs and other things," she said. "This is a critical part of our national security. "Think about West Virginia and FEMA. If we don't have a fully functioning FEMA, think of all the times we've had to access FEMA because of emergencies, and there again we're harming American citizens." CLARKSBURG, W.Va. - North Central West Virginia Airport is in the midst of recruiting a new airline to provide flights to Charlotte, North Carolina, as the airport is set to lose its current service in mid-April. Beginning April 14, the airport will provide flights to Chicago and Washington, D.C., via SkyWest Airlines - and no longer to Charlotte. But Airport Director Rick Rock is hopeful the airport can soon restore trips to North Carolina. "We know that our community likes the Charlotte service," Rock said. "[So] I'm trying to add back in Charlotte, which we're losing April 13." CKB has offered flights to Charlotte for a little more than three years via Contour Airlines after its original Essential Air Service (EAS) contract with SkyWest was canceled in 2022, and the airport came to be serviced by Contour at the end of that year. The airport's new contract with SkyWest is set to last four years, through 2030. But CKB will now offer the same flights as Morgantown Municipal Airport. "To us, that didn't make any sense for a lot of reasons," Rock said, noting the proximity of the two airports offering identical services. Airports can provide recommendations on which provider they would like the U.S. Department of Transportation to subsidize under Essential Air Service contracts, but the decision ultimately lies with the DOT. "We recruited five or six bidders to bid on our service," Rock said, noting that the airport had recommended American Airlines. But "the DOT, in its infinite wisdom," Rock said, chose to reinstate its contract with SkyWest, which had canceled its contract to serve CKB, along with dozens of other airports, in 2022 due to a pilot shortage. American Airlines had bid $5.7 million to continue the Chicago and Charlotte flights, Rock said. But SkyWest, which also operates in Morgantown, "came in and underbid [at] $4.7 million." Due to the DOT emphasizing low-cost EAS contracts, SkyWest was ultimately chosen, Rock said. Rock said he is hopeful CKB can work out a similar contract with an airline, as Yeager International Airport did to secure a contract with Breeze Airways. "We want Charlotte. We made that very clear that it's something that we were interested in as an airport, as a community. So we're out trying to find the best person to provide that service," Rock said. Securing a contract, however, has hurdles, including providing an airline with either a minimum revenue guarantee or some kind of subsidy. "If you look at how Yeager got Breeze Airways flights out there - basically [there] was a deal with [the West Virginia Department of] Tourism putting up some money towards it," Rock said. While there is "an interested airline willing to" provide Charlotte flights for CKB, Rock said, details of a deal are still in the works. "For a small airport to have multiple airlines like this, it creates a huge opportunity for your tourism, and it's something that we're lucky we were able to put together. We'd love to see it happen [here], but we've got to continue to seek partners to make it happen," Rock said. In other airport news, CKB is seeking donations of $10-$20 gift cards for Transportation Security Administration agents, who have been impacted by a lapse in federal funding to the Department of Homeland Security that has withheld their pay for more than a month. Because TSA agents cannot accept donations during screening operations or at the checkpoint, gift cards may be dropped off at CKB's administrative offices during normal business hours. Potential donors should note that cash and Visa gift cards cannot be accepted. During her Thursday press call, Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., decried the funding lapse at DHS and called the situation "dangerous." "We know that about 10% [of TSA agents] are beginning to walk off the job," she said. Capito called West Virginia "lucky" for having smaller airports, citing images of lines of travelers stretching out the doors at larger airports. But Capito said the situation - if not soon resolved - could begin to impact the local region as well.
