article_text: There are signs that commercial real estate activity is picking up following the long-tail disruption of the pandemic. Projects of all sizes are either restarting or starting a new and are making their way toward reshaping the area's commercial landscape. Buffalo Business First Publisher John Tebeau invited industry experts to discuss the status and future of commercial real estate in the Buffalo region. Joining Tebeau were: NOTABLE PROJECTS The new Trico Building Apartments project hits the city's needs on several fronts, Daly said. It preserved the historic architecture of the former windshield wiper plant while creating a mixed-use facility complex with 242 residential apartments and commercial space in the former brownfield site. Most importantly, it is bringing critical mass that is attractive to restaurants, stores and services, he said. The opportunity can only expand considering that the Trico complex, at 628 Ellicott St., is adjacent to the Buffalo Niagara Medical Campus. "The medical industry is not remote. They are all there. So there is a great opportunity on the medical campus that downtown does not have," Daly said. "Downtown needs to create those districts. They need to get that critical mass." Another project with similar potential is the planned conversion of the Bank of America building at 10 Fountain Plaza into 160 apartments, Daly said. "That is going to be interesting to see how that converts to residential," he said. "But you need big projects or a whole bunch of small ones in the area." Uniland, Hill said, is continuing its search for industrial sites to develop following its successes at the 230-acre Renaissance Commerce Park, the former location of the Bethlehem Steel Plant. The company also is working on converting the office building at 285 Delaware Ave. to accommodate the D'Youville University's College of Osteopathic Medicine. "Adding medical facilities and services to that building is probably going to be one of our largest projects over the next two to three years, and that is going to be transformational," Hill said. Carman applauded the developers for their thoughtful approach to their projects. "People are willing to reinvent their properties," he said. "Would you rather be in desperation mode and just try to fill the building with whatever rent you can get or reinvent yourself and enhance it and have something that you are going to have for a long time? I think that is where a lot of people's mindsets have advanced to." TENANT REQUIREMENTS Building that desired critical mass will be assisted by M&T and other like-minded businesses that are requiring once fully remote employees to return to their usual downtown offices for three or four days a week. Some companies that downsized their offices during the pandemic are expanding their workspaces to accommodate returning employees. During the past two years, the work has become more office-centric, but that does not mean a ricochet to traditional office spaces and functions, however. The traditional office operation is not functional in today's business environment, Hill said. "There have been some significant reductions in office space requirements for companies, because they are not looking to occupy as many square feet for the same number of people because they are not looking to have those people in the office as often," he said. "That becomes a challenge, reconfiguring their spaces, coming up for renewals, renegotiation and extensions, looking at those footprints and those layouts, and reconfiguring space so they can accommodate the number of people they expect within that office at any one point in time." Tenants are also asking for modernization of existing spaces and development with more open areas and buildings that provide for the hoteling format, which relies on shared offices and meeting areas. Hill said a recent client he has worked with has just two dedicated offices while using hoteling to accommodate the rest of the 800 employees. Creating those open spaces is not an inexpensive process. People want the open-ceiling, industrial look of older buildings, but achieving it is not a simple matter of removing dropped ceilings. Those tiles typically have been hiding years-old abandoned cables, wiring and ductwork that is not conducive for use in an office setting. Such conversions are a redevelopment challenge, particularly in the downtown area, Hill said. Uniland also has been converting suburban office space into mixed-use buildings for clients who want to relocate from downtown because staff no longer want the commute or to occupy urban buildings. Hill said businesses that downsized their office space during the pandemic might find that the return-to-work environment requires some expansion. One Uniland client went from about 1.2 headcount per space to 1.9 per space, he said. "Now, they do not need to double their space, but they do need to increase their space, so it becomes a challenge," Hill said. "Tenant improvements have skyrocketed because of the cost of labor and materials in the past three years. The cost has gone up exponentially, and clients do not want to spend their money to build out their space for their needs. They want the landlord to do it on their nickel. That is probably the biggest hurdle." Reconfiguring office space to meet the current demands might be worth the expense, Carman said. "It is unique and it is costly, but if you have an office that is occupied, the expense is probably worth it," he said. COST TRENDS The rent ceiling is a major concern to operators and lenders alike, Carman said. "Everybody is concerned about what is going to happen when the rate resets because there is a ceiling with rents," he said. "If the rate goes up too much, there is going to be a problem. A lot of people are trying to conceive where they can save money." Residential and office projects that had been sidelined are beginning to pencil out as rates improve. Conversion of buildings into multi-family units has been trending, but Carman is hopeful new construction will be on the horizon as well. "In Western New York tax credits are still utilized to make projects work and be viable. People are willing to stay for those five years, which is great," he said. Rising energy costs could offset the best laid money-saving plans, however. Daly said he and others who were proponents of sustainable design are rethinking that mindset with the rising energy costs. He predicts pushback on the state's initiatives as the cost to heat and cool buildings dramatically increases. Everyone has seen rates that were three times what they were last year, though consumption was the same, he said. "A lot of people went to these new energy-efficient heat pumps and that made sense. They could heat and cool space and it is cheaper than doing it with gas. With where the rates have gone now, it is not," Daly said. "The New York Clean Heat program made sense with the rates that we had last year. They do not make sense with the rates this year." He called on Gov. Kathy Hochul to push rates down to last year's levels, because the incentives are not worth it at the current rates. "It is just one more thing to look at when you are doing your pro forma and you are estimating what your operating costs are going to be and where your rents are going to be," Daly said. LABOR ISSUES Every contractor points to the labor shortage as a significant driver of project costs, Daly said. To counter that, Uniland has turned to pre-engineered or pre-constructed systems or materials, which are more expensive but are easier to assemble in the field. "That is really driving a lot of our decisions because contractors really do not have the labor," Daly said. Many say the labor shortage will end when the new football stadium is completed and workers filter back into the market, but Daly does not agree. "That shift would help it, but from what I have heard most of them are behind on other projects, so they are going to jump to those projects," he said. "I do not think you are going to see this big labor pool that is going to help bring any kind of cost down at all or help get things done faster." COLLABORATION Collaboration between developers and stakeholders seems to be improving toward strengthening the commercial real estate landscape, though the panelists believe more can only enhance commercial ventures. "I have always been really happy with the way the city has tried to collaborate and facilitate, getting lane closures and things like that," Daly said. "But the city has to be more creative and become an even bigger partner in facilitating projects," especially given the city's aging infrastructure. For example, he said, "Before you tie into a sewer, you have to scope out that sewer and make sure it is good all the way out to the street. If that sewer tie-in is broken, it is the development project's responsibility to fix that. Maybe that becomes a city infrastructure problem." Hill added that converting an office building into a mixed-use residential development puts extra strain on utilities, a situation that creates an opportunity for utility providers to collaborate with developers, "instead of looking at it as an opportunity to charge additional fees and rates." Working with the city and other partners to find parking locations during construction and for the development, is key, Hill said. "To bring in residentials or to convert a building into a mixed-use development, you need to have parking infrastructure capacity for those residents," he said. "Trying to lease or sell spaces to individuals without parking capacity is very difficult and that degrades the prices and rates you can get, which then impacts the loan that you are going to get for the construction or the permanent financing on that property." Carman agreed. He said parking increasingly has become a linchpin in financing major projects, not just in Buffalo or Western New York. "It is everywhere," he said. "Conversion is happening in all cities and urban areas and if they do not get on the same page and talk and think about the benefits, the economics and sustainability, it could ruin projects. Collaboration has to be there." POLICY CHANGES In addition to greater collaboration, the panelists would like further change in the city's policies that recognize the difficult market conditions in which developers are operating. One is property tax abatement, Daly said. The city begins phasing out the property tax abatement at year eight and ends it at year 12. That timeline might not be favorable for a mixed-use building required to have 15% commercial space. It takes time to find those tenants in a market with much available space downtown, and time without a commercial tenant is lost time in the abatement period, Daly said. He would like the policy to change so that the abatement clock begins when the commercial space is rented. For Hill, the slow permitting and review process is the biggest detractor to getting a project moving forward. It can take from 30 to 180 days to get a project reviewed and permitted depending on the municipality, which adds time to the client's time frame and could put them in jeopardy with their current location. "I would like to see an expedited review process in all municipalities to make it simpler and easier, not to short come any of the safety or design components of the project, but there has to be a better way," Hill said. It is operational policy overall that needs to change, Carman said. "It is not what is specifically on the books as the law. It is really - How do we operate more efficiently? How do you get things done the fastest?" he said. "That is really the issue."

Carman applauded the developers for their thoughtful approach to their projects. "People are willing to reinvent their properties," he said. "Would you rather be in desperation mode and just try to fill the building with whatever rent you can get or reinvent yourself and enhance it and have something that you are going to have for a long time? I think that is where a lot of people's mindsets have advanced to." TENANT REQUIREMENTS Building that desired critical mass will be assisted by M&T and other like-minded businesses that are requiring once fully remote employees to return to their usual downtown offices for three or four days a week. Some companies that downsized their offices during the pandemic are expanding their workspaces to accommodate returning employees. During the past two years, the work has become more office-centric, but that does not mean a ricochet to traditional office spaces and functions, however. The traditional office operation is not functional in today's business environment, Hill said. "There have been some significant reductions in office space requirements for companies, because they are not looking to occupy as many square feet for the same number of people because they are not looking to have those people in the office as often," he said. "That becomes a challenge, reconfiguring their spaces, coming up for renewals, renegotiation and extensions, looking at those footprints and those layouts, and reconfiguring space so they can accommodate the number of people they expect within that office at any one point in time." Tenants are also asking for modernization of existing spaces and development with more open areas and buildings that provide for the hoteling format, which relies on shared offices and meeting areas. Hill said a recent client he has worked with has just two dedicated offices while using hoteling to accommodate the rest of the 800 employees. Creating those open spaces is not an inexpensive process. People want the open-ceiling, industrial look of older buildings, but achieving it is not a simple matter of removing dropped ceilings. Those tiles typically have been hiding years-old abandoned cables, wiring and ductwork that is not conducive for use in an office setting. Such conversions are a redevelopment challenge, particularly in the downtown area, Hill said. Uniland also has been converting suburban office space into mixed-use buildings for clients who want to relocate from downtown because staff no longer want the commute or to occupy urban buildings. Hill said businesses that downsized their office space during the pandemic might find that the return-to-work environment requires some expansion. One Uniland client went from about 1.2 headcount per space to 1.9 per space, he said. "Now, they do not need to double their space, but they do need to increase their space, so it becomes a challenge," Hill said. "Tenant improvements have skyrocketed because of the cost of labor and materials in the past three years. The cost has gone up exponentially, and clients do not want to spend their money to build out their space for their needs. They want the landlord to do it on their nickel. That is probably the biggest hurdle." Reconfiguring office space to meet the current demands might be worth the expense, Carman said. "It is unique and it is costly, but if you have an office that is occupied, the expense is probably worth it," he said. COST TRENDS The rent ceiling is a major concern to operators and lenders alike, Carman said. "Everybody is concerned about what is going to happen when the rate resets because there is a ceiling with rents," he said. "If the rate goes up too much, there is going to be a problem. A lot of people are trying to conceive where they can save money." Residential and office projects that had been sidelined are beginning to pencil out as rates improve. Conversion of buildings into multi-family units has been trending, but Carman is hopeful new construction will be on the horizon as well. "In Western New York tax credits are still utilized to make projects work and be viable. People are willing to stay for those five years, which is great," he said. Rising energy costs could offset the best laid money-saving plans, however. Daly said he and others who were proponents of sustainable design are rethinking that mindset with the rising energy costs. He predicts pushback on the state's initiatives as the cost to heat and cool buildings dramatically increases. Everyone has seen rates that were three times what they were last year, though consumption was the same, he said. "A lot of people went to these new energy-efficient heat pumps and that made sense. They could heat and cool space and it is cheaper than doing it with gas. With where the rates have gone now, it is not," Daly said. "The New York Clean Heat program made sense with the rates that we had last year. They do not make sense with the rates this year." He called on Gov. Kathy Hochul to push rates down to last year's levels, because the incentives are not worth it at the current rates. "It is just one more thing to look at when you are doing your pro forma and you are estimating what your operating costs are going to be and where your rents are going to be," Daly said. LABOR ISSUES Every contractor points to the labor shortage as a significant driver of project costs, Daly said. To counter that, Uniland has turned to pre-engineered or pre-constructed systems or materials, which are more expensive but are easier to assemble in the field. "That is really driving a lot of our decisions because contractors really do not have the labor," Daly said. Many say the labor shortage will end when the new football stadium is completed and workers filter back into the market, but Daly does not agree. "That shift would help it, but from what I have heard most of them are behind on other projects, so they are going to jump to those projects," he said. "I do not think you are going to see this big labor pool that is going to help bring any kind of cost down at all or help get things done faster." COLLABORATION Collaboration between developers and stakeholders seems to be improving toward strengthening the commercial real estate landscape, though the panelists believe more can only enhance commercial ventures. "I have always been really happy with the way the city has tried to collaborate and facilitate, getting lane closures and things like that," Daly said. "But the city has to be more creative and become an even bigger partner in facilitating projects," especially given the city's aging infrastructure. For example, he said, "Before you tie into a sewer, you have to scope out that sewer and make sure it is good all the way out to the street. If that sewer tie-in is broken, it is the development project's responsibility to fix that. Maybe that becomes a city infrastructure problem." Hill added that converting an office building into a mixed-use residential development puts extra strain on utilities, a situation that creates an opportunity for utility providers to collaborate with developers, "instead of looking at it as an opportunity to charge additional fees and rates." Working with the city and other partners to find parking locations during construction and for the development, is key, Hill said. "To bring in residentials or to convert a building into a mixed-use development, you need to have parking infrastructure capacity for those residents," he said. "Trying to lease or sell spaces to individuals without parking capacity is very difficult and that degrades the prices and rates you can get, which then impacts the loan that you are going to get for the construction or the permanent financing on that property." Carman agreed. He said parking increasingly has become a linchpin in financing major projects, not just in Buffalo or Western New York. "It is everywhere," he said. "Conversion is happening in all cities and urban areas and if they do not get on the same page and talk and think about the benefits, the economics and sustainability, it could ruin projects. Collaboration has to be there." POLICY CHANGES In addition to greater collaboration, the panelists would like further change in the city's policies that recognize the difficult market conditions in which developers are operating. One is property tax abatement, Daly said. The city begins phasing out the property tax abatement at year eight and ends it at year 12. That timeline might not be favorable for a mixed-use building required to have 15% commercial space. It takes time to find those tenants in a market with much available space downtown, and time without a commercial tenant is lost time in the abatement period, Daly said. He would like the policy to change so that the abatement clock begins when the commercial space is rented. For Hill, the slow permitting and review process is the biggest detractor to getting a project moving forward. It can take from 30 to 180 days to get a project reviewed and permitted depending on the municipality, which adds time to the client's time frame and could put them in jeopardy with their current location. "I would like to see an expedited review process in all municipalities to make it simpler and easier, not to short come any of the safety or design components of the project, but there has to be a better way," Hill said. It is operational policy overall that needs to change, Carman said. "It is not what is specifically on the books as the law. It is really - How do we operate more efficiently? How do you get things done the fastest?" he said. "That is really the issue."

article_text: The data center construction revolution shows no signs of slowing down as the age of artificial intelligence ushers in even greater demand for computing power. The latest projections show that Arizona's current data center capacity is expected to double due to the number of data center projects on the books. The Business Journal spoke to top executives with Clune Construction and Wolverine Builders Commercial Construction to see where the industry is headed next. The Phoenix metro is home to 154 data centers, one of the biggest concentrations in the country. How much more runway exists to increase those numbers? Luke Plzak, Wolverine Builders: While 154 data centers sound like a large number, the market is really measured in watts - those 154 data centers currently represent about 2.7 gigawatts of capacity. We are fortunate to be living in the nation's #2 market for planned development with over 4 gigawatts currently under construction or in planning. With 2026 projects already 90% pre-leased and a vacancy rate of just 3%, the runway is laid out; it is now up to us to execute in a way that maximizes the upside for all of Arizona. Adam Wojack (Clune Construction): Phoenix still has significant runway for growth. The fundamentals that brought the industry there in the first place remain strong: land availability, relatively predictable permitting, strong fiber connectivity and proximity to major West Coast markets without the same seismic risk or coastal constraints. What we're seeing nationally is that demand for digital infrastructure continues to accelerate, largely driven by cloud computing and AI workloads. That demand doesn't show signs of slowing, but the pace of new development will increasingly be dictated by access to power rather than land. Phoenix has been proactive in planning for this growth, but like many major data center markets, future expansion will require thoughtful coordination between utilities, municipalities and developers. Markets that can reliably deliver power and infrastructure will continue to see investment. What has changed in the construction process for data centers, especially with power and cooling requirements? Adam: The biggest change in recent years has been the scale and density of equipment. That has direct implications for both power delivery and cooling strategies. From a construction standpoint, projects require larger electrical infrastructure, more robust power distribution and increasingly sophisticated (and efficient) cooling systems. We're also seeing much tighter integration between mechanical, electrical and structural systems because these facilities are designed to operate at extremely high loads from day one. Speed has probably become the most critical for our clients. Owner/operators want capacity online faster than ever before, which means builders need to plan procurement earlier, coordinate closely with utilities and structure projects in ways that allow certain systems to be installed or commissioned in parallel. The construction process has become more collaborative as a result. Luke: A data center's size is measured in terms of power; modern builds are now as much 'power plant' projects as they are data projects. Whether through solar, battery storage, or natural gas turbines, adapting to the unique code requirements of each medium is essential. The second largest and equally essential part of the data center build out is the cooling process. Obviously, data centers are at the center of the tech world, which means technology advances quickly. In a short time, we have seen the progression from air cooled racks, that required maintaining a very cold ambient temperature in the data center, to closed loop cooling where the heat transfer happens at the chip. Combining the speed of technological change with the need of speed to market means being able to forecast and leverage supply chain resources is essential in being a partner in these projects. What are your companies seeing from overall construction costs related to aluminum and steel for data center construction, and how comfortable are you with the current construction labor pool? Luke: The kickoff to the 2020s has been quite the lesson in supply chain costs and volatility. We have progressed through the Covid era, where supply chains were clogged and prices spiked, followed by another price spike in mid-2025 as a direct result of the 50% tariff on imported steel. While pricing stabilized briefly in late 2025, prices began a "step-up" climb in Q1 2026. We're in a unique cycle where the industry is its own biggest headwind. As the leading sector for non-residential construction, data centers are now driving metal prices rather than reacting to them. In Arizona, we've seen a 50% jump in cost-per-square-foot over two years. I tell my clients: 'waiting for prices to drop' is no longer a viable strategy. AI demand has set a new floor. Regarding labor, 1 in 5 construction workers in Arizona is over 55. We are losing institutional knowledge faster than the pipeline can replace it. We aren't just looking for more workers; we're looking for efficiency. The winners in this market will be those who use better tech and modular workflows to allow one skilled technician to do the work of 1.5 people. Adam: Material costs have stabilized mostly but procurement strategy still matters a lot. What we're seeing across the country is that early coordination with suppliers and long-lead equipment manufacturers has become essential. Successful projects are locking in procurement timelines early and maintaining flexibility where possible. On the labor side, data center construction requires a highly specialized workforce, particularly among electrical and mechanical trades. Phoenix has benefited from a growing pool of experienced workers as more projects have been built in the region, but demand remains high nationwide. Builders who invest in long-term trade partnerships and workforce development are in the best position to keep projects moving efficiently. Many cities in the Valley have shifted their attitudes about data centers and some have changed zoning laws to make sure data centers stay clear of neighborhoods. There is also resistance from some neighborhood groups regarding data centers and some pressure on cities to reduce incentives for data center developments in some cases. How do you think this will play out? Adam: As data centers become more visible, it's natural that communities and policymakers are asking more questions about how these projects fit into their long-term plans. We're seeing that conversation happen in many parts of the country as digital infrastructure becomes a larger part of the built environment. In our experience, the projects that move forward most successfully are the ones that engage with the community early. At Clune, we work with developers, local officials and neighbors before and during construction to explain what's being built, how it operates and what it means for the local economy. That kind of transparency goes a long way in building trust. We're also starting to see more policy frameworks that emerge to address community concerns directly. For example, agreements designed to protect ratepayers and ensure large energy users contribute appropriately to new infrastructure are becoming part of the conversation in several markets. Those kinds of approaches help communities feel confident that growth in digital infrastructure is happening responsibly. Data centers support the infrastructure behind nearly every digital service people rely on today, but communities understandably want to know how projects affect power infrastructure, land use and quality of life. When developers (and their builders) take the time to communicate clearly, listen to concerns and stay engaged throughout the process, these projects can become long-term economic assets while still respecting local priorities. Luke: Pushback to development is nothing new, especially large-scale development. The ecosystem of profit driven development and "NIMBY" concerns has pushed opposing sides to help generate win-wins that make our communities stronger. I've recently heard a new term for the most ardent opposition: BANANAs (Build Absolutely Nothing Anywhere Near Anyone). I believe there are two paths forward to mediate the need to grow the data center market in Arizona and ease the fears of Arizonans. First, data travels at the speed of light-building in remote areas is viable by extending the power and fiber infrastructure. Second, for sites that require proximity to population centers, we must engage the community early to fill knowledge gaps and show how these projects provide a personal, positive impact. A few quick examples would include better power infrastructure paid for by these projects, which results in attracting businesses that provide jobs and services. Data centers don't employ many people, wouldn't a better economic development case be to use this space for rooftops, manufacturing, and/or consumer services? Luke: We often hear about the concern related to job counts, while our focus should be about the tax-to-service ratio. A data center doesn't put 500 cars on the road at rush hour, doesn't add 200 children to an overcrowded school district, and doesn't require massive police or fire presence. Yet a single large campus can generate $10M-$40M in taxes annually. That is pure revenue for Arizona schools and first responders with almost zero strain on local services. When we talk about data centers, we aren't just talking about 'Big Tech', we're talking about the infrastructure that makes 2026 possible. Every telehealth appointment in rural AZ, every AI tool used by our local schools, and every digital transaction made by a small business in Mesa depends on this physical backbone. Arizona has become a global leader because we have the land, talent, and stability that few other states can match. We're seeing a massive shift toward 'behind-the-meter' power- solar/battery and even on-site generation. Are we moving toward a future where a 'successful' data center project in Arizona is defined less by its grid connectivity and more by its ability to operate as a self-contained microgrid? Luke: We haven't seen an exponential jump in power demand like is currently occurring in a lifetime and it is prudent for Arizonan's to not want to carry the personal burden of funding the power upgrades associated with the explosion in demand. In February of this year the Arizona House passed HB2756, this bill is the state's direct response to public anger over rising utility bills. It fundamentally changes the "contract" between data centers and the grid. The bill requires the Arizona Corporation Commission to ensure that the costs of new grid infrastructure (substations, transmission lines) are paid for entirely by the data centers themselves, rather than being "socialized" across the bills of residential customers. This is leading to projects evaluating the speed, cost and responsibility of that upgrade, and many are exploring the best solution for on-site power generation. As this shift is happening it is important as contractors that our expertise extends to building power plants as wells as building the data halls themselves. Public perception is now connecting data centers to the Urban Heat Island effect-whether that's scientifically nuanced or not. How should this industry change its approach to site selection and architectural design to prove we aren't just 'heating up' our local neighborhoods? Luke: A word that is constantly surrounding data centers is speed - we've seen this industry move forward at an exceptional pace. When things move quickly it is normal that questions can arise quicker than answers and solutions. The concerns that arise help drive innovation to ensure we steward our state correctly. Preliminary 2026 research suggests that a large data center campus can warm the immediate surrounding neighborhood by several degrees during the summer months. We have to be honest: if you put a 500,000-square-foot concrete box in the desert, it's going to hold heat. However, the 2026 approach is about thermal resilience. By using high-albedo materials that reflect solar radiation and moving toward liquid-cooling systems that capture heat more efficiently, we are creating facilities that have a smaller thermal footprint than the massive asphalt parking lots of the shopping centers around the valley. Our goal as contractors and developers in this space, is to ensure the neighborhood doesn't feel the building's presence after the sun goes down. Arizona has a record number of construction jobs, yet we still face a 20,000-worker deficit for megaprojects. How are we using technology, such as AI-driven estimating and modular 'off-site' pre-fabrication, to maintain project timelines without overstretching the local trade pool? Adam: Innovation is a core value at Clune, and we're constantly looking for ways to make our teams more efficient without compromising quality. We're leveraging AI-assisted tools where it makes sense, especially on highly repetitive scopes where we can drive speed and consistency. That said, no technology replaces experienced people. To support Phoenix's rapid growth, we're sourcing from local talent, Clune offices nationwide, and are also offering relocation to those looking for new opportunities and bringing in experienced travelers who are on-site during the week and home on weekends. That national flexibility allows us to deliver for our clients without putting unsustainable pressure on the local workforce. Luke: As mentioned before, 1 in 5 Arizonans in construction are over the age of 55. Arizona is on track to nearly triple our total data capacity by 2031. These two data points indicate a need to increase efficiency in the short term and training in the long term. We are currently working with groups that are focusing on modular buildings for their projects. In-house we are leveraging the very tools these data centers help provide, to increase our supply chain management and operational capacity to more accurately manage schedules and timing to limit the hidden inefficiencies in projects. How is your company engaging with communities as data center development grows more visible and sometimes more controversial? Luke: Conflicting information about data centers and what to do about them are being discussed from the local coffee shop to the halls of congress. As a contractor, our reach to the community isn't large but by partnering with local city economic development teams and chambers of commerce we can amplify the message that data centers aren't just windowless boxes. In reality, these data centers are the most important pieces of physical infrastructure Arizona will build this decade. They are the backbone of our schools, our healthcare, and our economy. Our challenge as developers and contractors isn't just to build them fast, it's to build them right. That means moving toward water-neutral systems and behind-the-meter energy solutions that don't just take from the grid but help modernize it. Our company goal is to ensure that when we look back at this 'boom' in ten years, we see an Arizona that is more resilient, more tech-forward, and where growth didn't just happen to our communities, but for them. Adam: In many markets, we're working directly with municipalities to build long-term, trust-based relationships. That means showing up early, being transparent, and staying engaged after construction is complete. We've participated in town halls to help educate the public on what a data center actually brings to their area, from jobs to infrastructure investment. We've also partnered on local job fairs, supported trade education programs, and even contributed to community efforts like road adoption and beautification. At the end of the day, we're not just building for our clients but we're building in someone's backyard. We take that seriously and strive to be the kind of partner cities want to work with again. How is your company attracting the next generation of talent? Adam: We're focused on creating careers, not just jobs. That starts with how we treat people: Clune is 100% employee-owned, and we pay 100% of medical premiums for employees and their families. That's rare in this industry and it reflects our belief that when people feel secure and valued, they build better, longer-lasting careers. We're especially focused on growing our talent pipeline in construction project management and field roles. We see a huge opportunity to bring people with mechanical, electrical and plumbing experience into MEP Coordinator roles, and we're investing in that transition with training and mentorship. At the end of the day, we want people to feel proud of the work they're doing and see a future here. That's how we build for the long haul.

article_text: Pittsburgh's shift from industrial powerhouse to a technology-driven economy began in the late 20th century. What followed was not a departure from infrastructure, but a redefinition of it. Today, the region depends as much on data systems as it once did on steel production. Companies like Evolution E-Cycling are operating within that shift, and data centers are at the core. Based in the Pittsburgh region, Evolution E-Cycling works on the downstream side of digital systems, providing an answer to the question, "What happens to technology, equipment, and data once it is no longer needed?" It's an issue that is becoming more urgent as digital infrastructure expands and electronic waste grows alongside it. E-Waste: A growing local consideration Globally, e-waste is among the fastest-growing categories of solid waste. In 2022, an estimated 62 million tons were generated, yet only 22.3% was formally collected and recycled. The remainder often enters informal or unregulated systems, where improper handling can release hazardous materials and pose serious health risks. While those figures are global, their implications are local. Western Pennsylvania's growth in healthcare, robotics, higher education, and advanced manufacturing has driven increased reliance on IT infrastructure. Systems are routinely upgraded or replaced, creating a steady volume of retired equipment, from laptops and mobile devices to servers and networking hardware. Understanding data centers and their lifecycle Data centers add another layer of complexity. Their lifecycle doesn't end at deployment; it includes ongoing cycles of upgrade and decommissioning. Servers, storage systems, and networking equipment are routinely replaced to meet performance and security demands, creating a steady stream of high-value, data-sensitive equipment that must be handled carefully at end of life. The rise of AI infrastructure is accelerating this cycle. AI servers, particularly those built around high-performance GPUs, are more expensive, more energy-intensive, and more specialized than traditional server hardware. As organizations scale AI capabilities, they are upgrading systems more frequently to keep pace with performance demands, shortening hardware lifecycles and increasing the volume of high-value equipment entering the IT asset disposition (ITAD) stream. These systems also introduce new complexities. GPU-based servers often retain significant residual value, but require more precise evaluation, handling, and resale pathways than standard equipment. At the same time, the intensity of AI workloads can place greater strain on components, affecting reuse potential and increasing the importance of responsible downstream processing. For ITAD providers, this shift is not just about volume; it's about adapting to a more technically demanding and higher-stakes category of infrastructure. This is not simply a disposal issue. It is a lifecycle management issue, with implications for data security, environmental compliance, and cost recovery. Where Evolution E-Cycling fits This is where specialized lifecycle management becomes critical. Evolution E-Cycling's services, including asset buyback and repurposing, secure data destruction, and responsible recycling, address the transition point between active infrastructure and retired equipment. Their client base mirrors the structure of the regional economy: healthcare, education, manufacturing, government, finance, and logistics. Across these sectors, the challenge is consistent. Equipment can't simply be discarded or written off. It must be tracked, processed, and accounted for. Evolution E-Cycling approaches this as a structured process rather than a one-time service. Standards such as R2v3 and RIOS certification, along with permitting through the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection, establish requirements for traceability, responsible downstream handling, and secure data destruction. article_text: CALDWELL, Ohio (AVC News) - After eight years serving Noble County, Gwynn Stewart is stepping into a new regional role following years of work in community and economic development. Stewart, an assistant professor of Community Development with Ohio State University Extension, has spent her time in Noble County helping connect local governments, organizations, and residents to resources aimed at strengthening communities and growing the local economy. During her tenure, Extension-led efforts in Noble County and the surrounding Appalachian region helped generate nearly $30 million in total project investments. Those projects include a new business park, a Vibrant Communities initiative, and redevelopment work at the former Mahle facility for Pinnacle Warehousing. Stewart also helped launch the Village Vistas program, which supports small businesses, nonprofits, and villages through matching funds for improvements such as building facades, signage, landscaping, and greenspace. The program has supported 37 projects totaling nearly $560,000 in investment. "Our efforts have also focused on supporting small business as they are the primary economic development driver in Noble," Stewart said. Her work extended into long-term planning and infrastructure development, including broadband expansion efforts, housing and land-use planning, and revitalization projects in Caldwell and Belle Valley. She also played a role in developing the Appalachian Byway of Ohio in partnership with the Ohio Department of Transportation to promote tourism across multiple counties. Stewart has been active in several organizations, including the Noble County Community Improvement Corporation, Chamber of Commerce Board, Planning Commission, Noble Community Foundation, and the Eastern Ohio Development Alliance, where she served as president. In 2025, she earned certification as an Ohio Certified Economic Developer through the Ohio Economic Development Association, a designation held by a small percentage of professionals in the field. In addition to her local work, Stewart has led grant writing training efforts across the state and Appalachian region, helping individuals and organizations secure funding for community projects. Stewart will now transition into a regional position serving 10 counties in eastern Ohio, including Belmont, Carroll, Columbiana, Coshocton, Guernsey, Harrison, Holmes, Jefferson, Muskingum, and Tuscarawas counties.

article_text: Jennifer Lawrence Founder and CEO - SEAT Center Jennifer Lawrence is the Founder & CEO of the Social Enterprise and Training Center (SEAT Center), where she's dedicated to creating opportunities for underrepresented young people. Passionate about workforce innovation, Jennifer connects businesses with an untapped talent pool to drive economic growth in the Capital Region. With over 20 years of experience in nonprofit management and workforce development, Jennifer is a leader in social entrepreneurship and a champion for opportunity youth. She founded SEAT Center to bridge gaps in the workforce by helping young people gain skills, re-enter the job market, and unlock their potential. Jennifer's career reflects her commitment to meaningful impact. She holds a master's degree in Social Work Administration from Fordham University, a bachelor's from Siena College, and coursework with the University at Albany Executive MBA program. She's also a graduate of the REDF Social Enterprise Accelerator and American Express Leadership Academy. Her leadership extends beyond SEAT Center, serving on the Capital Region Chamber Board of Directors and the Benhaven School in CT. Jennifer's contributions have earned her numerous awards, including the 2025 Key 4 Women ACHIEVE award, 2024 Albany Business Review Power 50 List, 2023 DEI Honoree, and 2022 Schenectady Community Award. Jennifer is a trailblazer creating pathways to success for individuals and communities while tackling workforce challenges with innovative solutions. These roles established a strong foundation in service standards, guest care, and operational discipline. After relocating to the Capital Region in 2007 to attend The College of Saint Rose, she continued her career across a range of restaurant concepts, from fast-casual to fine dining. Paula co-launched The Pony Show in 2022 with her partner, Anthony Angelicola. In 2025, Paula began a business partnership to open a restaurant in Troy, NY called First + Adams. The project is still under construction with plans to open in the middle of this year. First + Adams will bring a a new cornerstone of culinary and social heart to Troy and the surrounding areas, by way of a contemporary new American concept focusing on natural wine, local & seasonal products, and community. In 2022, she relocated to the Capital Region to begin the next chapter of her leadership journey. Her transition from clinical care to healthcare administration gives her a unique and powerful lens. Before joining Baltimore Community Lending, Watchen worked as Chief of Party/Country Director of the international USAID-funded project "Investing for Business Expansion" (IBEX) project to provide access to finance and economic development in Libera. article_text: Recent headlines have suggested that Ohio's population is destined for long-term decline, citing projections from a state development report that rely heavily on birth and death rates. While those demographic trends matter, they tell only part of the story and overlook one of the most important drivers of population growth: economic opportunity. The reality is that Ohio is growing, and it's growing because people follow jobs. The analysis in question focuses on natural population change (births minus deaths) but does not fully account for domestic migration, particularly the influx of workers and families moving to Ohio as a result of unprecedented economic investment. That omission leads to a misleading conclusion at a moment when Ohio's economy is doing exactly what strong economies do - attracting people. Recent national data from the U.S. Census Bureau show that while overall U.S. population growth slowed significantly in 2025, rising by just 0.5%, Ohio was one of the states with positive net domestic migration. In fact, Ohio recorded an 11,926 net domestic migration gain in 2025, a dramatic turnaround from a loss of more than 32,000 in 2021. Over the last several years, Ohio has secured some of the most significant economic development wins in the nation. Companies are choosing Ohio for large-scale manufacturing, technology, logistics and energy projects because of our workforce, infrastructure, location and business climate. Those investments are creating real jobs, in real communities, right now. Consider what's already underway. Anduril's planned hyperscale manufacturing facility in Columbus, the state's largest single job-creation project in history, is reinforcing Ohio's position as a leader in advanced technology and national security. Honda's electric vehicle and battery investments are anchoring the next generation of automotive manufacturing. Major expansions in logistics, aerospace, healthcare and advanced manufacturing are happening across the state, from Northwest Ohio to the Ohio River Valley. These projects require tens of thousands of workers, not just on construction sites, but in permanent, high-quality jobs. And those workers don't exist in a vacuum. They bring families, buy homes, enroll children in schools and become part of our communities. That is population growth driven by economic growth. We've seen this story before. States and regions that successfully attract large employers and invest in workforce development consistently outperform demographic projections that fail to account for migration. Ohio is no exception, and in many ways, we are uniquely positioned to benefit from this moment. Ohio offers affordability that coastal states can't match, world-class higher education and training institutions, reliable energy and infrastructure, amenities that contribute to a vibrant culture and sense of community, and a quality of life that resonates with workers across the spectrum. As companies look to reshore manufacturing, strengthen supply chains and invest in emerging technologies, Ohio checks the boxes they prioritize most. Ohio's economy is growing. Investment is accelerating. Jobs are being created. And people are moving here because of it. If we stay focused on policies that support business growth, workforce readiness, infrastructure investment, innovation and quality of life, Ohio will continue to attract talent from across the country. Growth is not something that happens by accident; it's the result of intentional choices. Ohio is making those choices, and the results are already visible. Ohio's future is not one of decline. It's one of opportunity, and that becomes clear when we examine the full picture. Steve Stivers in the president and CEO of the Ohio Chamber of Commerce.

WASHINGTON-The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), alongside the U.S. Department of Commerce (DOC), today announced a unique public-private partnership with SoftBank and AEP Ohio to redevelop DOE land, modernize energy infrastructure, and develop advanced computing in Southern Ohio. As part of the partnership, SB Energy, a SoftBank Group company, is planning to build 10 gigawatts (GW) of new power generation-including 9.2 GW of natural gas generation-that will connect to the local grid and provide power to a new 10 GW data center development at the Portsmouth Site in Pike County, Ohio at no cost to American families. These collective efforts will deliver lower electricity costs across the region, create thousands of American jobs, and strengthen America's national security. Portions of this announcement were previously announced as part of President Trump's U.S.-Japan Strategic Trade and Investment Agreement. This includes the $33.3 billion in Japanese funding for 9.2 GW of new natural gas generation. "Thanks to President Trump, the U.S. government is leveraging its assets-like our federal lands-to add power generation, create jobs, and ensure the United States wins the AI race," said U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright. "I'm pleased to be working with our partners at SoftBank and AEP Ohio on this important project. By bringing new power online and upgrading our existing infrastructure, this investment supports the AI boom and cutting-edge technologies while strengthening our energy system and helping keep costs down for the American people." "Our Japanese partnership is a direct result of President Trump's America First trade policies," said U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. "Japan has committed to invest $550 billion across America. With this historic trade deal we are reindustrializing the country through critical projects like this $33 billion dollar power project in Portsmouth, Ohio. Yesterday we announced additional mega projects in Alabama, Pennsylvania, Tennessee and Texas." Watch the Groundbreaking Here. This project complies with President Trump's Ratepayer Protection Pledge, which protects ratepayers from paying for energy infrastructure improvements needed to power the ongoing technological boom. In compliance with the pledge, SB Energy is investing $4.2 billion with AEP Ohio to upgrade and build new transmission lines in Southern Ohio. This critical grid investment, at no cost to the public, will help lower local utility rates for American families and businesses. SB Energy has committed to making excess transmission and generation capacity available to the grid. "AEP Ohio is proud that this partnership will bring critical infrastructure to Appalachian Ohio," said Bill Fehrman, AEP Chairman, President and Chief Executive Officer. "If it were not for the partnership between all parties - the Administration, SoftBank and our team - this type of investment would not be possible. This partnership unlocks billions of dollars of electric transmission infrastructure, all without increasing customer rates." "Our partnership with the Department of Energy strengthens America's AI leadership, secures the energy and compute needed for the future, and powers the next era of innovation for the United States," said Masayoshi Son, Chairman and CEO of SoftBank Group Corp. "AI will transform every industry, and the PORTS Technology Campus will help deliver the next-generation infrastructure needed to unlock those breakthroughs." The investment will support: Access to affordable energy through grid upgrades and the delivery of excess capacity onto the grid to help lower consumer electricity prices. Job creation and workforce development, delivering thousands of jobs and revitalizing the domestic manufacturing base that will support the project. Innovation and scientific discovery, developing a new large-scale data center that could have dedicated support of advanced research including around fusion, quantum computing, and national security. Environmental cleanup and remediation, advancing the revitalization of the Portsmouth site, that for decades played a pivotal role in our nation's security. Community and economic development initiatives, ensuring residents of Southern Ohio and the broader region benefit directly from the investment. "This partnership is a major step forward for Southern Ohio's economic and energy future," said Assistant Secretary of Environmental Management Tim Walsh. "By capitalizing on investments in America and federal land assets, the partnership will safely advance restoration and revitalization of the Portsmouth site with enormous economic benefit to the region and the country." Construction on the project is expected to begin this year.

"James, Lauren, Vincent, Michael, and Vips each bring valuable experience, strong community ties, and a deep appreciation for our state's outdoor traditions. I am confident they will help guide sound policies that balance conservation, access, and economic opportunity for generations to come." "These appointments reflect our commitment to protecting West Virginia's natural beauty while ensuring it remains accessible for our citizens and visitors," Governor Morrisey added. "We will continue to champion policies that strengthen our outdoor economy, and preserve these resources for the future." The meetings will be held in six locations across the state and can also be streamed online at the Commerce Department's YouTube Channel. article_text: MASON COUNTY, W.Va. -Mason County is seeing major economic growth with a new data and coal facility coming to the area, but that growth is also driving up costs. Fidelas and Frontieras plans to build a data center and coal facility in the area, along with a new campground for workers. "They bring their campers with them and they come into what we call temporary construction campsites, this has nothing to do with recreation campsites that we have in Mason County, but it's only temporary constriction campsites," Mason County Commission President Rick Handley said on MetroNews Midday Thursday. Nucor, which is building a steel plant in the county, has brought in nearly 2,000 temporary workers since construction began in 2024. Handley said they wanted to generate some revenue from workers staying in the county, but a bill to do so failed during the recently concluded 60-day legislative session. He added that the plan was to include campsites under the existing hotel and motel tax. "We were hoping to hug on with the hotel/motel, and we know they get six percent," Handley said. "If someone comes in and spends the night, let's say it's 100 dollars, and they go out of there paying 106 dollars they don't look at the bill and say where is the other six dollars going, you told me it was 100." He said the tax could have helped fund emergency personnel, who are currently struggling to meet demands. "We are needing more law enforcement officers, EMS workers, plus out volunteer fire department and it's only going to get worse with several thousand more construction workers in addition to what we down at Nucor now," Handley said. Handley said it's great to see growth coming to Mason County but added it would have been nice to generate some revenue from workers living there. "I love to see them here, they come here and spend money at the grocery stores and maybe at some of the restaurants, Walmart and all these places but again we just need to get tax money the same way hotel/motel would work," he said. He said that since the bill failed, the county is exploring other options.

article_text: News broke early Friday morning: Google has acquired land in Putnam County for a possible data center. While some - a minority, in my view - are less than enthusiastic, many in Putnam County see the announcement as a clear win... at least that's the read from the cacophony of social media. That's not surprising. Putnam County has a history of embracing new corporate investment, dating back to Toyota's decision to locate there. The county's economy is more diversified than most in West Virginia, and local leaders actively recruit investment with strong community backing. That approach has paid off - driving new development, raising property values, and generating more tax revenue for schools and public infrastructure, including recreational facilities. The greater Teays Metroplex - as I like to call it - is a great place to live. But as welcoming as the community is, that's not the primary reason Google is looking at Putnam County. The real driver is energy - specifically, available electric transmission capacity. And not just any capacity: 765,000 volts of it. American Electric Power, the largest transmission owner in the United States, operates a 765-kilovolt line near the property Google acquired. State Energy Tzar Nick Preservati said Friday on Talkline the Google facility will be powered by AEP's grid. That kind of high-voltage access - combined with available land, water, and other utilities - is the holy grail for data center development. It's the sweet spot in the Venn diagram. And it points to a bigger reality. The United States doesn't just need more generation to meet the demands of artificial intelligence - it needs more transmission infrastructure to move that power where it's needed. West Virginia is uniquely positioned here. Several major transmission projects are pending, including MARL and Valley Link. They're controversial, and the concerns from affected property owners are real and should not be dismissed. But Friday's announcement should sharpen the conversation. High-voltage transmission near viable sites attracts major investment. That doesn't erase legitimate concerns, but it absolutely belongs in the cost-benefit discussion. More transmission could mean more exports of energy from West Virginia. That's not necessarily a bad thing - megawatts may be the most valuable product we produce. But just as important, more transmission increases the likelihood that demand comes here. More end users. More load. More opportunity. That could mean data centers. It could mean manufacturing. It could mean commercial development we haven't even envisioned yet. And that would be a good thing - jobs, tax revenue, and a more diversified economy - all built on West Virginia's energy backbone. Not just power shipped out on a wire, but power used to create prosperity here at home. Call me a fanboy - everyone knows my first career was in energy - but this Google moment, made possible largely because that transmission line was already here, should be a wake-up call for the state.

article_text: BUFFALO, W.Va. - A leading name in the cyber world has made the decision to locate in West Virginia. Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced Friday Google has purchased property near Buffalo in Putnam County for a data center. MetroNews has learned the tech giant has acquired 1,700 acres of land on both sides of Route 62 to construct a data center. The announcement of the purchase means there are still many hurdles to cross and hoops to jump through before the company is in operation, but the announcement was enough to excite local leaders. "It will be transforming for the town of Buffalo. We're very excited about it and it's just a great announcement for the state," said state Senator Glen Jeffries, R-Putnam. "Google is the cream of the crop when you start talking about data centers and I think that's what's so important here. They're just a tremendous company and a tremendous partner, they do it the right way and they're interested in helping the community. To bring a partner like that into the state of West Virginia on a large scale signifies we are doing it right," said Deputy State Development Director Nick Preservati, who runs the state Office of Energy. The acreage where Google plans to put the site is on the west end of Buffalo, the opposite end from the Toyota West Virginia plant. Although not a deal breaker, the site was made much more attractive because of Appalachian Power's existing 765 KV transmission line which actually runs through the property. The location means power is already available in a sufficient quantity for what they hope to build. "Without the line they may still build the data center, but it makes it less attractive because they may have to put in additional transmission. That increases cost and increases timelines and the most important things to data centers is speed to power. Having that transmission there takes one of the largest issues off the table for them," Preservati said. Indications are the company has also embraced the state of West Virginia and more specifically the Buffalo community. Jeffries said Google has committed to paying for any and all infrastructure upgrades which might be needed for the operation. Increased water, sewer, and electrical transmission will not fall on ratepayers. They'll also take power directly off the grid rather than an on-site generating facility. The power will come directly from the coal fired John Amos power plant a few miles up the Kanawha River. Appalachian Power was an instrumental partner in the state in trying to attract the company to town. "None of that will be passed on to the people in West Virginia. They're going to work on sewer upgrades, water upgrades, all of that will be borne upon them," Jeffries. "It's 100 percent off the grid, that's one of the key things every bit of power will be pulled off the grid." "They are taking care of all of the infrastructure costs. None of that is being put on ratepayers and they're also looking to upgrade things throughout the community," said Del. Kathie Hess Crouse, R-Putnam. "It sounds like they are looking at being a very good neighbor to the people of Buffalo." Preservati said Google's commitment is one of the best economic development tools the state could have ever asked for. "A Google announcement sends a message to all other data center companies. If Google's willing to come to West Virginia and seize all the opportunities here, others should to. It's a multiplier," said Preservati. He added this is all a result of programs the legislature and the Morrisey administration put into place last year and it's proof they are working. "We put the building blocks in place and at this point, Governor Morrisey's message is to just keep doing what we're doing, the best is yet to come," he added.

article_text: Solar power proliferated in Indiana last year, despite roadblocks threatening the industry's future in the state. Last spring, an Amazon-backed renewable project began transforming 100-megawatts worth of sunshine into energy in Randolph County. Subaru of Indiana Automotive decked out a plant in Lafayette with rows of photovoltaic panels and businesses and homes across the state installed solar projects to save on utility bills and reduce carbon emissions. All in all, the state's solar capacity nearly doubled in 2025, according to a report from Wood Mackenzie and the Solar Energy Industries Association, a trade group. Indiana saw the 3rd largest solar capacity influx in the country last year, behind energy giants Texas and California. The renewable boom developed in the face of strong headwinds. Last year, the federal administration dismantled renewable energy tax incentives and canceled millions of dollars worth of grants for solar power. And finding physical space to put the panels remains an ordeal throughout the country: one rough night in a county zoning meeting can halt a project years-in-the-making. Building solar might be harder in 2026 than it was a couple of years ago, but state officials still see it as part of Indiana's solution to meet rising energy demand, lower the cost of electricity and keep the climate a little cleaner. "We benefit when we are open to a myriad of possibilities and solutions for energy sourcing," Secretary Suzanne Jaworowski, Indiana's Secretary of Energy and Natural Resources, wrote in an email to IndyStar. "Having a diverse portfolio will help us lower the cost of electricity." Solar is profitable, but tricky to build In the face of the country's increasing need for energy, some see Indiana's solar surge as common sense economics. It's a great way for developers to get a bang for their buck, said Topher Anderson, the director of programs and operations for the Indiana Conservative Alliance for Energy. Indiana is flat and sunny - possibly to the chagrin of the state's tourism board - and a complicated network of power lines operates like a massive expressway, shuttling electrons across the region. And many churches, schools and homeowners, burned by high utility bills or racked with climate concerns, have pursued residential solar projects. This has led to Indiana's biggest year of solar development yet: In 2025, the state installed about three gigawatts of solar power. Most states added less than one. Now, Indiana has about 6.5 gigawatts of solar capacity total, which the SEIA estimates is enough energy to power 770,052 homes. The trade group projects that Indiana is on track to install over 12 gigawatts of solar power over the next five years, but it won't be easy. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed last summer brought an early end to solar energy tax credits that eased high upfront installation costs. In addition, some rural counties can be hostile to renewable development. Almost 1/3 of Indiana counties have bans or moratoriums on new utility-scale solar parks. And projects still fail in counties that technically allow development. More: Big renewable projects mean big money for this small town On the other hand, communities that have welcomed solar projects often see financial gains. Renewable projects can boost county tax bases and provide stable income to farmers who lease land. Last spring, an Amazon-backed renewable project began transforming 100-megawatts worth of sunshine into energy in Randolph County. All in all, the state's solar capacity nearly doubled in 2025, according to a report from Wood Mackenzie and the Solar Energy Industries Association, a trade group. And finding physical space to put the panels remains an ordeal throughout the country: one rough night in a county zoning meeting can halt a project years-in-the-making. Building solar might be harder in 2026 than it was a couple of years ago, but state officials still see it as part of Indiana's solution to meet rising energy demand, lower the cost of electricity and keep the climate a little cleaner. "We benefit when we are open to a myriad of possibilities and solutions for energy sourcing," Secretary Suzanne Jaworowski, Indiana's Secretary of Energy and Natural Resources, wrote in an email to IndyStar. "Having a diverse portfolio will help us lower the cost of electricity." It's a great way for developers to get a bang for their buck, said Topher Anderson, the director of programs and operations for the Indiana Conservative Alliance for Energy. Indiana is flat and sunny - possibly to the chagrin of the state's tourism board - and a complicated network of power lines operates like a massive expressway, shuttling electrons across the region. And many churches, schools and homeowners, burned by high utility bills or racked with climate concerns, have pursued residential solar projects. This has led to Indiana's biggest year of solar development yet: In 2025, the state installed about three gigawatts of solar power. Most states added less than one. article_text: Not all degrees are created equal, and students across Kentucky and the surrounding states are starting to notice. Whether driven by job demand, personal interest, or just the desire for a steady paycheck after graduation, students are gravitating toward majors that feel practical, flexible, and rooted in reality. Gone are the days when a "safe" path meant law school or business. Now, it's nursing, tech, and even the trades that are quietly taking over classrooms, both in person and online. The data doesn't lie. Over the last few years, programs in healthcare, engineering, IT, and mental health have seen a sharp increase in enrollment, outpacing traditional liberal arts and even some business degrees. So what's behind this shift, and what majors are actually pulling ahead? Here's a look at what's growing, where the momentum is, and why. Nursing and Allied Health: Leading the Pack If there's one field that's consistently booming, it's nursing. The demand for nurses in both urban and rural areas continues to climb, and students are responding. Accelerated programs are also playing a big role. Online ABSN degrees in Ohio, for example, are giving students with non-nursing backgrounds a way to pivot into the field fast, and they're filling up quickly. Allied health programs like physical therapy assisting, respiratory therapy, and radiologic tech are also on the rise. These roles are often overlooked but highly employable, especially in areas that are underserved medically. The appeal? Shorter training periods, decent starting pay, and strong job security. Tech Majors: Less Flash, More Function Tech degrees aren't just for Silicon Valley hopefuls anymore. Cybersecurity, data analytics, and software development are becoming go-to choices for students who want a future-proof career but don't necessarily want to work for a big-name startup. The major takeaway here is practicality. These degrees tend to lead to remote or hybrid work, which appeals to a generation used to flexibility. Plus, with certificate and associate-level options becoming more common, some students are skipping the four-year route altogether and still landing solid entry-level jobs. Engineering: Still a Solid Bet While it might not be growing as explosively as nursing or tech, engineering programs are quietly expanding. Mechanical, civil, and electrical engineering continue to attract students who are good with math and want a job that pays well right out of the gate. What's changing is the focus. There's been a noticeable uptick in interest in renewable energy, infrastructure, and even environmental engineering. Areas that align with larger economic and climate concerns. It's not just about building bridges anymore; it's about building smart ones. Psychology and Counseling: The Mental Health Effect Increased attention on mental health has fueled major growth in psychology, social work, and counseling programs. Students aren't just drawn to these fields because they want to "help people." They're also seeing a wide range of job options and graduate pathways. Many who start with a psychology or social work degree don't necessarily plan to become therapists. School counseling, case management, behavioral health tech jobs, and community outreach work are all growing subfields. Unlike some majors that feel vague or abstract, this path feels grounded. There's a problem to solve and students want to be part of the solution. Education: Slowly Making a Comeback Yes, teacher shortages are real. But rather than scare students away, that reality seems to be drawing some in. Education majors are showing modest but consistent growth, especially in elementary and special education. Incentives in certain states, including loan forgiveness or guaranteed placement programs, are starting to shift the narrative. While teaching still isn't the most lucrative field, it's one that comes with a sense of purpose and students are taking note. Skilled Trades and "New Collar" Careers It's not just about college anymore. Career-minded students, especially those coming out of high school unsure about the traditional four-year route, are starting to explore skilled trades, vocational programs, and technical certifications. Think HVAC, welding, electrical work, and auto tech. What's different now is the branding. These aren't seen as fallback options; they're seen as strategic moves. Wages are competitive, training is relatively fast, and in some areas, the job openings outnumber the applicants. What's Driving the Shift? There's no single reason why these programs are growing, but a few key factors stand out: Job Market Alignment: Students want majors that lead to jobs. Simple as that. Flexibility: Programs that offer hybrid or online options are especially appealing. Cost vs. Outcome: The rising cost of education has made students more skeptical of majors that don't offer a clear return on investment. Social Influence: Gen Z is heavily influenced by trends, whether on TikTok or in their local communities. Seeing peers succeed in nursing, tech, or the trades makes those paths more attractive. Final Take If you're choosing a major in 2025, it's not just about passion anymore, it's about payoff. And while there's nothing wrong with following your heart, it turns out a lot of students are learning to follow the data, too. The fastest-growing majors in Kentucky and its neighboring states aren't always the flashiest, but they're getting results. They offer a clear path to a career, often without years of uncertainty or debt, and in today's world, that might be the most practical degree of all.
