article_text: As artificial intelligence fuels an unprecedented surge in data center development, Central Texas finds itself at the center of a broader infrastructure transformation. A recent Bloom Energy report, cited by the Texas Tribune, found Texas is poised to become the nation's largest data center market within two years, with power demand from Texas data centers projected to exceed 40 gigawatts by 2028. To examine what this rapid growth means for construction, water resources and workforce development, the Austin Business Journal convened a roundtable of industry leaders who are shaping the region's next chapter. Participants included Joe Navar, SVP of Sales at VVater (pronounced "water"); Bryan Kent, Central Texas Business Unit Leader at DPR Construction; and Billy Wright, President of Staffing and Business Development at Becker Wright Consultants. Together, they discussed how the data center boom is accelerating innovation, straining legacy systems and opening new opportunities across industries, reshaping the pace and scale of development in Texas and beyond. Abby Mellott, Market President & Publisher of the Austin Business Journal, moderated the conversation. Abby Mellott: Data center construction is experiencing an unprecedented boom. We're seeing thousands of projects and billions of dollars in investment across the country. Bryan, give us some insight into what this looks like for you at DPR in Texas. And more specifically, can you talk about what you're seeing in Central Texas? Bryan Kent: Yes, we've seen a lot of growth in the data center market in Texas, and a lot of it has been focused in Central Texas. From a DPR perspective, advanced technology is one of our core markets. Over the last decade, I would say that sector has been fairly quiet in Central Texas, but recently it has picked up. It used to be that a lot of the growth was centered in the San Antonio market. Now we're seeing a lot of activity not just in Central Texas, but across the state - in North Texas, West Texas and the Panhandle as well. There's been a ton of growth and a lot of new clients entering the market. In Central Texas, downtown commercial development was a big market over the past decade. With that sector slowing down somewhat, the advanced technology market has given DPR an opportunity to highlight our integrated approach to construction and provide value to clients in a different way. One thing that really sets DPR apart on these projects is our self-perform capabilities. In Texas, we have more than 1,300 craft professionals who do everything from concrete and drywall to specialties and electrical. That gives us the ability to bring our own people directly to the project. As this market continues to grow, that in-house expertise and capability helps us move faster, maintain quality, control the schedule and, ultimately, turn projects over on a tighter timeline than would otherwise be possible. Abby Mellott: On the labor front, this type of work requires highly specialized skill sets, both during construction and for ongoing operations. We all know there are talent gaps across the industry. Can you talk about where the biggest pain points are when it comes to those gaps, and how the staffing market is responding? Billy Wright: Yeah, we've seen talent gaps on both skilled trade roles and other construction or operations roles. What's unique about Becker Wright Consultants is that we're involved in both the direct placement side for all phases including site selection, construction, engineering, operations, as well as staffing all the skilled trades involved on the sites. We're seeing gaps at every level. On the technical side that might be engineers, MEP professionals or site selection roles. On the hourly skilled trades side, it's cable technicians, fiber optic splicers and similar positions. There's a real war for talent across the board and we are working hard to help integrators and general contractors win when it comes to staffing and recruiting talent. In response, we get creative to find top talent and use our nationwide candidate networks. At the end of the day, it comes down to industry knowledge, expertise and the strength of our network to find and place enough qualified people at every level and project phase. You have to respond quickly and be nimble. In staffing and recruiting, speed matters. On the construction side, especially with skilled trades in the field, there's often a quick turnaround. That means coordinating housing, travel expenses, background checks and onboarding processes to make sure everyone is cleared before going on-site and to ease the administrative burden for our clients. We also use workforce pooling, building groups from specific programs or recruiting channels and moving them from project to project, often in teams. There are really two sides to it. On the hourly and skilled trades side, you have to constantly build and maintain referral networks and talent pipelines. On the higher-level, direct placement side, you can't simply post a job and expect to find an experienced MEP engineer. You have to rely on relationships, referrals and knowing exactly where to go to find that talent. Abby Mellott: We've talked about the skills gap and the broader workforce challenges. Are teams being pulled from other sectors to support data center projects? Billy Wright: Yes, as we are seeing the data center sector grow, companies are pulling talent from other mission critical projects in sectors like energy, oil and gas, semiconductor manufacturing, healthcare, and more. This is where Becker Wright Consultants adds value, with over twenty years of experience recruiting in those fields and our recruiting team having the deep industry knowledge and time to dedicate to finding, screening, and vetting those with similar skillsets who've been working outside of the data center industry. From a future hiring standpoint, you also have to be as proactive as possible. That means identifying candidates with similar skill sets or the right aptitude, bringing them in at an entry level and training them. You might teach them how to run cable, teach them how to splice, or train them to handle other technical aspects of the work. Abby Mellott: Bryan, how does DPR handle this? Bryan Kent: One of the benefits of DPR being not just a local contractor but also a national and international company is the ability to move talent where it's needed. With the growth happening in Texas, we've been able to bring in professionals from across the country to support these projects, drawing from markets that may not be as dominant. That allows us to continue serving our local clients that we have long-standing relationships with while also supporting this rapid expansion of data center construction in Texas, particularly in Central Texas. At the same time, we're actively recruiting top talent who want to work on these projects, and we're offering competitive packages that make those opportunities attractive. Abby Mellott: Joe, let's shift to you. What does VVater do and how does your technology differ from traditional water treatment systems? Joe Navar: At its core, VVater is a water treatment company. We remove contaminants from water supplies and treat it to specific quality standards. That can range from meeting discharge requirements to producing water suitable for industrial reuse or even human consumption. We operate across several verticals, including wastewater treatment, on-site applications and food and beverage applications. More recently, we've found a strong and growing opportunity in the data center space. Essentially, data centers face the same fundamental issue as many other industries: We're running out of fresh water for potable use, and we have to get more creative about how we reuse our water supplies after the initial purpose has been served. Our approach to water shortages and water treatment is more disruptive than traditional systems. We don't rely on chemicals, membranes or filters, so there are fewer moving parts. Instead, we use targeted electric pulses to destroy contaminants and alter the chemistry of the incoming water, which allows us to achieve different treatment grades on the outgoing water. From a water perspective, we're actually fairly agnostic when it comes to customer segment. Data centers are attractive because of the pace of development, but the broader impact is that rapid growth is putting pressure on municipal water infrastructure. We're seeing increased demand from both private and public organizations that want to protect their water supply. Abby Mellott: As data center demands surge, how scalable is VVater's approach as a long-term solution?= Joe Navar: All of our systems are modular and designed to scale incrementally. In most capital projects, there's a headline investment number, but that full amount isn't typically deployed on day one. Even well-funded organizations often raise capital in phases and build out capacity over time. When you look at how quickly data centers can come online, you're often talking about one to two years for initial operations, and four to five years for a full-blown data center. A lot of the constraints are tied to interconnection, whether that's tying into the power grid or local water infrastructure. Because we eliminate many of the dynamic components and chemicals, the systems are simpler so the learning curve for a new team is much shorter. That matters when we're talking about scaling quickly and staffing up fast. The footprint is also relatively small, which helps from a construction standpoint. From a cash flow standpoint, it's important for our customers to work with a supplier that can scale incrementally alongside their demand. For example, if a site is ultimately designed for a gigawatt of power and may require between 1 million and 3 million gallons of water per day at full capacity, they don't need that volume on day one. Initial demand is typically much lower, and it ramps up over the next two to three years into that top-end capacity. So being modular and scalable is mission critical. It allows us to expand treatment capacity in step with construction, staffing and operational needs. It also helps customers adapt as regulatory requirements continue to evolve. Abby Mellott: When communities push back on data center projects over power, noise or water concerns, what does effective engagement look like from a development standpoint? And how are you working with local municipalities and other stakeholders to address concerns? Bryan Kent: The biggest thing is communication. It's about being involved in the community, keeping people informed and getting them engaged in the project as much as possible. Following the client's lead, we try to be clear about what we're building, how it will operate and how it may affect the local area. From our side, transparency is key. We have to be upfront about what we're doing and how we plan to work within the community. That can be as simple as partnering with local restaurants to provide food for the project teams or working with smaller local contractors on part of the job. Those efforts demonstrate that we're not just building in a community, we're trying to be a partner. Abby Mellott: Joe, you touched on concerns around water loss and conservation. What are you doing to address those issues? Joe Navar: Involving all of the stakeholders early on is critical. For example, we're currently working on a direct potable reuse project south of Austin. It's designed not just to address a specific segment, but also to benefit surrounding communities. We're not living in bubbles. Even if a data center comes in and builds its own microgrid, it's still tapping into the same aquifers as the rest of the community. In Austin, we've dealt with drought conditions forever. And when you layer in population growth and a surge in data centers, it only compounds the strain on limited freshwater supplies. That's why bringing stakeholders in early and clearly communicating what's coming and how reuse applications work is essential. Nobody likes surprises. Abby Mellott: Billy, when you're deploying teams to job sites, are you tapping into local workers as well? Billy Wright: Yes, we use local talent when we can, but it can also depend on the type of role or the turnaround time for the need. Like I mentioned earlier, it's a tight market pretty much everywhere. Sometimes we're able to tap into local talent, and sometimes we're bringing people in from outside the area on the project teams. For the direct placement roles we work on, both in the construction phase and for the long-term operation of a data center, we focus primarily on finding local talent or those that are looking to relocate to a market for these long-term opportunities. From a boots-on-the-ground perspective, a big part of what we manage when it comes to the hourly, skilled trade roles we fill is keeping the local community top of mind. On some of these projects, there can be hundreds or even thousands of workers in one location. If you're bringing that many people into a smaller city, like Abilene, or a more rural town it's important that the hourly employees working for us are respectful of the community. They're pumping in a lot of revenue to the local economy - staying in hotels, eating at restaurants, shopping at grocery stores - and they're working long hours. We're in constant communication with the employees about the need to be professional and respectful, both on the job and out in the local communities. If that doesn't happen then we won't use them on another project. You have to look at it from the perspective of the community. We make sure the people coming in for the construction project phases aren't becoming an issue for local residents. Abby Mellott: Bryan, can you talk about infrastructure-related delays? What are you seeing on that front, and how is DPR working to mitigate those risks? Bryan Kent: The biggest factor is power; however, as a construction company, we're not typically part of that decision-making process. Usually, the developer is the one making those agreements to get power brought onto the site. From our side, when we think about delays or risk on a project, it really comes down to preconstruction and supply chain management. On large projects like data centers, electrical and mechanical equipment is key to the success of the job. We have a dedicated team focused on tracking those materials, monitoring lead times, staying current on pricing and understanding where things stand in the industry. That allows us to provide accurate input back to the client and make informed decisions about what we can deliver and how quickly. A lot of times we're installing items the owners are furnishing. So we work closely together to make sure those materials get to the site when they're needed. That can include coordinating temporary storage or warehouse space, so equipment is ready to go as soon as construction reaches that point. Our preconstruction team is working on that from day one, long before we ever break ground, to make sure everything is in place and ensure we're able to meet the project schedule Abby Mellott: Joe, do you run into many infrastructure-related delays? Joe Navar: Yeah, we do run into some infrastructure delays. With a data center project, one of the first questions is whether you're pulling water from a municipal feed or sourcing from your own well. From there, it usually comes down to piping and permitting. Water permits in particular are often overlooked. The industry is starting to pay more attention to it now, but early on, it was mostly just a race for power - where is the power that's readily available? Now, folks are realizing that a lot of these site selections and projects could actually be killed due to lack of extensive water due diligence. Abby Mellott: How far in advance do you start evaluating infrastructure to determine a project's viability? Joe Navar: Pretty early on. We recommend looking at water hand-in-hand with power. If you find a pipeline out in West Texas, you'd better figure out where the water is coming from also. Without water, you don't have power. Community buy-in is another critical factor. There are a couple areas that have embraced water reuse applications but are still quite hostile to data center build outs, largely because stakeholders weren't engaged early in the process. So yeah, we definitely recommend that as soon as site selection starts you should be looking at water simultaneously. Abby Mellott: Beyond the headline capital investment numbers, what tangible local economic impact do data center projects create? Bryan Kent: For me, the most exciting part is how this boom is shining a light on construction jobs as an attractive career opportunity. These projects give people - whether they're starting out or looking for a career change - a way to provide value for themselves and their families. That's why we've focused on outreach to community colleges, universities, and even high schools, promoting construction as a viable and lucrative trade. There are opportunities on both the administrative side and the skilled craft side, and we're trying to get counselors and students to see the diversity of opportunities for a meaningful career path. At DPR, we run a Builder Development Program for new hires just out of college to prepare them for the technical aspects of these projects. We also have craft apprenticeship programs to help tradespeople learn new skills and advance in their careers. It's exciting to see this kind of growth across the construction industry. Even if the work isn't done in someone's hometown, many of these workers return to their communities, helping to address labor shortages. So the data center and advanced technology boom is giving us a chance to promote construction to people who may not have seen it as an opportunity before. Abby Mellott: Joe, you mentioned something I found interesting - the impact on water quality for local communities. Beyond the data center itself, these projects can actually benefit the areas around them. Can you expand on that? Joe Navar: Yeah, it's actually pretty remarkable. The last time the United States saw this kind of broad infrastructure upgrade was probably 40 or 50 years ago. What we're deploying now is new, disruptive technology. A lot of it is being driven by demand from the data center sector, but it's carrying over into adjacent markets as well. Municipalities are being pushed to adopt more modern infrastructure. We're even talking with school districts about upgrading water systems on a much smaller scale. There's a massive infrastructure build out happening right now, and it's centered on adopting new technology. Abby Mellott: Bryan, do you have anything you'd like to add to that? Bryan Kent: It's important to think about the ongoing employment these data centers create. There's a major influx during construction, and we've talked about the impact on hotels, restaurants, retail and grocery stores in local communities. On one of the recent projects we were involved with, local hotels were operating at 98 percent capacity. But it doesn't stop when construction wraps up. Once the facility is operational, there's continued demand for local services. That can include security, landscaping and ongoing maintenance, along with other support roles needed to keep the site running. The construction is the big ramp-up, but the economic impact continues well beyond that. Each of these facilities requires long-term support, which creates sustained opportunities within the community Abby Mellott: Joe, from an operational standpoint, how should developers be thinking about water security 10 or 20 years down the road? And how do treatment systems and on-site staffing factor into that long-term reliability? Joe Navar: A lot of times during development, the focus is on upfront capital expenditure. But when you're thinking 10 or 20 years out, the bigger consideration becomes operational expenditure. Most of our systems are designed to last more than 30 years, so longevity isn't the issue. The question is what it costs to operate and maintain them over time. How much hands-on attention does the system require? How much downtime are you dealing with? Is it sustainable from both a personnel and a monetary standpoint? Those are the factors that really matter long term. We focus heavily on reducing OpEx for customers, not just in data centers but across all sectors. As construction winds down and staffing levels normalize, operators need systems that don't require large teams to manage ongoing infrastructure. We design with that in mind. That includes condition-based monitoring and incorporating artificial intelligence into monitoring platforms. We're also looking at supply chain intelligence and identifying components that are more prone to failure so we can minimize disruptions. Abby Mellott: This question is for all of you. If AI demand continues on its current trajectory, what structural changes need to happen to sustain that growth? What are some of the key pain points you're seeing right now that will need to be addressed? Bryan, let's start with you. Bryan Kent: DPR has spent years building a suite of services designed to make complex projects run more efficiently. So the cool thing about this data center boom is really putting that into action. These projects are larger and moving faster than what we've seen in the past, which is forcing everyone to innovate and think differently. From a DPR perspective, we have a family of companies that covers everything from structural engineering and electrical to prefabrication and self-perform work, in addition to general construction. Packaging all of that together helps us meet the ambitious schedule and demands of the client. Meanwhile, the prefabrication and manufacturing components don't have to happen on-site. They can take place in more controlled environments elsewhere across the country, which improves safety, quality and scalability. Then we deliver those components to the job site, where they can be installed more efficiently. That approach not only supports the rapid growth we're seeing in Texas, but it also keeps other offices and facilities active across other markets. Joe Navar: It really comes down to priorities. Where do you focus first? As a country, we're already operating near the limits of much of our infrastructure. If you look specifically at water treatment, there are still a lot of antiquated technologies in use. At the same time, new challenges are emerging, and the public is much more aware of what's in their water. Years ago, people didn't think twice about drinking from a plastic bottle that had been sitting in a hot car. Now there's much more scrutiny around water quality and contaminants. The strain on infrastructure was already there before the data center boom accelerated the conversation. What the boom has done is bring urgency. It's pushing more organizations to evaluate and upgrade their systems. Billy Wright: Over the past 20 years in Austin, I've seen skilled trades and production talent dwindle as more people gravitated toward computers, IT and coding. Those are great career paths, but there are also strong opportunities in the trades that many people simply don't know about. For example, a fiber optic splicer can make around $40 an hour. Someone with two to three years of experience might start at $28 an hour and quickly move up. So there's real earning potential, and there's steady demand. With workforce development, we've been fairly reactive as a whole, and we need to become more proactive when it comes to creating awareness. That means working closely with trade schools, being present in high schools and partnering with local manufacturers and industry groups. In the Austin area, organizations like ARMA - the Austin Regional Manufacturing Association - have done a good job promoting manufacturing careers. In smaller markets though, how many locals truly understand what jobs are available or what that career path looks like? Probably not enough. Training and upskilling is another piece. It's not always easy for construction companies to bring on new workers and create training programs, but we have to get creative and develop more accessible pathways into these roles. Abby Mellott: Any final thoughts before we close? Bryan Kent: A lot of what we've talked about today around the advanced technology boom is already influencing other sectors, like life sciences, advanced manufacturing and healthcare. These projects are bigger and moving faster than the construction industry was used to, and the resulting learnings and innovations are catching the attention of other industries. They're watching what's happening in the data center space, and the hope is that those lessons continue to trickle out and transform how we do our work in other areas as well.

article_text: Sheena Collier Founder & CEO - Boston While Black Sheena Collier is a superconnector, convener, and strategic planner. Sixteen years ago, she moved to the Boston area to attend Harvard Graduate School of Education, after attending Spelman College in Atlanta. As a Black woman, she struggled to feel a sense of belonging at school and in the city. She didn't know anyone or have a network, so she built one. Sheena started & joined organizations, became civically engaged, and hosted events that connected her to lots of different worlds, including education, politics, arts, community organizing, & business. She made connections that changed her life and learned techniques to navigate the city. This helped her build a broad network that she now leverages to benefit others. As Founder & CEO of The Collier Connection (TCC), Sheena is designing a portfolio of solutions that disrupt the ways that Black professionals seek information, access, and belonging in cities. TCC also specializes in helping companies to engage employees, customers, & suppliers of color through strategic events and inclusive business practices. She has 15 years of experience in education, economic development, community organizing, & event planning, and uses her ability to navigate different environments to broker partnerships within and across sectors. Sheena consults with a number of companies, most notably as the Senior Economic Opportunity Advisor at the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce. At the Chamber, she supports initiatives to engage the private sector in advancing economic inclusion. She led the creation of the Pacesetters program - a partnership of large and mid-sized companies & anchor institutions that commit to increase their spending with local, ethnic minority-owned businesses. In addition, for the past 3 years Sheena has curated Fierce Urgency of Now (F.U.N.), a City Awake festival designed to highlight the experiences, challenges, and possibilities for young professionals of color in Greater Boston. Sheena is a 2020 recipient of the Harvard Club Boston's Most Influential Women award; 2020 recipient of YW Boston's Academy of Women Achievers Sylvia Ferrell-Jones Award; 2018 recipient of the GK25 - Who is Who Millennial Leaders of Color Awards; 2017 and 2018 nominee of the Ad Club's Rosoff Awards; and a 2016 recipient of the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce's Ten Outstanding Young Leaders Award. She received her BA from Spelman College and her Ed.M. from Harvard Graduate School of Education. Sheena is a proud board member of Jeremiah Program Boston & Union Capital Boston, advisory board member of Boston Harbor Now, investor in the Boston Ujima Fund, and member of the Black Economic Council of Massachusetts (BECMA). Geri Denterlein Founder and CEO - Denterlein Named a recipient of the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce's Pinnacle Award and to the Harvard Club of Boston's "Most Influential Women" list, Geri Denterlein founded the firm that bears her name in 2000. In the years since, Denterlein has grown to become a 25-person, full-service strategic communications and public relations consulting firm that helps businesses, non-profits, and institutions promote and protect their reputations. Leveraging a 30-year career in public affairs and journalism, Geri serves as a close, trusted advisor to CEOs and boards of many of the region's most respected companies and organizations, guiding them through major newsmaking initiatives, leadership transitions, and situations of actual or potential crisis. She has successfully sought to build, in her words, "an agency that is strong in all the areas where New England is strong," including longstanding Denterlein engagements with clients in healthcare, education, professional services, real estate, sustainability, and public affairs. Geri is a devoted mentor and coach to staff at all levels of the agency. Prior to becoming a strategic communications and PR consultant, Geri was editorial director at WBZ Television (Boston's Channel 4), where she presented on-air commentary on major issues of the day and led the station's government outreach. Geri's government experience included serving as an associate press secretary to then-Governor Michael S. Dukakis and as communications director for the Massachusetts Department of Mental Health. In board rooms, the political arena, and the local community, Geri is well known as a champion for women. As an active volunteer leader for several of Boston's nonprofit organizations, including MassINC, the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce, A Better City, and the American Red Cross, Geri advocates for civic and philanthropic engagement and civil discourse. Geri was appointed to the Bridgewater State University Board of Trustees by Governor Charlie Baker and to the board of the Boston Main Streets Foundation by Mayor Martin J. Walsh. Among many other awards and honors, Geri received the Abigail Adams Award from the Massachusetts Women's Political Caucus for her outstanding leadership in achieving parity for women. She was inducted into the Academy of Women Achievers by YW Boston, received the Hall of Fame Award from Boston Women's Business, and won the Workplace Innovations Award from Bentley University. Geri earned her Bachelor of Science degree from the University of Cincinnati and a Master of Public Administration from Harvard's Kennedy School of Government. She also holds a certificate in leadership from the Executive Education Program at the Harvard Kennedy School and serves on the faculty of Harvard's Executive and Continuing Professional Education Program. Jen Faigel Co-founder and Executive Director - Commonwealth Kitchen Jen Faigel is a passionate advocate for community economic development that promotes asset building, wealth creation, and meaningful investment in low-income communities. She is the co-founder and Executive Director of CommonWealth Kitchen, Boston's only nonprofit food business incubator and food manufacturing social enterprise. CommonWealth Kitchen (CWK) provides shared kitchen space and business support to more than 55 entrepreneurs-75% of whom are women, people of color, or immigrants-who collectively employ over 160 local residents. CWK's small-batch contract manufacturing operation offers recipe development, production, and value-added processing for more than 25 wholesalers, restaurants, and farms, and also partners with several local colleges and Boston Public Schools. Jen also brings deep expertise in commercial real estate and community economic development in the City of Boston. She served as the lead real estate consultant for the $15 million Pearl Project, now home to CWK's flagship kitchen facility. Over the course of her career, Jen has helped develop more than 500 affordable homes and over 225,000 square feet of commercial real estate-valued at more than $200 million-leveraging development as a catalyst for job creation and economic opportunity. Her leadership and impact have been widely recognized. In 2015, CommonWealth Kitchen was named "Best Incubator" by Boston Magazine and a "Game-Changer" by The Boston Globe. Jen has been recognized by The Boston Globe as one of nine nonprofit leaders to watch, named one of Boston Magazine's "50 on Fire," and honored as one of eight Regional Food Economies Fellows by The Wallace Center's National Food Systems Leadership Network. She was selected as a 2019 Barr Fellow by the Barr Foundation for her leadership at CWK and across Greater Boston, and most recently was named one of Boston Business Journal's Power 50 leaders in the city. Sandy Lish Principal / Co-Founder - The Castle Group People always ask me if my crisis management work is stressful. Not for me. It's where I thrive - drawing upon my natural resourcefulness, decades managing risk and crises for clients, and passion for developing communication strategies. I help my clients by focusing on connections... how they reach their audiences, how their audiences reach them, how my teams and I can facilitate those interactions. After decades working with companies to build a crisis communications plan or tackle their latest controversy, I've seen it all - national high-profile, high-stakes crises for organizations of all sizes, including corporate, public sector, nonprofit, education and healthcare clients. I've successfully managed sensitive and highly charged crisis communications around data breaches, acts of God, sexual harassment, Title IX discrimination, free speech, leadership misconduct, mergers & acquisitions, workforce reduction, violence & workplace accidents, regulatory action and more. Castle was named a Forbes 2021 Best PR Agency, Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce 2021 Small Business of the Year, PRNEWS' Agency Elite Top 100, and is a five-time Boston Business Journal Best Place to Work. I've been honored with the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce Pinnacle Award for Entrepreneurship, Women's Business Enterprise Hall of Fame Trailblazer Award, Enterprising Women Magazine Enterprising Women of the Year, Women's Enterprise USA Top WBE CEO, Tomorrow's Women TODAY Woman of the Year, WBENC Women's Business Enterprise Star Award, Center for Women and Enterprise Rising Star Award and March of Dimes Franklin Delano Roosevelt Humanitarian Award. I was also named a Boston Business Journal "40 under 40 (although I would no longer be eligible!). I've had the privilege of speaking at regional and national conferences, including Association of Independent Colleges and Universities of Massachusetts, University Risk Management and Insurance Association and the Automotive Public Relations Council. Other speaking engagements include Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce, Boston Business Journal, Association of American Colleges and Universities, National Association of Independent Schools, Commonwealth Institute, Council for Advancement and Support of Education, Center for Women and Enterprise, CBRE Women's Initiative and more. I'm also a contributor to Forbes, an active member of the New England Council and a founding member of the Boston Business Journal Leadership Trust. In 2018, I was appointed by Governor Charlie Baker to the Massachusetts Bay Community College Board of Trustees. For more than 15 years, I have served on the boards of Center for Women and Enterprise and WGBH Corporate Council. I also serve on the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce Board of Directors and Executive Committee, and am on the Executive Committee of the Public Relations Global Network - interacting almost daily with my "sister" (and "brother") agency principals in every major media market to develop world-class relationships for our clients and teams. When I'm not doing all of that? I was a hockey, lacrosse and field hockey mom to my son and daughter for many years and now that they're college-aged, I'm busy sending them "helpful" articles with my two Wheaten Terrier mixes by my side. I look forward to the times my husband and I can travel with them. My favorite place to be is the beach - any beach with a great book and great company. I'm a musical theater geek and am always checking out the latest Broadway hit or returning classic. What else do you want to know? Before Wendy and I founded Castle in 1996, I held in-house marketing positions at KPMG, Lesley University and the Massachusetts Bar Association, and was an executive at IQ & J, a premier Boston agency. I've worked on everything from pita chips to online travel to medical imaging to student lending. I grew up in Brookline, Mass. and am a proud alumna of UMass Amherst. Let me know if you have any questions. Kris May Executive Director - Ravi K. Mehrotra Institute for Business, Markets, and Society Boston University Questrom School of Business Dr. Kris May is the Executive Director of the Mehrotra Institute for Business, Markets, and Society at Boston University's Questrom School of Business. In this role, she builds bridges between research, students, and business leaders to explore how companies can drive both performance and positive social impact. Before joining BU, Kris worked in senior leadership roles in EdTech companies such as Instructure, Pluralsight, and Mantra Health. For almost a decade, Kris directed the Professional MBA and MBA Online programs at the University of Utah, where she oversaw recruiting and admissions, student experience, alumni relations, career coaching, and the Women's MBA Association. Kris has served on multiple nonprofit boards and currently chairs the board of YWCA Vermont. Kris's path to leadership has been anything but linear: she worked her way through college and graduate school to eventually complete an MBA and a PhD in Communication while balancing a full-time career. She teaches graduate students at DePaul University, focusing on courses in positive leadership and in helping adults thrive academically and professionally. At Mentoring Monday, Kris is especially excited to support women who are first-generation professionals, career switchers, or leaders stepping into bigger roles and to talk candidly about confidence, boundaries, and building a career that aligns with both your values and your life. Carla McCall Managing Partner - AAFCPAs Carla is Managing Partner of AAFCPAs, a U.S. Top 100 CPA and consulting firm based in New England. article_text: New York State's energy policy has bottom-line impacts on businesses. Over the past decade, New York has prioritized renewable energy generation to decarbonize the energy sector. At the same time, the State has been less proactive in maintaining gas infrastructure and has decommissioned nuclear and gas-fired power plants. Since 2019, New York has focused on implementing the Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA), which, along with related legislation, has accelerated the State's pursuit of a zero-emissions grid. However, there has been a noticeable shift in the State's energy policy approach recently. This shift can be explained as a response to increasing energy costs and the State's lagging growth in energy supply, which is forecasted to fall short of steeply rising energy demand. The result: New York is now embracing an all-of-the-above energy approach. In its 2025 State Energy Plan, the State expressed three primary goals: affordable, reliable and clean energy. The focus on affordability is due to rising energy costs for consumers, coupled with sudden (and likely long-term) growth in energy demand. Who pays for energy system investments has become a major political issue. To address affordability, the Energy Plan acknowledged that natural gas and petroleum fuels should be supported and may require further investment in pipeline delivery and gas-fired power plants. Further, the Energy Plan highlighted that energy-intensive businesses need low-cost power to stay competitive. The Energy Plan reiterated that maintaining fossil fuel infrastructure will be additive and not in replacement of planned growth of renewable energy. The second goal of reliability is to ensure a sufficient supply of energy to meet demand year-round. New York has forecasted increased demand due to electrification and large loads and a shifting of peak demand to the winter months. This forecast, combined with lagging development of renewables and transmission lines, as well as planned fossil-fuel generation retirements, means new challenges to keep the lights on. Here, the Energy Plan embraced nuclear energy as a tool to achieve a reliable zero-emissions electric grid-a policy change from a decade ago when the State closed Indian Point, seemingly placing nuclear energy in the rearview. In the past year, Governor Hochul has initiated a 5GW nuclear energy capacity target by 2040. The final goal is cleaner energy. While the State will build on existing efforts to promote renewable energy, the Energy Plan made clear that the State's energy transition must be put on a sustainable financial footing and that renewable energy development is lagging behind CLCPA targets. The Energy Plan echoed calls for permitting reforms as well as innovations in State tax policy and other financial strategies to better deploy private capital. The State's focus on these three goals demonstrates a pivot to a more pragmatic and heedful energy policy. The Phillips Lytle team will be monitoring and working with leaders from across the State to ensure New York's energy future is affordable, reliable and clean.

article_text: There are signs that commercial real estate activity is picking up following the long-tail disruption of the pandemic. Projects of all sizes are either restarting or starting a new and are making their way toward reshaping the area's commercial landscape. Buffalo Business First Publisher John Tebeau invited industry experts to discuss the status and future of commercial real estate in the Buffalo region. Joining Tebeau were: NOTABLE PROJECTS The new Trico Building Apartments project hits the city's needs on several fronts, Daly said. It preserved the historic architecture of the former windshield wiper plant while creating a mixed-use facility complex with 242 residential apartments and commercial space in the former brownfield site. Most importantly, it is bringing critical mass that is attractive to restaurants, stores and services, he said. The opportunity can only expand considering that the Trico complex, at 628 Ellicott St., is adjacent to the Buffalo Niagara Medical Campus. "The medical industry is not remote. They are all there. So there is a great opportunity on the medical campus that downtown does not have," Daly said. "Downtown needs to create those districts. They need to get that critical mass." Another project with similar potential is the planned conversion of the Bank of America building at 10 Fountain Plaza into 160 apartments, Daly said. "That is going to be interesting to see how that converts to residential," he said. "But you need big projects or a whole bunch of small ones in the area." Uniland, Hill said, is continuing its search for industrial sites to develop following its successes at the 230-acre Renaissance Commerce Park, the former location of the Bethlehem Steel Plant. The company also is working on converting the office building at 285 Delaware Ave. to accommodate the D'Youville University's College of Osteopathic Medicine. "Adding medical facilities and services to that building is probably going to be one of our largest projects over the next two to three years, and that is going to be transformational," Hill said. Carman applauded the developers for their thoughtful approach to their projects. "People are willing to reinvent their properties," he said. "Would you rather be in desperation mode and just try to fill the building with whatever rent you can get or reinvent yourself and enhance it and have something that you are going to have for a long time? I think that is where a lot of people's mindsets have advanced to." TENANT REQUIREMENTS Building that desired critical mass will be assisted by M&T and other like-minded businesses that are requiring once fully remote employees to return to their usual downtown offices for three or four days a week. Some companies that downsized their offices during the pandemic are expanding their workspaces to accommodate returning employees. During the past two years, the work has become more office-centric, but that does not mean a ricochet to traditional office spaces and functions, however. The traditional office operation is not functional in today's business environment, Hill said. "There have been some significant reductions in office space requirements for companies, because they are not looking to occupy as many square feet for the same number of people because they are not looking to have those people in the office as often," he said. "That becomes a challenge, reconfiguring their spaces, coming up for renewals, renegotiation and extensions, looking at those footprints and those layouts, and reconfiguring space so they can accommodate the number of people they expect within that office at any one point in time." Tenants are also asking for modernization of existing spaces and development with more open areas and buildings that provide for the hoteling format, which relies on shared offices and meeting areas. Hill said a recent client he has worked with has just two dedicated offices while using hoteling to accommodate the rest of the 800 employees. Creating those open spaces is not an inexpensive process. People want the open-ceiling, industrial look of older buildings, but achieving it is not a simple matter of removing dropped ceilings. Those tiles typically have been hiding years-old abandoned cables, wiring and ductwork that is not conducive for use in an office setting. Such conversions are a redevelopment challenge, particularly in the downtown area, Hill said. Uniland also has been converting suburban office space into mixed-use buildings for clients who want to relocate from downtown because staff no longer want the commute or to occupy urban buildings. Hill said businesses that downsized their office space during the pandemic might find that the return-to-work environment requires some expansion. One Uniland client went from about 1.2 headcount per space to 1.9 per space, he said. "Now, they do not need to double their space, but they do need to increase their space, so it becomes a challenge," Hill said. "Tenant improvements have skyrocketed because of the cost of labor and materials in the past three years. The cost has gone up exponentially, and clients do not want to spend their money to build out their space for their needs. They want the landlord to do it on their nickel. That is probably the biggest hurdle." Reconfiguring office space to meet the current demands might be worth the expense, Carman said. "It is unique and it is costly, but if you have an office that is occupied, the expense is probably worth it," he said. COST TRENDS The rent ceiling is a major concern to operators and lenders alike, Carman said. "Everybody is concerned about what is going to happen when the rate resets because there is a ceiling with rents," he said. "If the rate goes up too much, there is going to be a problem. A lot of people are trying to conceive where they can save money." Residential and office projects that had been sidelined are beginning to pencil out as rates improve. Conversion of buildings into multi-family units has been trending, but Carman is hopeful new construction will be on the horizon as well. "In Western New York tax credits are still utilized to make projects work and be viable. People are willing to stay for those five years, which is great," he said. Rising energy costs could offset the best laid money-saving plans, however. Daly said he and others who were proponents of sustainable design are rethinking that mindset with the rising energy costs. He predicts pushback on the state's initiatives as the cost to heat and cool buildings dramatically increases. Everyone has seen rates that were three times what they were last year, though consumption was the same, he said. "A lot of people went to these new energy-efficient heat pumps and that made sense. They could heat and cool space and it is cheaper than doing it with gas. With where the rates have gone now, it is not," Daly said. "The New York Clean Heat program made sense with the rates that we had last year. They do not make sense with the rates this year." He called on Gov. Kathy Hochul to push rates down to last year's levels, because the incentives are not worth it at the current rates. "It is just one more thing to look at when you are doing your pro forma and you are estimating what your operating costs are going to be and where your rents are going to be," Daly said. LABOR ISSUES Every contractor points to the labor shortage as a significant driver of project costs, Daly said. To counter that, Uniland has turned to pre-engineered or pre-constructed systems or materials, which are more expensive but are easier to assemble in the field. "That is really driving a lot of our decisions because contractors really do not have the labor," Daly said. Many say the labor shortage will end when the new football stadium is completed and workers filter back into the market, but Daly does not agree. "That shift would help it, but from what I have heard most of them are behind on other projects, so they are going to jump to those projects," he said. "I do not think you are going to see this big labor pool that is going to help bring any kind of cost down at all or help get things done faster." COLLABORATION Collaboration between developers and stakeholders seems to be improving toward strengthening the commercial real estate landscape, though the panelists believe more can only enhance commercial ventures. "I have always been really happy with the way the city has tried to collaborate and facilitate, getting lane closures and things like that," Daly said. "But the city has to be more creative and become an even bigger partner in facilitating projects," especially given the city's aging infrastructure. For example, he said, "Before you tie into a sewer, you have to scope out that sewer and make sure it is good all the way out to the street. If that sewer tie-in is broken, it is the development project's responsibility to fix that. Maybe that becomes a city infrastructure problem." Hill added that converting an office building into a mixed-use residential development puts extra strain on utilities, a situation that creates an opportunity for utility providers to collaborate with developers, "instead of looking at it as an opportunity to charge additional fees and rates." Working with the city and other partners to find parking locations during construction and for the development, is key, Hill said. "To bring in residentials or to convert a building into a mixed-use development, you need to have parking infrastructure capacity for those residents," he said. "Trying to lease or sell spaces to individuals without parking capacity is very difficult and that degrades the prices and rates you can get, which then impacts the loan that you are going to get for the construction or the permanent financing on that property." Carman agreed. He said parking increasingly has become a linchpin in financing major projects, not just in Buffalo or Western New York. "It is everywhere," he said. "Conversion is happening in all cities and urban areas and if they do not get on the same page and talk and think about the benefits, the economics and sustainability, it could ruin projects. Collaboration has to be there." POLICY CHANGES In addition to greater collaboration, the panelists would like further change in the city's policies that recognize the difficult market conditions in which developers are operating. One is property tax abatement, Daly said. The city begins phasing out the property tax abatement at year eight and ends it at year 12. That timeline might not be favorable for a mixed-use building required to have 15% commercial space. It takes time to find those tenants in a market with much available space downtown, and time without a commercial tenant is lost time in the abatement period, Daly said. He would like the policy to change so that the abatement clock begins when the commercial space is rented. For Hill, the slow permitting and review process is the biggest detractor to getting a project moving forward. It can take from 30 to 180 days to get a project reviewed and permitted depending on the municipality, which adds time to the client's time frame and could put them in jeopardy with their current location. "I would like to see an expedited review process in all municipalities to make it simpler and easier, not to short come any of the safety or design components of the project, but there has to be a better way," Hill said. It is operational policy overall that needs to change, Carman said. "It is not what is specifically on the books as the law. It is really - How do we operate more efficiently? How do you get things done the fastest?" he said. "That is really the issue."

article_text: The data center construction revolution shows no signs of slowing down as the age of artificial intelligence ushers in even greater demand for computing power. The latest projections show that Arizona's current data center capacity is expected to double due to the number of data center projects on the books. The Business Journal spoke to top executives with Clune Construction and Wolverine Builders Commercial Construction to see where the industry is headed next. The Phoenix metro is home to 154 data centers, one of the biggest concentrations in the country. How much more runway exists to increase those numbers? Luke Plzak, Wolverine Builders: While 154 data centers sound like a large number, the market is really measured in watts - those 154 data centers currently represent about 2.7 gigawatts of capacity. We are fortunate to be living in the nation's #2 market for planned development with over 4 gigawatts currently under construction or in planning. With 2026 projects already 90% pre-leased and a vacancy rate of just 3%, the runway is laid out; it is now up to us to execute in a way that maximizes the upside for all of Arizona. Adam Wojack (Clune Construction): Phoenix still has significant runway for growth. The fundamentals that brought the industry there in the first place remain strong: land availability, relatively predictable permitting, strong fiber connectivity and proximity to major West Coast markets without the same seismic risk or coastal constraints. What we're seeing nationally is that demand for digital infrastructure continues to accelerate, largely driven by cloud computing and AI workloads. That demand doesn't show signs of slowing, but the pace of new development will increasingly be dictated by access to power rather than land. Phoenix has been proactive in planning for this growth, but like many major data center markets, future expansion will require thoughtful coordination between utilities, municipalities and developers. Markets that can reliably deliver power and infrastructure will continue to see investment. What has changed in the construction process for data centers, especially with power and cooling requirements? Adam: The biggest change in recent years has been the scale and density of equipment. That has direct implications for both power delivery and cooling strategies. From a construction standpoint, projects require larger electrical infrastructure, more robust power distribution and increasingly sophisticated (and efficient) cooling systems. We're also seeing much tighter integration between mechanical, electrical and structural systems because these facilities are designed to operate at extremely high loads from day one. Speed has probably become the most critical for our clients. Owner/operators want capacity online faster than ever before, which means builders need to plan procurement earlier, coordinate closely with utilities and structure projects in ways that allow certain systems to be installed or commissioned in parallel. The construction process has become more collaborative as a result. Luke: A data center's size is measured in terms of power; modern builds are now as much 'power plant' projects as they are data projects. Whether through solar, battery storage, or natural gas turbines, adapting to the unique code requirements of each medium is essential. The second largest and equally essential part of the data center build out is the cooling process. Obviously, data centers are at the center of the tech world, which means technology advances quickly. In a short time, we have seen the progression from air cooled racks, that required maintaining a very cold ambient temperature in the data center, to closed loop cooling where the heat transfer happens at the chip. Combining the speed of technological change with the need of speed to market means being able to forecast and leverage supply chain resources is essential in being a partner in these projects. What are your companies seeing from overall construction costs related to aluminum and steel for data center construction, and how comfortable are you with the current construction labor pool? Luke: The kickoff to the 2020s has been quite the lesson in supply chain costs and volatility. We have progressed through the Covid era, where supply chains were clogged and prices spiked, followed by another price spike in mid-2025 as a direct result of the 50% tariff on imported steel. While pricing stabilized briefly in late 2025, prices began a "step-up" climb in Q1 2026. We're in a unique cycle where the industry is its own biggest headwind. As the leading sector for non-residential construction, data centers are now driving metal prices rather than reacting to them. In Arizona, we've seen a 50% jump in cost-per-square-foot over two years. I tell my clients: 'waiting for prices to drop' is no longer a viable strategy. AI demand has set a new floor. Regarding labor, 1 in 5 construction workers in Arizona is over 55. We are losing institutional knowledge faster than the pipeline can replace it. We aren't just looking for more workers; we're looking for efficiency. The winners in this market will be those who use better tech and modular workflows to allow one skilled technician to do the work of 1.5 people. Adam: Material costs have stabilized mostly but procurement strategy still matters a lot. What we're seeing across the country is that early coordination with suppliers and long-lead equipment manufacturers has become essential. Successful projects are locking in procurement timelines early and maintaining flexibility where possible. On the labor side, data center construction requires a highly specialized workforce, particularly among electrical and mechanical trades. Phoenix has benefited from a growing pool of experienced workers as more projects have been built in the region, but demand remains high nationwide. Builders who invest in long-term trade partnerships and workforce development are in the best position to keep projects moving efficiently. Many cities in the Valley have shifted their attitudes about data centers and some have changed zoning laws to make sure data centers stay clear of neighborhoods. There is also resistance from some neighborhood groups regarding data centers and some pressure on cities to reduce incentives for data center developments in some cases. How do you think this will play out? Adam: As data centers become more visible, it's natural that communities and policymakers are asking more questions about how these projects fit into their long-term plans. We're seeing that conversation happen in many parts of the country as digital infrastructure becomes a larger part of the built environment. In our experience, the projects that move forward most successfully are the ones that engage with the community early. At Clune, we work with developers, local officials and neighbors before and during construction to explain what's being built, how it operates and what it means for the local economy. That kind of transparency goes a long way in building trust. We're also starting to see more policy frameworks that emerge to address community concerns directly. For example, agreements designed to protect ratepayers and ensure large energy users contribute appropriately to new infrastructure are becoming part of the conversation in several markets. Those kinds of approaches help communities feel confident that growth in digital infrastructure is happening responsibly. Data centers support the infrastructure behind nearly every digital service people rely on today, but communities understandably want to know how projects affect power infrastructure, land use and quality of life. When developers (and their builders) take the time to communicate clearly, listen to concerns and stay engaged throughout the process, these projects can become long-term economic assets while still respecting local priorities. Luke: Pushback to development is nothing new, especially large-scale development. The ecosystem of profit driven development and "NIMBY" concerns has pushed opposing sides to help generate win-wins that make our communities stronger. I've recently heard a new term for the most ardent opposition: BANANAs (Build Absolutely Nothing Anywhere Near Anyone). I believe there are two paths forward to mediate the need to grow the data center market in Arizona and ease the fears of Arizonans. First, data travels at the speed of light-building in remote areas is viable by extending the power and fiber infrastructure. Second, for sites that require proximity to population centers, we must engage the community early to fill knowledge gaps and show how these projects provide a personal, positive impact. A few quick examples would include better power infrastructure paid for by these projects, which results in attracting businesses that provide jobs and services. Data centers don't employ many people, wouldn't a better economic development case be to use this space for rooftops, manufacturing, and/or consumer services? Luke: We often hear about the concern related to job counts, while our focus should be about the tax-to-service ratio. A data center doesn't put 500 cars on the road at rush hour, doesn't add 200 children to an overcrowded school district, and doesn't require massive police or fire presence. Yet a single large campus can generate $10M-$40M in taxes annually. That is pure revenue for Arizona schools and first responders with almost zero strain on local services. When we talk about data centers, we aren't just talking about 'Big Tech', we're talking about the infrastructure that makes 2026 possible. Every telehealth appointment in rural AZ, every AI tool used by our local schools, and every digital transaction made by a small business in Mesa depends on this physical backbone. Arizona has become a global leader because we have the land, talent, and stability that few other states can match. We're seeing a massive shift toward 'behind-the-meter' power- solar/battery and even on-site generation. Are we moving toward a future where a 'successful' data center project in Arizona is defined less by its grid connectivity and more by its ability to operate as a self-contained microgrid? Luke: We haven't seen an exponential jump in power demand like is currently occurring in a lifetime and it is prudent for Arizonan's to not want to carry the personal burden of funding the power upgrades associated with the explosion in demand. In February of this year the Arizona House passed HB2756, this bill is the state's direct response to public anger over rising utility bills. It fundamentally changes the "contract" between data centers and the grid. The bill requires the Arizona Corporation Commission to ensure that the costs of new grid infrastructure (substations, transmission lines) are paid for entirely by the data centers themselves, rather than being "socialized" across the bills of residential customers. This is leading to projects evaluating the speed, cost and responsibility of that upgrade, and many are exploring the best solution for on-site power generation. As this shift is happening it is important as contractors that our expertise extends to building power plants as wells as building the data halls themselves. Public perception is now connecting data centers to the Urban Heat Island effect-whether that's scientifically nuanced or not. How should this industry change its approach to site selection and architectural design to prove we aren't just 'heating up' our local neighborhoods? Luke: A word that is constantly surrounding data centers is speed - we've seen this industry move forward at an exceptional pace. When things move quickly it is normal that questions can arise quicker than answers and solutions. The concerns that arise help drive innovation to ensure we steward our state correctly. Preliminary 2026 research suggests that a large data center campus can warm the immediate surrounding neighborhood by several degrees during the summer months. We have to be honest: if you put a 500,000-square-foot concrete box in the desert, it's going to hold heat. However, the 2026 approach is about thermal resilience. By using high-albedo materials that reflect solar radiation and moving toward liquid-cooling systems that capture heat more efficiently, we are creating facilities that have a smaller thermal footprint than the massive asphalt parking lots of the shopping centers around the valley. Our goal as contractors and developers in this space, is to ensure the neighborhood doesn't feel the building's presence after the sun goes down. Arizona has a record number of construction jobs, yet we still face a 20,000-worker deficit for megaprojects. How are we using technology, such as AI-driven estimating and modular 'off-site' pre-fabrication, to maintain project timelines without overstretching the local trade pool? Adam: Innovation is a core value at Clune, and we're constantly looking for ways to make our teams more efficient without compromising quality. We're leveraging AI-assisted tools where it makes sense, especially on highly repetitive scopes where we can drive speed and consistency. That said, no technology replaces experienced people. To support Phoenix's rapid growth, we're sourcing from local talent, Clune offices nationwide, and are also offering relocation to those looking for new opportunities and bringing in experienced travelers who are on-site during the week and home on weekends. That national flexibility allows us to deliver for our clients without putting unsustainable pressure on the local workforce. Luke: As mentioned before, 1 in 5 Arizonans in construction are over the age of 55. Arizona is on track to nearly triple our total data capacity by 2031. These two data points indicate a need to increase efficiency in the short term and training in the long term. We are currently working with groups that are focusing on modular buildings for their projects. In-house we are leveraging the very tools these data centers help provide, to increase our supply chain management and operational capacity to more accurately manage schedules and timing to limit the hidden inefficiencies in projects. How is your company engaging with communities as data center development grows more visible and sometimes more controversial? Luke: Conflicting information about data centers and what to do about them are being discussed from the local coffee shop to the halls of congress. As a contractor, our reach to the community isn't large but by partnering with local city economic development teams and chambers of commerce we can amplify the message that data centers aren't just windowless boxes. In reality, these data centers are the most important pieces of physical infrastructure Arizona will build this decade. They are the backbone of our schools, our healthcare, and our economy. Our challenge as developers and contractors isn't just to build them fast, it's to build them right. That means moving toward water-neutral systems and behind-the-meter energy solutions that don't just take from the grid but help modernize it. Our company goal is to ensure that when we look back at this 'boom' in ten years, we see an Arizona that is more resilient, more tech-forward, and where growth didn't just happen to our communities, but for them. Adam: In many markets, we're working directly with municipalities to build long-term, trust-based relationships. That means showing up early, being transparent, and staying engaged after construction is complete. We've participated in town halls to help educate the public on what a data center actually brings to their area, from jobs to infrastructure investment. We've also partnered on local job fairs, supported trade education programs, and even contributed to community efforts like road adoption and beautification. At the end of the day, we're not just building for our clients but we're building in someone's backyard. We take that seriously and strive to be the kind of partner cities want to work with again. How is your company attracting the next generation of talent? Adam: We're focused on creating careers, not just jobs. That starts with how we treat people: Clune is 100% employee-owned, and we pay 100% of medical premiums for employees and their families. That's rare in this industry and it reflects our belief that when people feel secure and valued, they build better, longer-lasting careers. We're especially focused on growing our talent pipeline in construction project management and field roles. We see a huge opportunity to bring people with mechanical, electrical and plumbing experience into MEP Coordinator roles, and we're investing in that transition with training and mentorship. At the end of the day, we want people to feel proud of the work they're doing and see a future here. That's how we build for the long haul.

article_text: Pittsburgh's shift from industrial powerhouse to a technology-driven economy began in the late 20th century. What followed was not a departure from infrastructure, but a redefinition of it. Today, the region depends as much on data systems as it once did on steel production. Companies like Evolution E-Cycling are operating within that shift, and data centers are at the core. Based in the Pittsburgh region, Evolution E-Cycling works on the downstream side of digital systems, providing an answer to the question, "What happens to technology, equipment, and data once it is no longer needed?" It's an issue that is becoming more urgent as digital infrastructure expands and electronic waste grows alongside it. E-Waste: A growing local consideration Globally, e-waste is among the fastest-growing categories of solid waste. In 2022, an estimated 62 million tons were generated, yet only 22.3% was formally collected and recycled. The remainder often enters informal or unregulated systems, where improper handling can release hazardous materials and pose serious health risks. While those figures are global, their implications are local. Western Pennsylvania's growth in healthcare, robotics, higher education, and advanced manufacturing has driven increased reliance on IT infrastructure. Systems are routinely upgraded or replaced, creating a steady volume of retired equipment, from laptops and mobile devices to servers and networking hardware. Understanding data centers and their lifecycle Data centers add another layer of complexity. Their lifecycle doesn't end at deployment; it includes ongoing cycles of upgrade and decommissioning. Servers, storage systems, and networking equipment are routinely replaced to meet performance and security demands, creating a steady stream of high-value, data-sensitive equipment that must be handled carefully at end of life. The rise of AI infrastructure is accelerating this cycle. AI servers, particularly those built around high-performance GPUs, are more expensive, more energy-intensive, and more specialized than traditional server hardware. As organizations scale AI capabilities, they are upgrading systems more frequently to keep pace with performance demands, shortening hardware lifecycles and increasing the volume of high-value equipment entering the IT asset disposition (ITAD) stream. These systems also introduce new complexities. GPU-based servers often retain significant residual value, but require more precise evaluation, handling, and resale pathways than standard equipment. At the same time, the intensity of AI workloads can place greater strain on components, affecting reuse potential and increasing the importance of responsible downstream processing. For ITAD providers, this shift is not just about volume; it's about adapting to a more technically demanding and higher-stakes category of infrastructure. This is not simply a disposal issue. It is a lifecycle management issue, with implications for data security, environmental compliance, and cost recovery. Where Evolution E-Cycling fits This is where specialized lifecycle management becomes critical. Evolution E-Cycling's services, including asset buyback and repurposing, secure data destruction, and responsible recycling, address the transition point between active infrastructure and retired equipment. Their client base mirrors the structure of the regional economy: healthcare, education, manufacturing, government, finance, and logistics. Across these sectors, the challenge is consistent. Equipment can't simply be discarded or written off. It must be tracked, processed, and accounted for. Evolution E-Cycling approaches this as a structured process rather than a one-time service. Standards such as R2v3 and RIOS certification, along with permitting through the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection, establish requirements for traceability, responsible downstream handling, and secure data destruction. As regulatory scrutiny and data security expectations increase, these processes are a necessary part of infrastructure management. Infrastructure, reconsidered

article_text: CLYDE, Ohio - For months, State Rep. Gary Click (R-Vickery) told anyone who would listen that he wasn't worried about his Republican primary challenger. Now he's asking donors for help because "this is a tough primary." Click's campaign sent a fundraising email this week promoting his campaign kickoff event Saturday at the Historic Octagon House in Clyde - and the tone was a sharp departure from the confident dismissals that have defined his public response to Eric Watson's insurgent challenge. "This is a tough primary, and your contributions will make the difference in keeping a commonsense conservative in this House seat!" Click wrote in the email to supporters. That language is difficult to square with the posture Click has struck since Watson entered the race. When former U.S. Senate candidate Mark Pukita commented on Facebook that Click "really has his panties in a wad" over the primary challenge, Click replied: "You're funny, Markie. Not concerned at all." When the Fremont News-Messenger asked him about Watson's campaign, Click responded: "You move to the right of Gary Click and you're in the ditch." And when Watson and others called for a public debate, Click dismissed the idea entirely: "It's always the guy losing that wants the debate. They are trying to grift off of the leader's name ID." Now, with the May primary approaching, Click is telling donors the race is tough - and he's lining up heavy reinforcements to prove it. Moreno out, Statehouse leadership in Saturday's kickoff will feature Ohio House Speaker Jason Huffman, State Treasurer Robert Sprague, and Majority Whip Nick Santucci, along with representatives from Turning Point Action. It's a show of force from the Statehouse Republican establishment - but it's also a downgrade. U.S. Sen. Bernie Moreno was originally expected to headline the event before being quietly dropped. Whether Moreno's withdrawal was his decision or Click's, the shift from a sitting U.S. Senator to state-level officials tells its own story about the dynamics of this race. Click's campaign did not respond to a request for comment. While Republicans fight over ideology, Jones focuses on kitchen-table issues As Click and Watson battle over who is the more authentically conservative candidate - trading attacks over digital IDs, gun ratings, and abortion politics - the Democratic candidate in the race has staked out notably different ground. Aaron Jones, a U.S. Army veteran, manufacturing supervisor, and Tiffin City Councilman, has built his campaign around the economic issues that most directly affect working families in the 88th District: jobs, economic development, cost of living, property tax relief, and fair and equal funding for public schools. The contrast is sharp. While the Republican primary has centered on culture war credentials and intra-party loyalty tests, Jones has focused on the issues voters in Seneca and Sandusky counties confront daily - stagnant wages, rising costs, and a manufacturing sector under pressure from plant closures like the potential TMD/First Brands shutdown that could eliminate 407 jobs in Tiffin. The winner of the May Republican primary will face Jones in November.
